1.q: Which file formats can I convert to PDF?
1.a: Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files (including the older DOC, XLS, and PPT formats), OpenDocument text, spreadsheets, presentations, and drawings, RTF, plain text, Markdown, CSV, XML, ebooks in EPUB, MOBI, FB2, and CBZ, XPS, Publisher, Visio, WordPerfect, Microsoft Works, Apple Pages, and images in JPG, PNG, HEIC, WebP, TIFF, BMP, SVG, and PSD. If you have a folder of mixed image types, [0]Images to PDF[/0] accepts them all in one batch and puts each image on its own page.

2.q: What can I convert a PDF into?
2.a: Word (DOCX), Excel (XLSX), CSV, plain text, Markdown, SVG, and page images in JPG, PNG, WebP, TIFF, or BMP, with multi-page PDFs delivered as a ZIP holding one image per page. For long-term archiving, [0]PDF to PDF/A[/0] outputs PDF/A-1b, 2b, or 3b, and a separate tool turns a color PDF into a grayscale one.

3.q: Does PDF to Word keep the layout?
3.a: [0]PDF to Word[/0] rebuilds the document with its text, basic formatting, and general layout, and it can convert a batch of files in one run. Pages with multiple columns, embedded forms, or heavy graphics may not come across perfectly, so expect to tidy those up in your word processor.

4.q: Why is my converted Word or text file empty?
4.a: The PDF is almost certainly a scan, which stores each page as a picture with no text layer, so PDF to Word, PDF to Text, and the table converters have nothing to pull out. Run the file through [0]OCR PDF[/0] first to add a searchable text layer, then convert the result.

5.q: Can I get tables out of a PDF into Excel?
5.a: [0]PDF to Excel[/0] scans every page for tables and writes each one to its own worksheet, named after the page it came from. If it reports that no tables were found, the PDF lays the data out as loose text rather than a real table structure; PDF to CSV and Extract Tables rely on the same detection, so try PDF to Text to grab the raw content instead.

6.q: Do I need Microsoft Office installed to convert Word, Excel, or PowerPoint files?
6.a: No. Those files, along with Publisher, Visio, RTF, and WordPerfect, are converted by a LibreOffice engine that runs inside your browser, so there's nothing to install; [0]Word to PDF[/0], for example, also takes DOC, ODT, and RTF directly. The engine downloads once per session, which makes the first conversion take a few seconds longer than the ones after it.

7.q: Will converting a PDF to JPG or PNG lose quality?
7.a: Pages are rendered at twice their native size, so a letter-size page becomes an image of roughly 1,224 by 1,584 pixels. [0]PDF to JPG[/0] is lossy with a quality slider that defaults to 90%, which keeps a good balance between sharpness and file size; PDF to PNG and PDF to TIFF are lossless, and PNG adds a scale control from 1x to 3x for print-quality output.

8.q: Are my files uploaded to a server during conversion?
8.a: No. Every converter on this page, including the Office, ebook, and image converters, runs as WebAssembly inside your browser tab, so the file is read from your device and the result is written straight back to it. There's no upload queue, no server copy, and nothing to delete afterward.

1.q: Can I change the existing text in a PDF?
1.a: [0]Edit PDF Text[/0] lets you click any paragraph and rewrite it in place, with the surrounding text reflowing as you type and controls for fonts and styling. For adding new text boxes, comments, highlights, shapes, or images on top of the page, use the general Edit PDF tool instead.

2.q: What can I do in the Edit PDF tool?
2.a: The [0]Edit PDF[/0] toolbar covers highlighting, underlining, strikethrough, freehand drawing, text and comments, shapes and images, permanent redaction, and full-text search. It keeps the original PDF structure, so fonts, layouts, and form fields stay intact, and you can keep up to 10 documents open in tabs and switch between them.

3.q: How do I make a PDF smaller?
3.a: [0]Compress PDF[/0] strips unused structure, downsamples images, and subsets fonts while keeping text selectable and links working. Start with the Medium level, or enter a target file size, and only step up to High if the file is still too large.

4.q: Which editing tools keep my text selectable?
4.a: Page-level tools such as Rotate, Organize, Delete Pages, Background Color, and Remove Annotations work on the PDF structure and leave text searchable. Invert Colors, Change Text Color, and PDF to Greyscale re-render every page as an image, so text in their output can no longer be selected or searched. If you need searchable text after one of those, run the result through [0]OCR PDF[/0].

5.q: Can I add page numbers or a header and footer?
5.a: [0]Page Numbers[/0] puts a number in any of six positions on every page, in plain or "page X of Y" style, with your choice of font size and color. Header and Footer adds text to six slots per page (left, center, and right at top and bottom), understands {page} and {total} placeholders so a footer like "Page {page} of {total}" fills in correctly on each page, and can be limited to a page range.

6.q: Can I put a watermark on every page?
6.a: [0]Add Watermark[/0] stamps text or an image onto your pages, and you position it by dragging on a live preview, then set opacity, rotation, and size. A tiled mode repeats the mark across the whole page so it's much harder to crop out, and you can apply one watermark to all pages, restrict it to a page range, or set a different watermark on each page.

7.q: Can I rotate a single page, or fix a slightly tilted scan?
7.a: [0]Rotate PDF[/0] shows a thumbnail of every page with its own left and right buttons for 90-degree turns, plus a bulk control for the whole document. For a scan that's off by a few degrees, Rotate by Custom Degrees accepts any angle, per page or for all pages at once.

8.q: Does editing a PDF here upload it anywhere?
8.a: No. The editor and every other tool on this page run as WebAssembly inside your browser, so the file is opened, changed, and saved on your own device without a server in between. Nothing is stored, so there's no copy to delete when you're done.

1.q: How do I combine several PDFs into one file?
1.a: Add two or more files to [0]Merge PDF[/0] and drag them into the order you want. File Mode joins whole documents, with an optional page range per file such as 1-3, 5, while Page Mode lays out every page as a thumbnail so you can build the exact sequence. There's no cap on file count or total pages, and pages are copied without re-encoding, so quality doesn't change.

2.q: What are the different ways to split a PDF?
2.a: [0]Split PDF[/0] has six modes: page ranges, visual selection from thumbnails, even or odd pages only, one file per page, splitting at bookmark boundaries with a choice of bookmark level, and fixed chunks of every N pages. A single range downloads as one PDF, while multiple ranges or per-page output arrive as a ZIP. Bookmark mode needs a PDF that actually contains bookmarks.

3.q: What's the difference between Split, Extract Pages, and Delete Pages?
3.a: [0]Extract Pages[/0] keeps only the pages you list and saves them as a new file, Delete Pages removes the pages you list and keeps everything else, and Split breaks one document into several files. Extract and Delete are inverses of each other, so pick whichever needs the shorter list of page numbers.

4.q: Can I reorder pages or duplicate a page?
4.a: [0]Organize PDF[/0] shows every page as a draggable thumbnail with a duplicate and a delete button on each one. You can also type a complete page order such as 3, 1, 2, 4 to rearrange everything in one step, and Reverse Pages flips an entire document, or a batch of them, in one click.

5.q: My scanner put all the front pages first and all the backs after. How do I fix the order?
5.a: [0]Duplex Collate[/0] handles exactly that: it interleaves the two blocks into front 1, back 1, front 2, back 2 order, with an option to reverse the back block for stacks that were flipped before the second pass. If the fronts and backs are in two separate files, Alternate Merge interleaves pages from multiple PDFs the same way.

6.q: How do I print a PDF as a folded booklet?
6.a: [0]PDF Booklet[/0] reorders the pages into saddle-stitch imposition and shows a preview of each sheet before you download. Print the result double-sided with "flip on short edge", fold the stack in half, and staple at the spine; if the page count isn't a multiple of four, blank pages are added automatically to fill the last sheet.

7.q: Can I see what changed between two versions of a PDF?
7.a: [0]Compare PDFs[/0] pairs up the pages of two documents and highlights differences in text, images, annotations, headers and footers, and formatting, in either a side-by-side or an overlay view. Filters let you hide the change types you don't care about, OCR can be switched on for scanned documents, and the comparison can be exported as a PDF report.

8.q: Are my files uploaded when I merge or split them?
8.a: No. Merging, splitting, and reordering run as WebAssembly inside your browser, so the files are read from your disk and the result is written back to it without passing through a server. That holds for large scans and multi-file batches too.

1.q: What's the difference between protecting a PDF with a password and restricting its permissions?
1.a: A user password, set with [0]Protect PDF[/0], is required to open the file at all. Permissions are flags stored inside the encryption that control what a reader can do after opening, such as printing, copying, editing, annotating, or filling forms, and they only take effect when an owner password is set. Change Permissions lets you allow or deny each action individually, while Protect PDF applies the strictest set as soon as you add an owner password.

2.q: How strong is the password protection?
2.a: Protect PDF and Change Permissions use 256-bit AES encryption, the PDF 2.0 standard, applied by QPDF running in your browser. The encryption itself isn't practical to brute-force, so the weak point is the password: use a long passphrase and send it through a different channel than the file. Permission flags are a separate matter, since they rely on the reader honoring them and some third-party tools ignore them.

3.q: Can I remove a password from a PDF if I don't know it?
3.a: No. [0]Unlock PDF[/0] needs the password and then saves a copy with no encryption or restrictions left, and none of the tools crack or brute-force passwords. For a file that opens fine but blocks printing or copying, use Remove Restrictions instead, which asks for the owner password if the file has one.

4.q: What's the difference between Sign PDF and a digital signature?
4.a: Sign PDF places a drawn, typed, or uploaded signature image on the page, with an option to flatten it so nobody can move or delete it later. [0]Digital Signature[/0] applies a cryptographic signature with your own X.509 certificate (.pfx, .p12, or .pem), which proves who signed and that the file hasn't changed since, and Validate Signature checks signatures already in a file. Certificate signing may need an internet connection to fetch the certificate chain, and self-signed certificates will show warnings in Adobe Reader.

5.q: How do I redact text so it's actually gone?
5.a: Use the redaction tool in the [0]PDF Editor[/0]. Marking text or an area only flags it. Once you apply the redaction, the marked content is permanently removed from the page instead of just being covered with a box, and if you download with marks that haven't been applied yet, the editor offers to apply them first. When you redact selected text, copies of it in the file's properties, bookmarks, comments, and attachments are removed on download too, unless the file is encrypted. Area redactions have no text to search for, so if the file's properties, comments, or attachments could reveal the same information, run Remove Metadata or Sanitize PDF on the result as well.

6.q: What's the difference between Remove Metadata and Sanitize PDF?
6.a: [0]Remove Metadata[/0] strips only the document properties: title, author, dates, producer, XMP data, document IDs, and application-specific data, and it leaves pages, forms, links, and bookmarks untouched. Sanitize PDF goes further and can also flatten forms and delete annotations, embedded JavaScript, attachments, layers, links, and structure tags, with each item selectable. Both are irreversible, so keep your original file.

7.q: What does flattening a PDF do, and when should I use it?
7.a: [0]Flatten PDF[/0] burns form fields and annotations (comments, highlights, stamps, sticky notes, signature fields) into the page content, so they look the same but can no longer be edited, moved, or removed. Use it after a form is filled in or a signature is placed and before you send the file, because there's no way to unflatten. Text stays selectable and searchable, and bookmarks are kept.

8.q: Are my passwords, certificates, or files sent to a server?
8.a: No. Encrypting, unlocking, sanitizing, and signing all run as WebAssembly in your browser, so the document, the password you type, and your certificate's private key stay on your device. The one network exception is Digital Signature, which may contact your certificate authority's servers to fetch the certificate chain; the document itself is still never sent.

1.q: What kinds of files can I embed in a PDF?
1.a: Any file type: spreadsheets, images, ZIP archives, CAD drawings, even executables. The tool doesn't inspect or convert the file; it stores the bytes inside the PDF under the original file name, and you can embed several files in one pass.

2.q: What's the difference between document-level and page-level attachments?
2.a: Document-level attachments belong to the PDF as a whole and appear in the reader's attachments panel. Page-level attachments are tied to the pages you list in the page range field (for example 1,3,5-7), and the same file is attached to every page in that range. Document level is the safer choice, since some viewers never show page-level attachments.

3.q: Where do the attached files show up when someone opens the PDF?
3.a: In readers that have an attachments panel, such as Adobe Acrobat Reader or Firefox's built-in viewer, they're listed by file name and can be opened or saved from there. Viewers without that panel won't show them at all, although the files are still inside the PDF.

4.q: Does embedding files make the PDF bigger?
4.a: Yes, by roughly the size of each attachment, since the file's bytes are stored inside the PDF. A 40 MB spreadsheet attached to a 1 MB report yields a PDF of about 41 MB, so keep attachment size in mind before emailing the result.

5.q: Is the file I attach uploaded anywhere when I embed it?
5.a: No. The PDF and the attachments are read and combined in your browser by the CoherentPDF WebAssembly module, and the result is downloaded straight from the page. Nothing is sent to a server.

6.q: Why does the tool say an advanced processing module is required?
6.a: Embedding uses the CoherentPDF (cpdf) module, which loads on demand from a CDN the first time you use it rather than shipping with the main site. If you self-host BentoPDF or work in an air-gapped setup, you can point the tool at your own copy of the module on the [0]Advanced Features settings[/0] page.

7.q: Can I remove an attachment later?
7.a: Yes. [0]Edit Attachments[/0] lists every embedded file and lets you remove individual ones or all of them, and Extract Attachments saves them back out as separate downloads.

8.q: Will attaching files break a digital signature on the PDF?
8.a: Yes. Adding attachments rewrites the file, which invalidates any existing digital signature. Attach the files first, then sign the finished PDF with [0]Digital Sign PDF[/0].

1.q: Where will the blank page be inserted?
1.a: The position number is how many existing pages come before the new blank pages. Enter 0 to put them at the very start, 3 to insert them after page 3, or the total page count to append them at the end.

2.q: What size are the blank pages?
2.a: Each blank page copies the width and height of your document's first page, so a Letter document gets Letter blanks and an A4 document gets A4 blanks. If your PDF mixes page sizes, the blanks still match page 1 rather than the pages next to them.

3.q: Can I add more than one blank page at a time?
3.a: Enter any count of 1 or more and all of them are inserted together at the same position. To add blanks at several different spots, run the tool again on the output, or use [0]PDF Multi Tool[/0] to arrange pages visually.

4.q: Does it keep bookmarks and document properties?
4.a: Page content, images, text, and annotations on the pages are kept as they are. The document is rebuilt page by page, so bookmarks (the outline panel) and properties such as title and author aren't carried over to the new file.

5.q: Is the inserted page completely empty?
5.a: Yes. It has no text, no page number, and no printed note, just a white page of the same size as page 1. If you want page numbers on it afterward, run the result through [0]Page Numbers[/0].

6.q: Can I use this to make every chapter start on a right-hand page for double-sided printing?
6.a: You can, one position per run. Insert a blank after each chapter that ends on an odd page, download, then repeat on the new file for the next chapter. The output keeps the original filename, so rename copies as you go to avoid mixing them up.

7.q: Can I add blank pages to a password-protected PDF?
7.a: If the file needs a password to open, the tool asks for it before reading the page count. The new file is saved without the password, so protect it again afterward if you need to.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded to add the page?
8.a: No. The page count is read and the new document is assembled in your browser with pdf-lib, a JavaScript PDF library, and the download comes straight from memory. Nothing is sent to a server.

1.q: How do I label appendix pages A-1, A-2, A-3?
1.a: Add a rule for the appendix page range, keep Decimal Arabic as the style, and type A- in the Label Prefix field. With the default start value of 1 the pages become A-1, A-2, A-3, and a second rule with the prefix B- handles the next appendix.

2.q: Can page numbering start at 0 or at a number other than 1?
2.a: Each rule has a Start Value field that defaults to 1. Set it to 0 for zero-based numbering, or to any other number, for example 15 so a chapter extracted from a longer book keeps its original page numbers.

3.q: What does 'Continue numbering across disjoint ranges' do?
3.a: Turn it on when one rule covers pages that aren't contiguous, such as 1-9,30-40 or odd, and you want the labels to keep counting in sequence across the gap. With it off, each separate block of pages starts again from the start value.

4.q: What happens to the page labels the PDF already has?
4.a: The 'Remove existing page labels' box is checked by default, so the old labels are cleared before your rules are applied. Uncheck it if you only want to relabel some pages and keep the existing labels on the rest.

5.q: Which page range formats can I type?
5.a: Leave the field empty to cover every page, or use forms like 1-4, 7, odd, or 1-9,30-40. Page numbers refer to physical positions in the file, not to labels the PDF may already display.

6.q: Can I add labels to a password-protected PDF?
6.a: Not directly. The tool stops with a Protected PDF message, so remove the password first with [0]Unlock PDF[/0] and then upload the copy that no longer needs one.

7.q: Why does the tool ask me to configure CoherentPDF?
7.a: Page labels are written by the CoherentPDF engine, which normally loads from a CDN the first time you use the tool. If that default has been turned off in a self-hosted build, you'll be prompted to point [0]WASM Settings[/0] at a copy of the library.

8.q: How do I check that the labels were applied?
8.a: Open the downloaded PDF in a reader that displays page labels, such as Adobe Acrobat or Firefox's built-in viewer, and look at the page number box in the toolbar. It shows the label, for example iv or A-1, instead of the plain page index.

1.q: What kind of stamps can I add with this tool?
1.a: This tool places image stamps, so you pick an image file such as a PNG or JPG (a company seal, an APPROVED graphic, a scanned notary stamp) and drop it onto the page. For text-only marks like a diagonal DRAFT label, [0]Add Watermark[/0] is the better fit.

2.q: What does the Stamp Username field do?
2.a: The name you enter is recorded on each stamp you create as its author, so reviewers can see who placed it. Set it before you upload the PDF. It's optional, and leaving it blank creates stamps without a name attached.

3.q: Can I put the same stamp on every page at once?
3.a: No. Stamps are placed one at a time on the page you're viewing, and you can move and resize each one before saving. If you need an identical mark on all pages, use the image mode in [0]Add Watermark[/0], which can apply one image to every page in a single step.

4.q: Are the stamps permanent, or can they be removed later?
4.a: Stamps are saved as PDF stamp annotations, so a PDF editor can still select, move, or delete them. If you want them merged into the page content so they can't be lifted off, run the saved file through [0]Flatten PDF[/0].

5.q: How do I move or resize a stamp after placing it?
5.a: Click the stamp in the viewer to select it, then drag it to a new position or pull its corner handles to change the size. Nothing is final until you click Save Stamped PDF, so you can adjust as much as you like first.

6.q: What's the difference between this and Sign PDF?
6.a: [0]Sign PDF[/0] is built for signatures: you draw one, type one, or upload one and place it on the page. Add Stamps is for reusable image marks such as seals, RECEIVED stamps, or QC stamps, with your name recorded as the author of each one.

7.q: Does the stamp tool work on password-protected PDFs?
7.a: If the file needs a password to open, the tool asks for it before loading the viewer. You need the open password; the tool doesn't bypass encryption.

8.q: Is my document uploaded when I stamp it?
8.a: No. The viewer, the stamp editor, and the export all run in your browser, and the stamped PDF is written on your device. Nothing is sent to a server, which matters when you're stamping contracts, inspection reports, or notarized documents.

1.q: Can I watermark only certain pages of a PDF?
1.a: Yes. Type a range such as 1-3, 5, 7-9 in the Page Range field, or leave it set to "all". If you want different text or a different position on individual pages, uncheck "Apply to all pages" and use the page arrows above the preview to set each page separately.

2.q: How do I add a diagonal CONFIDENTIAL or DRAFT watermark across the page?
2.a: Stay in Text mode, type the word, and raise the font size (10 to 200 points, default 72) until it spans the page. The angle slider already defaults to -45 degrees for the classic diagonal look, so usually you only need to enlarge the text and drag it to the center of the preview.

3.q: Can I use a logo image as the watermark?
3.a: Switch to Image mode and upload a PNG or JPG; other image formats aren't accepted. A PNG with a transparent background blends best with the page. You can scale it from 10% to 200%, set its opacity and angle, and drag it into position on the preview.

4.q: What does the Tiled layout do?
4.a: Tiled repeats the watermark across the whole page in a diagonal grid that follows the rotation angle, so the mark runs edge to edge. The horizontal and vertical gap sliders control the spacing between tiles as a percentage of the watermark size. Lower the opacity when tiling so the document underneath stays readable.

5.q: Can someone remove the watermark afterward?
5.a: The watermark is drawn into the page content rather than added as a separate annotation, so it can't be deleted with one click in a PDF viewer. It isn't tamper-proof though. For a harder-to-strip result, use Tiled mode, or check "Flatten watermark" to bake every page into pixels, which also makes the document's text unselectable.

6.q: Does adding a watermark change the original text or image quality?
6.a: No. The pages keep their original text, images, and dimensions, and the watermark is placed on top, so text stays selectable and searchable. The exception is the "Flatten watermark" option, which re-renders every page as an image at 2.5x scale and removes selectable text.

7.q: What opacity should I use for a watermark?
7.a: The slider runs from 0.05 to 1 and defaults to 0.3. Values between 0.2 and 0.4 keep the mark visible without hiding the content beneath it; go higher only for small marks placed in a margin or corner.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded when I add a watermark?
8.a: No. The live preview, the drag-and-drop editor, and the final rendering all run inside your browser with pdf-lib, so neither the PDF nor a logo image you add leaves your device.

1.q: How do I brighten a dark scanned PDF?
1.a: Move the Brightness slider (range -100 to +100) up to lighten the page, and raise Contrast if the text still looks washed out. When only the midtones are too dark, the Gamma slider (0.2 to 5.0) lifts them without blowing out the white background. The preview updates as you drag, so you can check the first page before applying the settings to all of them.

2.q: Can I convert a color PDF to grayscale with this tool?
2.a: Drag the Saturation slider all the way to -100 and every page becomes grayscale, which also cuts ink use when printing. If you don't need any of the other adjustments, the [0]grayscale conversion tool[/0] does the same thing in one step.

3.q: What do the hue, temperature, and tint sliders do?
3.a: Hue Shift rotates every color around the color wheel by 0 to 360 degrees while leaving whites, grays, and blacks untouched. Temperature (-50 to +50) shifts the page toward blue on the cool end or yellow-orange on the warm end, and Tint (-50 to +50) shifts between green and magenta, which is useful for photos scanned with a color cast.

4.q: Will the text still be selectable after adjusting colors?
4.a: No. To apply the changes, each page is rendered to an image at 2x resolution and saved into a new PDF, so the output is image-based and text can't be selected or searched. Keep your original for editing, or run the result through [0]OCR[/0] to add a searchable text layer.

5.q: Why is my PDF larger after adjusting the colors?
5.a: Every page is stored as a full-page PNG image instead of text and vector drawing commands, so the file usually grows, especially for text-heavy documents. Running the result through [0]Compress PDF[/0] afterward brings the size back down.

6.q: Can I give a PDF a sepia or vintage look?
6.a: Raise the Sepia slider (0 to 100) to add a brown tone; higher values give a stronger antique look. Combine it with a small drop in Contrast or Saturation to soften the result, and click Reset at any point to return every slider to its default.

7.q: Does the preview show every page or only the first one?
7.a: The live preview renders the first page only, so you can test settings quickly. When you click Apply, the same settings are processed on every page of the document and the adjusted PDF downloads.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded anywhere when I adjust its colors?
8.a: No. The page rendering and the color math run in your browser, and the adjusted PDF is assembled on your device, so the file never leaves your computer.

1.q: What does alternate merge do that a normal merge doesn't?
1.a: A normal merge appends whole files one after another. Alternate merge takes page 1 from each file in turn, then page 2 from each, and so on, so the pages of two or more PDFs are interleaved into a single document. If you only need files back to back, use [0]Merge PDF[/0].

2.q: How do I fix a double-sided scan where the fronts and backs are in separate PDFs?
2.a: Upload the fronts PDF first and the backs PDF second, then click Mix Pages. The output alternates front 1, back 1, front 2, back 2 and so on. If the backs were scanned last page first, flip that file with [0]Reverse Pages[/0] before mixing.

3.q: The fronts and backs are in the same PDF, not separate files. Which tool do I need?
3.a: This tool interleaves separate files. If one PDF holds all the fronts followed by all the backs, [0]Duplex Collate[/0] splits that single file at the midpoint and interleaves the two halves, with an option to reverse the back block.

4.q: What happens if the PDFs have different page counts?
4.a: Interleaving continues until the shorter file runs out, and the remaining pages from the longer file are appended in order at the end. No pages are dropped.

5.q: Can I interleave more than two PDFs?
5.a: Any number of files from two upward. With three files the output goes A1, B1, C1, A2, B2, C2 and so on, following the order shown in the file list, which you can change by dragging the grip handles.

6.q: Does the output keep bookmarks and page numbers from the original files?
6.a: Bookmarks from each source file are carried into the mixed PDF. Page labels are reset to a plain 1 to N sequence by default; turn on the option to keep original page labels if you want each file's own labels, which can produce duplicates such as two pages both labeled 1.

7.q: Can I alternate pages from password-protected PDFs?
7.a: If a file is encrypted you're asked for its password when it loads, and the decrypted copy is used for mixing. The output isn't encrypted, so use [0]Protect PDF[/0] afterward if it needs a password again.

8.q: Are the PDFs uploaded to a server while they're being interleaved?
8.a: No. The files are read in your browser and interleaved by a WebAssembly build of cpdf running in a background worker on your device, and the finished alternated-mixed.pdf is saved straight from the browser.

1.q: How do I change the background color of a PDF without losing the text?
1.a: Upload the PDF, pick a color, and the tool draws a solid rectangle behind each page and places the original page content on top of it. The text stays real text, so it remains selectable and searchable, and the page dimensions don't change.

2.q: Why didn't the background color show up on some pages?
2.a: The color sits underneath the existing content, so any page that already has an opaque background covers it up. Scanned pages, which are usually one full-page image, and pages with a drawn white background are the most common cases.

3.q: Does the color apply to every page or can I pick specific pages?
3.a: There's no page range option, so the same color is applied to every page in the document. To color only certain pages, pull them out with [0]Split PDF[/0], color that file, and merge it back.

4.q: What colors work best as a PDF background?
4.a: Light, muted tones such as cream, ivory, or pale yellow keep black text readable, which is why the default is a light yellow (#FFFFCC). A dark background makes normal black text hard to read because the text color isn't changed; use [0]Change Text Color[/0] on the result if you want light text on a dark page.

5.q: Will links, form fields, or bookmarks survive the color change?
5.a: No. Each page is re-embedded as a drawing on top of the color layer and written into a new file, so link annotations, form fields, comments, and bookmarks aren't carried over. Change the background first and add those elements afterward.

6.q: Does changing the background turn my pages into images or make the file bigger?
6.a: Pages aren't rasterized. The tool works at the PDF object level and only adds a filled rectangle per page, so fonts and vector graphics stay intact and the file size stays close to the original.

7.q: Is my PDF uploaded when I change its background color?
7.a: No. The color layer is added by code running in your browser and the finished file is saved directly from the page to your device. The document isn't sent to a server at any point.

8.q: Can I change the background color of a password-protected PDF?
8.a: If the PDF needs a password to open, the tool prompts you for it and then processes the file as usual. The output is saved without that password, so protect it again with [0]Protect PDF[/0] if you still need it locked.

1.q: What does the Bates number look like on the page?
1.a: By default it's a six-digit zero-padded number such as 000001 placed at the footer center in 10 pt Helvetica. Presets can add an exhibit number, a case label, and a page number, for example Exhibit 1 Case XYZ 000001 Page 1, and the preview box shows the exact text before you process anything.

2.q: Can I use my own prefix or case number instead of the presets?
2.a: Yes. Pick Custom style and write a template with placeholders: [BATES] for the sequential number, [PAGE] for the page number within the file, [FILE] for the file counter, and [FILENAME] for the source file name. A template like SMITH-[BATES] produces SMITH-000001, SMITH-000002, and so on.

3.q: Does the numbering continue across multiple PDFs or restart for each file?
3.a: It continues. If the first file has 30 pages and numbering starts at 1, the second file begins at 000031, following the order of the file list, which you can rearrange by dragging. There's no option to restart the count per file; process the files separately if you need that.

4.q: How many digits can the number have?
4.a: Zero padding can be 3, 4, 5, or 6 digits, or turned off so 1, 2, 3 print without leading zeros. The count itself isn't capped; if it grows past the padding width, the extra digits are still printed.

5.q: Where does the stamp go, and will it cover my content?
5.a: You choose one of six spots: header or footer, at the left, center, or right. The margin scales with the page, roughly 4 percent of the width or height with a floor of 8 points and a cap of 40, so the stamp sits in the same relative place on Letter, A4, and oversized exhibits. Existing content isn't shifted, so on pages printed edge to edge the stamp can overlap it.

6.q: Are Bates numbers searchable text or an image?
6.a: They're real text drawn in Helvetica, Times New Roman, or Courier, so they can be selected, searched, and read by review software without OCR. These are the built-in PDF standard fonts, which cover Latin characters only, so a template containing other scripts will fail.

7.q: Are my discovery documents uploaded to a server for stamping?
7.a: No. Stamping happens inside your browser and the numbered files are written straight to your downloads folder. Nothing about the documents, the case name, or the numbering leaves the machine, which matters for privileged material.

8.q: What do I get when I stamp several files at once?
8.a: Each PDF is numbered as its own file and keeps its original name; a single file downloads directly, and two or more download together as bates_numbered.zip. The files aren't merged, so the page counts and order inside each document stay as they were.

1.q: Can I combine several BMP files into one PDF?
1.a: Yes. Every BMP you add becomes its own page in a single PDF, in the order shown in the file list. There's no option to produce one PDF per file, so convert files separately if you need them split.

2.q: Why is the PDF smaller than my BMP files?
2.a: BMP stores uncompressed pixels, so the files are large. The converter redraws each image and stores it in the PDF as lossless PNG, which usually shrinks it considerably without changing a single pixel.

3.q: Is any image quality lost in the conversion?
3.a: No. Pixels are stored losslessly and there's no quality setting on this tool, so the output has the same resolution and colors as the source. If you need a smaller file afterward, run the PDF through [0]Compress PDF[/0].

4.q: What page size does the PDF get when I convert a BMP?
4.a: Each page is sized to the image's pixel dimensions at one point per pixel, so a 2480 by 3508 pixel scan produces a page about 34 by 49 inches rather than A4. Viewers and printers scale it to fit, and [0]Fix Page Size[/0] can resize every page to A4 or Letter afterward.

5.q: Why does it say one of my files is invalid?
5.a: Images are decoded by your browser, which handles standard Windows bitmaps. Unusual variants such as OS/2 headers or rare compression modes can fail; re-saving the file as a standard 24-bit BMP or as PNG in any image editor fixes it.

6.q: Can I mix BMP with JPG or PNG files?
6.a: This tool accepts only .bmp files and skips anything else you add. Use [0]Images to PDF[/0] when you need to combine several formats into one document.

7.q: Does the BMP's DPI setting affect the result?
7.a: No. The resolution stored in the file header is ignored and page size comes purely from pixel count, so two images with the same pixel dimensions produce identical pages regardless of their DPI.

8.q: Are my BMP files uploaded anywhere?
8.a: No. Decoding uses your browser's own image support and the PDF is assembled locally with pdf-lib, so scanner or medical imaging exports never leave your computer.

1.q: How do I add bookmarks to a PDF that doesn't have any?
1.a: Upload the PDF, go to a page, type a title, and click Add to Page; drag entries to nest or reorder them. Click Save PDF with Bookmarks to download the result. For a printed contents page inside the document rather than sidebar navigation, use [0]Table of Contents[/0] instead.

2.q: Will my existing bookmarks be kept?
2.a: Only if you check Auto-extract existing bookmarks before uploading, or use the extract button afterward, so they load into the panel. When you save, the panel's contents replace the PDF's bookmark tree entirely, so anything not loaded into the editor is dropped.

3.q: What is the CSV format for importing bookmarks?
3.a: A header row followed by one line per bookmark with three columns: title,page,level. Titles containing commas go in double quotes, page is the 1-based page number, and level controls nesting, with the lowest number for top-level entries and each deeper child adding one.

4.q: Can a bookmark jump to a specific spot on a page instead of the top?
4.a: Open the bookmark's edit dialog, turn on Set custom destination, and either type X and Y coordinates plus a zoom percentage or click the pick button and then click the exact spot on the page preview. The bookmark is saved as an XYZ destination, which most readers honor.

5.q: Can I color or bold bookmarks?
5.a: Each bookmark can be red, blue, green, yellow, purple, or a custom hex color, and styled bold, italic, or bold italic. Turn on Batch Mode to select several bookmarks and apply a color or style to all of them at once.

6.q: How do I get bookmarks out of a PDF for editing in a spreadsheet?
6.a: Load them with Auto-extract, then use Export to CSV or Export to JSON; the file is named after your PDF with a -bookmarks suffix. The CSV opens in Excel or Google Sheets, and once you've edited it you can import it back and save a new PDF.

7.q: Does the editor work on password-protected PDFs?
7.a: You'll be asked for the password when you upload the file, and the editor opens once it's entered. The saved PDF is written without the password, so protect it again afterward if you need to.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded while I edit bookmarks?
8.a: No. The page preview, the bookmark tree, and the final save are all handled in your browser with PDF.js and pdf-lib, so the file never leaves your computer.

1.q: Does converting a CBZ to PDF reduce the image quality?
1.a: JPEG and PNG pages are copied into the PDF as they are, with no re-encoding, so the artwork looks exactly like the original and the file size stays about the same. Other formats such as WebP, GIF, or BMP are decoded and re-saved as lossless PNG before embedding.

2.q: How does the tool decide the page order?
2.a: Pages are sorted by filename using natural ordering, so page2.jpg comes before page10.jpg. Files in subfolders are included and sorted by their full path, and non-image files such as ComicInfo.xml are ignored.

3.q: What page size do the comic pages get in the PDF?
3.a: Each page is sized to the pixel dimensions of its image, one point per pixel, so a double-page spread comes out as a wide landscape page and single pages stay portrait. There's no option to force one size here; if you need uniform pages, run the result through [0]Fix Page Size[/0].

4.q: Can I convert CBR files as well as CBZ?
4.a: .cbr archives are accepted and can be mixed with .cbz files in the same batch. CBR files are routed through the PyMuPDF engine, which downloads on first use, so they take a little longer than CBZ files, which are unpacked directly in the browser.

5.q: Which image formats inside the archive are supported?
5.a: JPEG and PNG are embedded directly. GIF, BMP, WebP, AVIF, TIFF, HEIC, and JXL are converted to PNG by your browser first, so those less common formats only work if your browser can display them; TIFF, HEIC, and JXL fail in some browsers. The converter checks the actual image data rather than the extension, so a PNG named .jpg still works.

6.q: Is there a limit on archive size or page count?
6.a: A single CBZ can hold up to 2,000 images, with each image capped at 100 MB and 500 MB of uncompressed image data per archive. Those limits keep the browser from running out of memory, and they're far above a typical comic issue.

7.q: What happens when I convert several comics at once?
7.a: Each archive becomes its own PDF named after the original file. One file downloads directly; two or more are bundled into comic-converted.zip.

8.q: Are my comic files uploaded anywhere?
8.a: No. CBZ archives are unzipped and rebuilt as PDFs entirely inside your browser, and CBR files are handled by an engine that also runs locally. Nothing from your collection leaves your device.

1.q: What is the difference between a user password and an owner password?
1.a: The user password is required to open the PDF at all. The owner password protects the permission settings and is what someone needs to change or remove them later. Set only an owner password if anyone should be able to open the file but with printing, copying, or editing restricted.

2.q: Why does the tool ask for an owner password when I set permissions?
2.a: Permission flags are only enforced when an owner password exists; without one, PDF readers treat the file as unrestricted. The tool therefore requires a New Owner Password whenever you set permissions or a user password.

3.q: How do I stop people from copying text or printing my PDF?
3.a: Uncheck "Allow Copying Text" and "Allow Printing", enter a New Owner Password, and click Change Permissions. Adobe Reader and other compliant viewers will then block those actions. Some third-party tools ignore permission flags, so for sensitive material consider [0]rasterizing the pages[/0] as well.

4.q: Which permissions can I control?
4.a: Seven checkboxes: printing, copying text, modifying content, annotating, filling forms, document assembly (inserting, deleting, or rotating pages), and page extraction. An unchecked box means the action is not allowed.

5.q: What encryption does Change Permissions use?
5.a: The output is encrypted with 256-bit AES. That also makes this a quick way to upgrade an old RC4-encrypted PDF: enter its current password, set new passwords, and the file is rewritten with AES-256.

6.q: Can I change permissions on a PDF that is already password protected?
6.a: Yes, enter the existing password in the Current Password field. The tool opens the file with it, then re-encrypts it with your new passwords and permission settings; a wrong current password produces an error and nothing is changed.

7.q: How do I remove all restrictions instead of changing them?
7.a: Leave both new password fields empty and click Change Permissions. The output is fully decrypted with no passwords and no permission flags. If you don't have the current password, use [0]Remove Restrictions[/0] instead, which works without one when the PDF opens freely.

8.q: Is my PDF or its owner password sent anywhere when I change permissions?
8.a: No. The encryption is done by QPDF compiled to WebAssembly inside your browser tab, so the file and every password you type stay on your device.

1.q: How do I merge all pages of a PDF into one long page?
1.a: Upload the PDF, keep Layout Direction set to Vertical, and click the process button. Every page is placed top to bottom on one continuous page, with the output width matching the widest source page and narrower pages centered.

2.q: Can I put the pages side by side instead of stacked?
2.a: Choose Horizontal (Left to Right) in Layout Direction. Pages are laid out in order from left to right on a single wide page, and pages shorter than the tallest one are centered vertically.

3.q: Can I add a gap or a line between the pages?
3.a: Spacing (0 by default) adds a gap between pages, measured in the PDF's own units where 72 equals one inch, and Background Color fills that gap. Turn on Add Separator Lines to draw a line through the middle of each gap, with its own thickness (0.5 units and up, in steps of 0.5) and color.

4.q: Does the background color apply to the whole page or only the gaps?
4.a: It fills the whole output page underneath the source pages, so it shows in the spacing between pages and in any margin where a narrower page is centered. With white selected, the default, no fill is drawn at all.

5.q: Will the text in the combined page still be selectable?
5.a: No. Each source page is rendered to an image at 2x resolution and drawn onto the new page, so the result is a picture of your pages rather than live text. Keep the original PDF if you need to copy or search text later.

6.q: Is there a limit to how many pages I can stitch together?
6.a: The tool doesn't set one, but the output grows with every page you add: a 100-page document becomes a page roughly 100 pages tall. Some readers struggle with very large pages; Adobe Reader, for example, doesn't display pages larger than 200 inches on a side.

7.q: What is a single long-page PDF useful for?
7.a: It suits scrolling previews for the web, design mockups, comic strips, and storyboards where the reader scrolls instead of flipping pages. If you want several pages printed on one sheet in a grid, [0]N-Up PDF[/0] is the better fit.

8.q: Does the combined PDF get uploaded to a server?
8.a: No. Rendering the pages and building the new single-page PDF both happen in your browser, and the file stays on your device the whole time.

1.q: How do I see what changed between two versions of a PDF?
1.a: Upload the original as the first PDF and the revised version as the second. The tool pairs matching pages, then highlights added, deleted, modified, and moved content on each page pair, with counters showing how many changes of each kind were found.

2.q: What is the difference between side-by-side and overlay mode?
2.a: Side-by-side shows the two pages next to each other with synchronized scrolling, which is easiest for reading text changes. Overlay stacks the revised page on top of the original with an opacity slider, so shifted or resized elements stand out, and the Flicker button switches the top page on and off to make small moves visible.

3.q: Can it compare scanned PDFs that have no text layer?
3.a: With OCR turned on, page images are run through Tesseract in your browser and the recognized text is compared, so scanned documents can be checked. OCR currently uses the English language model, and it's slower than comparing PDFs that already contain text.

4.q: Can I filter out formatting changes and only see text differences?
4.a: Changes are grouped into text, image, header/footer, annotation, formatting, and background categories, each with its own toggle. Turn off the categories you don't care about, and use the text search box to find a specific changed word or phrase.

5.q: What happens when pages were added, removed, or reordered between versions?
5.a: Pages are paired by content similarity rather than by page number, so an inserted page doesn't throw off everything after it. A page with no counterpart is reported as added or removed, and the page navigation steps through the pairs the tool built.

6.q: Does it detect changes to comments and annotations?
6.a: Annotation changes are their own category, so added or removed comments, highlights, and markup are flagged separately from body text and can be shown or hidden with the annotation filter.

7.q: Can I save the comparison as a report?
7.a: The Export as PDF menu produces a PDF of the comparison. In side-by-side mode you can choose a split view, alternating pages, or only the left or right document with highlights; in overlay mode it exports the overlay view.

8.q: Are the two PDFs sent anywhere to be compared?
8.a: No. Rendering, page pairing, OCR, and change detection all run in your browser with WebAssembly and web workers, and nothing is transmitted, so contracts and other confidential drafts stay on your machine.

1.q: What size should an email attachment be?
1.a: Under 10MB is safe for virtually every recipient, including strict corporate servers. Under 5MB is courteous for recipients on mobile connections.

2.q: Why does my 24MB PDF bounce with a 25MB limit?
2.a: Email encodes attachments in a format that adds roughly 33% overhead, so a 24MB file becomes a 32MB message. Compress the PDF to about 18MB or less to fit a 25MB limit.

3.q: Is it safe to compress confidential documents here?
3.a: Yes. this is the point of BentoPDF. The file is processed by WebAssembly inside your browser and is never uploaded, so the only copies are on your device and in the email you choose to send.

1.q: Can every PDF be compressed to 100KB?
1.a: Not always. Short text-based PDFs almost always can. Long or heavily scanned documents may bottom out above 100KB, and the result message tells you when that happens. In that case split the file or rescan at a lower DPI and compress again.

2.q: Which compression level should I pick for 100KB?
2.a: You can leave it on Medium. The 100 KB target is already filled in, so Hyper Compress steps image quality down only as far as it needs to. Pick Low instead if you want it to start from higher quality, and for image-only scans that still won't fit, turn on Rasterize pages. Nothing is uploaded, so retries are instant.

3.q: Will my text stay selectable?
3.a: Yes. Text, links, and form fields are preserved. Rasterize pages only applies to scans with no text layer, so it never turns selectable text into an image unless you turn on Override content protection.

4.q: Is my document private?
4.a: Yes. Compression runs entirely in your browser using WebAssembly. The file never leaves your device, which matters for the ID documents and applications that 100KB limits usually involve.

1.q: How much can compression reduce my PDF?
1.a: Typical reductions are 50 to 90%. Image-heavy files shrink the most; already-optimized PDFs shrink the least. You see the exact before-and-after size instantly, and nothing counts against a quota.

2.q: Is there a file size limit for what I can compress?
2.a: No hard limit. processing happens on your own machine, so capacity depends on your device rather than a server plan. Files of several hundred megabytes work on a typical laptop.

3.q: Does compressing affect signatures or form fields?
3.a: Compression preserves form fields. A digitally signed PDF is left exactly as it is, because any change would invalidate the signature, so compress before signing, not after. If you need it smaller anyway, turn on Override content protection under Custom Settings to remove the signatures and compress it.

1.q: What quality should I expect at 200KB?
1.a: Typed documents look identical. Scans keep readable text; photos inside the PDF will look slightly softer but remain clear on screen.

2.q: The portal wants under 200KB but my file is 10MB. possible?
2.a: Usually yes, if most of the weight is images. With the 200 KB target set, Hyper Compress keeps lowering image quality and resolution until the file fits, and tells you if it can't get there.

3.q: Do I need to sign up or pay?
3.a: No. Every BentoPDF tool is free with no account, and because the work happens in your browser there are no server costs to pass on to you.

1.q: Which level keeps the best image quality?
1.a: Lossless keeps images exactly as they are, and Low keeps them at high quality. With the 2 MB target set, Hyper Compress starts from the level you pick and lowers image quality only if the file doesn't fit.

2.q: Why is my exported PDF so large in the first place?
2.a: Design tools often embed full-resolution images and complete font files. Compression subsets the fonts and re-encodes images at sensible resolution, which is where the large savings come from.

3.q: Can I check the result before downloading?
3.a: You see the compressed size immediately after processing, and you can re-run with a different level or target as many times as you like. Nothing is uploaded, so iteration is instant.

1.q: Will 500KB compression change how my PDF prints?
1.a: Print quality stays excellent for text and vector graphics, which compression never degrades. Photos are optimized for screen-and-print use; only large-format printing would show the difference.

2.q: Can I compress multiple PDFs to 500KB at once?
2.a: Yes. add several files and each is compressed independently in your browser, with no queue and no per-file fee.

3.q: Why is my compressed file already smaller than 500KB but the portal still rejects it?
3.a: Some portals measure size in mebibytes or reject certain PDF versions. Re-check the exact limit wording, and try the Sanitize PDF tool to strip unusual metadata if a compliant file is still rejected.

1.q: Why is my PDF still large after compressing it?
1.a: Most of a PDF's size comes from images, so a file with few images, or images that are already small, won't shrink much, and the result message tells you when the size couldn't be reduced. Try the High level, set a target file size, or turn on Convert to grayscale under Custom Settings. For an image-only scan, turn on Rasterize pages there too.

2.q: How much does each compression level reduce image quality?
2.a: Low re-encodes images at JPEG quality 80 and downsamples anything above 200 DPI, Medium uses quality 50 and 150 DPI, and High uses quality 20 and 72 DPI. Lossless leaves images untouched and only optimizes fonts and file structure. Medium is the default and reads fine on screen; Low is the safer choice for anything that will be printed.

3.q: Will I still be able to select and search text after compression?
3.a: Yes. Compression recompresses images, subsets fonts, and cleans up the file structure without touching the text layer, so selection, search, and links keep working. Rasterize pages only applies to image-only scans and is skipped whenever a document has selectable text, unless you turn on Override content protection under Custom Settings.

4.q: Does compressing remove metadata from my PDF?
4.a: Compression keeps document details such as the title and author. It drops embedded page thumbnails and private data that editing apps leave behind, and a PDF/A file loses its PDF/A label unless you turn on Preserve PDF/A under Custom Settings. To strip document details as well, use [0]Remove Metadata[/0].

5.q: Can I compress a scanned PDF?
5.a: Scanned PDFs are full-page images, so they respond well to compression. Medium or High downsamples the scans in place and keeps any OCR text layer. If the scan has no text layer at all, turning on Rasterize pages under Custom Settings can make it smaller still.

6.q: What do the Custom Settings do?
6.a: They fine-tune Hyper Compress. You can set image quality and maximum resolution, control how fonts are subset and merged, flatten annotations, form fields, or links, remove thumbnails and other hidden data, rasterize image-only scans, keep PDF/A conformance, and turn on Brotli. Override content protection lets you compress signed PDFs by removing their signatures and rasterize pages that have text. Picking a compression level resets the rest to that level's values.

7.q: Can I compress a PDF to a specific size like 1 MB?
7.a: Yes. Enter the size under Target File Size and Hyper Compress searches for the best image quality that still fits. If the file can't get that small, you get the smallest version it can make and a note saying so. For common limits there are pages with the target already filled in, such as [0]Compress PDF to 1MB[/0].

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded to a server for compression?
8.a: No. Compression runs [0]Hyper Compress[/0], BentoPDF's own engine, compiled to WebAssembly and served with the app, so everything happens on your device. You can compress one file or a whole batch, which comes back as compressed-pdfs.zip, and none of them leave your computer.

1.q: Does cropping permanently delete the part of the page outside the box?
1.a: Not in the default mode. The tool sets each page's crop box, so viewers and printers show only the selected area while the full page content stays in the file and can be restored by resetting the crop box in a PDF editor. Turn on Flattening Crop if the trimmed area has to be gone for good, for example before sharing an excerpt.

2.q: Will my text still be selectable after cropping?
2.a: In the default mode, yes: nothing is re-rendered, so text, links, and vector graphics stay exactly as they were. Flattening Crop renders each cropped page as an image, which removes selectable text and usually makes the file larger.

3.q: Can I crop different pages by different amounts?
3.a: Yes. Use the page navigation to move through the document and draw a separate box on each page; the tool remembers every box you set, and pages you never drew on keep their original size. To use one box everywhere, check Apply to all pages and the box on the current page is copied to every page.

4.q: What page size will the cropped PDF have?
4.a: Each cropped page takes on the size of its box, so trimming a 1-inch margin from every side of a Letter page leaves a 6.5 x 9 inch page. If you need a standard size like A4 or Letter afterward, run the result through [0]Fix Page Size[/0].

5.q: Is there a way to type exact crop measurements?
5.a: No. Cropping is done by dragging the corners or edges of the overlay on the page preview; there's no numeric input for margins or dimensions in this tool. Zooming the browser in helps when a margin is only a few millimeters wide.

6.q: Does cropping reduce image quality or file size?
6.a: The default mode changes neither: the content is untouched, so quality is identical, and the file stays about the same size because the hidden margin data is still inside. Flattening Crop replaces cropped pages with images, which typically makes the file bigger rather than smaller.

7.q: Is my document uploaded while I crop it?
7.a: No. The page previews are rendered in your browser and the crop is applied locally, so the file never leaves your computer; the cropped copy is saved under the original file name.

8.q: Can I crop a scanned PDF to remove black edges?
8.a: Yes. Draw the box inside the dark border on each page, or set it once and use Apply to all pages if every scan has the same border. Because the default crop only hides the edges, use Flattening Crop if the border must be physically removed, and straighten tilted scans first with [0]Deskew PDF[/0].

1.q: How is the CSV laid out in the PDF?
1.a: The first row becomes a bold header with a blue background and the remaining rows become striped table rows in 9-point text on landscape A4 pages. Long tables continue over as many pages as needed, with the header repeated on each page.

2.q: My file uses semicolons or tabs instead of commas. Will it work?
2.a: Yes. The parser detects the delimiter automatically, so comma, semicolon, tab, and pipe separated files all convert. Quoted fields containing commas or line breaks are handled according to standard CSV rules.

3.q: My CSV has many columns. Why is the table squashed?
3.a: All columns are shrunk to fit the page width and cell text wraps onto extra lines, so very wide files end up with narrow columns. There's no setting for page size or orientation, so split wide datasets into several files or drop columns you don't need.

4.q: Can I convert several CSV files at once?
4.a: Yes. A single file downloads as a PDF with the same base name, while several files are packaged into csv-converted.zip with one PDF per file.

5.q: Does it handle accented or non-Latin characters?
5.a: The file is read as UTF-8 and the PDF uses the built-in Helvetica font, which covers Latin characters including accents. Text in scripts such as Chinese, Arabic, or Cyrillic may not display correctly, and files saved in other encodings can show garbled characters.

6.q: Why does it say the CSV file is empty?
6.a: Rows that are completely blank are dropped before the table is built, so a file containing only empty lines or whitespace triggers that error. Open the file in a text editor and confirm it has at least a header row with values.

7.q: Can I keep spreadsheet formatting such as column widths, colors, or multiple sheets?
7.a: No. CSV holds only raw values, so there's no formatting to preserve. For .xlsx or .xls files with formatting and several sheets, use [0]Excel to PDF[/0] instead.

8.q: Is my spreadsheet data sent anywhere?
8.a: No. The CSV is parsed and the PDF is generated in your browser with JavaScript libraries (PapaParse and jsPDF), so financial or customer data in the file stays on your machine.

1.q: How do I delete specific pages from a PDF?
1.a: Upload the file, then either type the pages in the box using ranges like 2, 4-6, 9 or click the page thumbnails to mark them. Marked pages are highlighted so you can double-check before clicking the button, and the result downloads as a new PDF with those pages gone.

2.q: Can I delete every page in the file?
2.a: No. At least one page has to remain, and the tool refuses with an error if your selection covers the whole document.

3.q: Do the remaining pages lose quality or formatting?
3.a: No. The kept pages are copied over unchanged, including their text, images, fonts, and order, so nothing is re-rendered or recompressed.

4.q: Are bookmarks and links kept after deleting pages?
4.a: Links and annotations that live on the kept pages come along, but the document's bookmark tree isn't carried over because the pages are copied into a fresh PDF. If you need bookmarks afterward, rebuild them with [0]Edit Bookmarks[/0].

5.q: Can I delete pages from a password-protected PDF?
5.a: You'll be prompted for the password when you upload the file. The downloaded PDF is saved without the password, so add protection again with [0]Protect PDF[/0] if the document still needs it.

6.q: Will the PDF get smaller after removing pages?
6.a: Usually, if the removed pages carried their own images or fonts, since only the resources the kept pages reference are written to the new file. Pages that share resources with the rest of the document free up less space.

7.q: Is my PDF uploaded to a server to delete the pages?
7.a: No. The thumbnails are rendered and the new file is assembled in your browser, so the document stays on your device from upload to download.

8.q: What if I want to keep only a few pages instead of deleting many?
8.a: Use [0]Extract Pages[/0], which does the reverse: you list the pages to keep and everything else is left out. The output is the same kind of clean copy.

1.q: How does the tool detect that a page is tilted?
1.a: Each page is rendered to an image at the DPI you choose, then OpenCV analyzes it: it fits a minimum-area rectangle around the dark pixels and, as a fallback, measures the angle of dominant text lines with a Hough transform. The resulting angle is what the results panel reports for that page.

2.q: What does the Skew Threshold setting do?
2.a: Pages whose detected tilt is below the threshold are left alone. The default of 0.5 degrees catches visible tilt without touching pages that are already straight; drop it to 0.1 degrees when you want the tightest alignment before OCR, or raise it to 1 or 2 degrees to correct only clearly crooked pages.

3.q: Does deskewing keep the text selectable?
3.a: No. Every page in the output, including pages that didn't need correction, is written as an image at the processing DPI, so any existing text layer is lost. Run the result through [0]OCR PDF[/0] afterward if you need searchable text; OCR works better on straightened pages anyway.

4.q: Which DPI should I use when deskewing a scan?
4.a: 150 DPI is fast and accurate for ordinary letter-sized scans. Use 200 or 300 DPI for small print or fine detail, and 100 DPI when speed matters more than precision. The setting also controls the resolution of the output pages, so higher values produce larger files.

5.q: Will the page size change after rotation?
5.a: Output pages keep the original page dimensions. The rotated image is padded with white in the corners exposed by the rotation and then fitted onto the page, so content may shrink by a hair but nothing is pushed off the sheet.

6.q: Does it work on every kind of scan?
6.a: It works best on pages with clear horizontal lines of text. Pages that are mostly photos, drawings, or diagonal design elements give the detector little to measure, so the angle can be off; check the results panel and keep your original for those.

7.q: How do I know which pages were corrected?
7.a: After processing, a results panel lists every page with its detected angle and marks the ones that were rotated; pages under the threshold show their angle but are labeled as untouched. If you queued several PDFs, each downloads under its original name and the panel shows the last file processed.

8.q: Are my scans uploaded for processing?
8.a: No. The PDF rendering and the OpenCV analysis both run in your browser through WebAssembly. The engine is downloaded the first time you use it, but your documents never leave your computer.

1.q: What is the difference between Digital Signature and Sign PDF?
1.a: [0]Sign PDF[/0] places a drawn, typed, or uploaded picture of your signature on the page; it's visual only. This tool applies a cryptographic PKCS#7 signature using your X.509 certificate, so a PDF reader can verify who signed and detect any change made afterward. You can also show a visible signature block at the same time.

2.q: Can I sign with a PEM certificate instead of a .pfx or .p12 file?
2.a: Yes. Upload a single .pem file that contains both the certificate and the private key. Encrypted private keys work too; enter the key password in the Certificate Password field. If your certificate and key are in separate PEM files, paste them into one file first.

3.q: Do I need an internet connection to sign?
3.a: Often, yes. The signing library fetches the issuer certificate chain from the URLs in your certificate's Authority Information Access extension, and if those servers can't be reached, signing fails for certificates that need chain validation. Your PDF and private key are never part of those requests; only the certificate URLs are fetched.

4.q: Why does Adobe Reader say the signature validity is unknown?
4.a: The reader can't trace the certificate back to a root it trusts. That's expected for self-signed certificates, which are fine for testing but always show a warning. For documents other people need to rely on, use a certificate issued by a Certificate Authority that PDF readers trust.

5.q: Do I have to add a visible signature on the page?
5.a: No. The cryptographic signature is embedded whether or not the visible block is enabled. Turn on Visible Signature if you want a stamp on the page: pick the first, last, all, or a specific page, set the position and size in points, and add a PNG, JPG, or WebP image or a line of text; with neither, the tool writes the certificate's common name and the current date.

6.q: What are the Reason, Location, and Contact Info fields for?
6.a: They're optional metadata stored inside the signature itself. Reason records why you signed, such as "Approved" or "Reviewed", Location where it happened, and Contact Info how to reach you. PDF readers display them in the signature panel.

7.q: Can a digitally signed PDF still be edited?
7.a: The file can still be opened and edited, but any change made after signing breaks the integrity check and readers will report the document as modified. If the PDF has form fields or annotations that should be fixed in place, run it through [0]Flatten PDF[/0] before signing, not after.

8.q: How can I check that the signature was applied correctly?
8.a: Open the signed file in [0]Validate Signature[/0]. It lists every signature, shows the signer and issuer, checks the certificate dates, and confirms whether the bytes have changed since signing. You can also load your CA certificate there to verify the trust chain.

1.q: How do I split a two-page book scan into separate pages?
1.a: Upload the PDF, choose Vertical (Left & Right) as the split type, and process it. Each page is cut at the exact midpoint into a left page followed by a right page, so a book scanned two pages per sheet becomes one page per sheet in reading order.

2.q: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal division?
2.a: Vertical cuts each page down the middle into left and right halves, which suits landscape pages with side-by-side content. Horizontal cuts across the middle into top and bottom halves, top half first, which suits tall pages such as posters or stacked forms.

3.q: Can I divide only some pages and leave the rest alone?
3.a: Enter a page range such as 1-5, 8, 11-13 in the page range box. Only those pages are divided; every other page is copied into the output unchanged and in its original position. Leave the box blank to divide all pages.

4.q: Does dividing pages lower the quality or change the text?
4.a: No. The tool copies each page twice and sets a different crop box on each copy rather than re-rendering anything, so text stays selectable, vector graphics stay sharp, and images keep their original resolution.

5.q: Can I choose where the cut happens instead of the middle?
5.a: No, the split is always at the midpoint of the page. If the content is off-center or you need an uneven cut, use [0]Crop PDF[/0] to set the exact area you want for each half.

6.q: How many pages will the output have?
6.a: Each divided page becomes two pages, so a 10-page document with every page divided produces 20 pages. Pages outside your range still count once, and the halves keep the same order as the original.

7.q: The halves come out sideways. What should I do?
7.a: Divide Pages doesn't rotate anything, so fix the orientation with [0]Rotate PDF[/0] either before dividing or on the divided output, depending on how the scan was made.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded when I divide its pages?
8.a: No. The page copying and crop-box changes happen in your browser, and the divided file is written on your device without any upload.

1.q: What kind of scan is this tool for?
1.a: A PDF produced by feeding a stack through a single-sided scanner twice, once for the fronts and once for the backs, which gives one file with all front pages first and all back pages after. The tool interleaves the two blocks into front 1, back 1, front 2, back 2 order. If the fronts and backs are in two separate PDFs, use [0]Alternate & Mix Pages[/0] instead.

2.q: How do I know where to set the split point?
2.a: The split is the last page of the front block, which for a normal two-pass scan is exactly half the total. Click Auto-detect split (half) to fill that in, then read the preview summary, which shows the size of each block and the resulting page count before you commit.

3.q: What does the grouped export option do?
3.a: If the stack held several short documents, such as two-page forms, enter the pages per document and the collated output is cut into chunks of that length. Multiple chunks download as a ZIP with one PDF per document; a single chunk downloads as a plain PDF.

4.q: What filename does the collated PDF get?
4.a: A single collated file downloads under your original name with _collated added, for example scan_collated.pdf. Grouped output is a ZIP named scan_collated_grouped.zip containing the separate PDFs.

5.q: Can I preview the result before downloading?
5.a: The page shows a summary line as you change the split point and back order, including the front and back block sizes and the output page count, and it warns when the blocks are uneven. There is no thumbnail preview, so check the first few pages of the download and switch the back block order if the backs come out reversed.

6.q: Does it keep bookmarks from the scanned PDF?
6.a: The output is rebuilt page by page, so page content and rotation are preserved but document-level bookmarks aren't carried across. Scanner output rarely has any, but if yours does you can add them again with [0]Edit Bookmarks[/0].

7.q: Is my scanned document uploaded to be reordered?
7.a: No. The PDF is opened in your browser, the pages are copied into a new document on your device, and the result is downloaded directly, so scans of forms and records never leave your computer.

1.q: How do I see what files are attached to a PDF?
1.a: Upload the PDF and the tool scans it and lists every embedded file by name, marking each one as a document-level attachment or as a page attachment with its page number. If nothing is embedded, it tells you so instead of showing an empty list.

2.q: Can I remove just one attachment instead of all of them?
2.a: Click the trash icon next to any attachment to mark it, and click again to unmark it before saving. Remove All Attachments selects everything at once, and the new PDF is written with only the marked files taken out.

3.q: Does removing attachments change the rest of the PDF?
3.a: The pages, text, and images are untouched. The attachments you keep are re-embedded under their original names and, for page attachments, on their original pages, but any description text stored with them isn't carried over.

4.q: Will deleting attachments make my PDF smaller?
4.a: Usually, and often by a lot, because embedded files are stored in full inside the PDF. A document carrying a large spreadsheet or image attachment can drop to a fraction of its size once that file is removed.

5.q: What is the difference between a document-level and a page-level attachment?
5.a: Document-level attachments live in the PDF's embedded files list and show up in a viewer's attachments panel. Page-level attachments are file attachment annotations pinned to a spot on one page, usually shown as a paperclip or pushpin icon. The tool lists and removes both kinds.

6.q: Can I download the attachments before deleting them?
6.a: This tool only lists and removes them. To save the embedded files to your computer first, run the PDF through [0]Extract Attachments[/0], then come back here to strip them.

7.q: Can I add or replace an attachment here?
7.a: No, this tool only removes attachments. Use [0]Add Attachments[/0] to embed new files, and combine the two steps when you want to swap an outdated attachment for a newer version.

8.q: Are the attachments uploaded anywhere when I edit them?
8.a: No. The PDF is parsed by a cpdf engine running as WebAssembly in your browser, the attachment list is built locally, and the cleaned file is saved straight from your browser. Neither the document nor its attachments is sent to a server, which matters when the attachments are the sensitive part.

1.q: Which metadata fields can I change?
1.a: Title, Author, Subject, Keywords, Creator, Producer, Creation Date, and Modification Date, plus any custom key-value pairs you add. The form loads with the file's current values, so you only edit what needs changing.

2.q: How do I delete a field like Author completely?
2.a: Clear the box and save. Whatever is in the form is written back, so an emptied field is stored as empty. To strip every field at once, including hidden ones, use [0]Remove Metadata[/0] instead.

3.q: Why does the modification date change even though I didn't touch it?
3.a: If the Modification Date box is left empty, the tool stamps the current date and time when it saves. Set a specific date in the picker if a particular value needs to be kept.

4.q: Can I add my own fields such as Department or Project ID?
4.a: Yes. Click the add button, enter a key and a value, and the pair is written into the PDF's info dictionary alongside the standard fields. Not every reader lists custom entries, but they stay in the file and show up in tools that read the full info dictionary, such as [0]View Metadata[/0].

5.q: I changed the title but Acrobat still shows the old one. Why?
5.a: The tool writes to the document info dictionary. Some PDFs also carry an XMP metadata stream, and readers like Acrobat prefer XMP when both exist, so the old title can still appear there. Run [0]Remove Metadata[/0] first, then edit, to avoid the conflict.

6.q: How should I enter keywords?
6.a: Separate them with commas, for example invoice, 2026, Q3. They're saved as a keyword list that document management systems and desktop search can index.

7.q: Does editing metadata alter the pages or send my file anywhere?
7.a: No. Only the info dictionary is rewritten; pages, fonts, links, and bookmarks are untouched, and the whole edit happens in your browser, so the document never leaves your device.

8.q: Can I edit metadata on a password-protected PDF?
8.a: If the file needs a password to open, the tool asks for it and then loads the document normally. Without the password the file can't be opened here.

1.q: Can I edit the text in a scanned PDF?
1.a: Not with this tool. A scanned page is a picture, and even after OCR the text is an invisible layer over that picture, so there are no glyphs to edit. The editor detects this and shows a notice that the page's text blocks are an OCR layer, searchable and selectable but not editable.

2.q: Does the text reflow when I add or delete words?
2.a: Within the paragraph you are editing, lines rewrap live as you type and the block grows or shrinks to fit. Other paragraphs and pages stay where they are, so check that a much longer paragraph doesn't run into the content below it.

3.q: Can I use a font from my computer?
3.a: Open the Font menu and choose System fonts to list the fonts installed on your machine. This relies on the Local Font Access API, which is currently available in Chrome and Edge; in other browsers you can still use the fonts already embedded in the document.

4.q: Is there a find and replace across the whole document?
4.a: The Find & Replace bar offers Next, Replace, and Replace All, with Match case, Whole word, and Ignore accents options. Replace All works through every page of the document, not just the one on screen.

5.q: Can I edit images and shapes, not just text?
5.a: Use the Edit menu to choose Text, Images, Shapes, or Edit All, which controls what is selectable on busy pages. Images can be moved, rotated in 90 degree steps, flipped, or replaced while keeping their placement, you can add new images and text boxes, and shapes expose their path stroke settings.

6.q: What happens if the PDF is digitally signed or is PDF/A?
6.a: Editing a signed document invalidates its signature, so the editor warns you and saves your changes as an appended revision, which keeps the original signed version verifiable. For PDF/A files it warns that edits may break conformance.

7.q: Will the editor open a password-protected PDF?
