7.a: It asks for the password first and then opens the document for editing. The saved copy is written from the decrypted document, so if you still need protection, add it again with [0]Protect PDF[/0].

8.q: How is this different from the PDF Editor tool?
8.a: This tool changes the text, images, and shapes that are already part of the page, with fonts, spacing, alignment, lists, and right-to-left support. The [0]PDF Editor[/0] is for annotating: highlights, comments, drawings, and other markup layered on top of the page.

1.q: Can I change the existing text in my PDF with this editor?
1.a: This editor works on top of the page: highlights, comments, shapes, images, freehand drawing, redaction, and new text boxes. To rewrite text that's already in the document, use [0]Edit PDF Text[/0], which lets you click a paragraph and edit it in place.

2.q: Will my annotations show up in Acrobat, Preview, or Chrome?
2.a: Yes. Highlights, comments, shapes, and drawings are saved as standard PDF annotations, so other viewers display them and can usually edit or delete them. Text boxes are written into the page as regular text on download, so they look identical everywhere but can't be moved afterward.

3.q: Is the redaction permanent?
3.a: Yes, once it's applied. Marking text or an area only flags it. Applying a redaction removes the content underneath the marked area from the file rather than covering it with a box, so the text can't be recovered by copying or searching. If you download with marks that haven't been applied yet, the editor offers to apply them first. When you redact selected text, copies of it in the file's properties, bookmarks, comments, and attachments are removed on download too, unless the file is encrypted. Open the downloaded file and check before you share it.

4.q: Can I open more than one PDF at a time?
4.a: Up to 10 documents can be open at once, each in its own tab above the viewer. Adding more files opens more tabs, and removing a file from the list closes its tab.

5.q: Does the editor save my changes automatically?
5.a: No. Everything stays in your browser's memory until you click Download Edited PDF, and closing or refreshing the tab discards the changes. Download before you leave the page.

6.q: Why can't I highlight text on my scanned PDF?
6.a: Highlight, underline, and strikethrough attach to real text, and a scanned page is only an image. Run the file through [0]OCR PDF[/0] first to add a text layer, or mark it up visually with the pen or rectangle tools.

7.q: Can I add text in Chinese, Japanese, Arabic, or other non-Latin scripts?
7.a: Yes. When a text box contains characters outside the basic Latin set, the editor fetches a matching Noto font and embeds it in the PDF so the text renders correctly in other viewers.

8.q: Does the editor upload my PDF?
8.a: No. The editor runs a PDF engine (PDFium compiled to WebAssembly) inside your browser. The only network requests are for the editor's code and optional font files; the document itself never leaves your device.

1.q: How do I get an .eml or .msg file out of my email client?
1.a: In Gmail, open the message, use the three-dot menu, and choose Download message to save an .eml file. Outlook for Windows saves a .msg when you drag a message to a folder or use Save As; Apple Mail and Thunderbird save .eml through their Save As commands. Drop the saved file into the tool.

2.q: Do inline images and formatting survive the conversion?
2.a: HTML emails keep their layout, fonts, and colors, and images embedded in the message itself (the cid: kind used for signatures and pasted screenshots) are included. Images that the email loads from a web server aren't downloaded, so those spots come out empty.

3.q: Can I hide the CC and BCC lines?
3.a: Turn off Include CC and BCC before converting and the header block shows only From, To, Date, and Subject. The same panel has a toggle for the attachments list at the bottom of the PDF.

4.q: Which page sizes are available?
4.a: A4, US Letter, and Legal, with a 50-point margin on every side. Long emails flow onto as many pages as needed. The page size applies to the whole batch, so pick it before you click Convert.

5.q: Can I convert a whole thread or mailbox (.mbox, .pst) at once?
5.a: The tool reads individual message files only, one email per PDF. It doesn't open .mbox or .pst mailboxes, so export the messages you need as separate .eml or .msg files first; you can then drop them all in together and get a ZIP of PDFs.

6.q: Are links in the email clickable in the PDF?
6.a: Web and mailto links are re-created as clickable links wherever the link text can be matched on the page. Very short link text (three characters or fewer) isn't matched, so those particular links appear as plain text.

7.q: What is the converted email's PDF named?
7.a: A single email becomes a PDF with the same base name as the .eml or .msg file. Several emails are packaged into emails-converted.zip with one PDF per message.

8.q: Does converting an email trigger tracking pixels or contact the sender's server?
8.a: No. The message is parsed and rendered entirely in your browser, and no remote images, scripts, or stylesheets referenced by the email are fetched. Open-tracking pixels never fire, and the email's contents never leave your device.

1.q: Will the PDF keep the formatting, images, and fonts from my EPUB?
1.a: Text, images, tables, and embedded fonts carry over. Because the reflowable book is laid out into fixed pages, the page breaks won't match what you see in an ebook reader. For heavily styled EPUBs, check the first few pages of the output to confirm the layout.

2.q: Can I convert a DRM-protected EPUB from Kindle, Apple Books, or Kobo?
2.a: No. The tool reads the EPUB file directly and doesn't remove DRM, so protected books fail to convert. It works with DRM-free EPUB files.

3.q: Does it support both EPUB 2 and EPUB 3?
3.a: Yes, both versions convert. EPUB 3 extras such as embedded audio and video have no PDF equivalent and are dropped, while the text, images, and tables are kept.

4.q: Can I convert several EPUB files at once?
4.a: Yes. Add multiple files and click Convert to PDF; the results download as epub-converted.zip with one PDF per book. A single file downloads directly as a PDF with the same base name.

5.q: Can I choose the page size, margins, or font size?
5.a: Not in this tool. There are no settings; the PyMuPDF engine renders the book with its default layout into standard page dimensions.

6.q: Is the text in the converted PDF selectable and searchable?
6.a: Yes. The EPUB text is written into the PDF as real text rather than page images, so you can search, select, copy, highlight, and annotate it in any PDF reader.

7.q: Is my ebook uploaded to a server for conversion?
7.a: No. The PyMuPDF engine loads into your browser as WebAssembly and renders the book there, so the EPUB never leaves your device. Large books with many images just take a little longer on slower machines.

8.q: Why does the first conversion take longer than later ones?
8.a: On the first run the browser downloads the PyMuPDF engine before it can start. After that the engine stays loaded, so converting more books in the same session starts right away.

1.q: Which spreadsheet formats can I convert to PDF?
1.a: The tool accepts .xlsx and .xls Excel workbooks, OpenDocument .ods files from LibreOffice Calc, and .csv files. You can mix formats in the same batch and convert them all at once.

2.q: Does it convert all sheets in the workbook or just the first one?
2.a: All sheets are included in the PDF. The LibreOffice engine follows each sheet's own page setup, print area, and scaling, so Print Preview in Excel is a good guide to what you'll get.

3.q: Will formulas and charts survive the conversion?
3.a: Charts are rendered into the PDF, and formulas appear as their computed values rather than the formula text. Cell formatting such as fills, borders, fonts, and number formats is preserved.

4.q: How do I stop a wide spreadsheet from being cut across several pages?
4.a: There are no layout options in the tool itself, so set the orientation, print area, and fit-to-width scaling in Excel or LibreOffice Calc before uploading. The converter reads those settings from the file and lays out the PDF accordingly.

5.q: Why does the first conversion take a while to start?
5.a: The browser-based LibreOffice engine is downloaded the first time you convert, which can take a moment on a slow connection. After that it stays cached for the session, so further conversions start right away.

6.q: What do I get when I convert several spreadsheets at once?
6.a: One file downloads directly as a PDF with the same name as the spreadsheet. Two or more files are bundled into excel-converted.zip with one PDF per spreadsheet.

7.q: Should I use Excel to PDF or CSV to PDF for a .csv file?
7.a: Excel to PDF runs a CSV through the full LibreOffice layout engine, which is heavier but handles long rows and print settings the way a spreadsheet would. [0]CSV to PDF[/0] is a lighter, faster option for plain tabular data without formatting.

8.q: Is my spreadsheet uploaded to a server for conversion?
8.a: No. The LibreOffice engine runs inside your browser through WebAssembly, so the workbook is opened, rendered, and saved as a PDF on your own device. Financial data and personal records never leave your computer.

1.q: What counts as an attachment in a PDF?
1.a: Files embedded inside the PDF, either at the document level (the paperclip panel in Acrobat) or attached to a specific page as a file attachment annotation. Images drawn on the page, fonts, and form data are not attachments; for pictures use [0]Extract Images[/0].

2.q: Why does it say the PDF has no attachments?
2.a: It means cpdf found no embedded files at either the document or page level. Pictures on the page, hyperlinks to external files, and form field data can look like attachments in a viewer but aren't stored as embedded files, so there is nothing to extract.

3.q: How are the extracted files named?
3.a: Each file keeps the name it was embedded with. Attachments tied to a specific page get the PDF's name and page number added as a prefix, and if two attachments share a name the second gets a _1 suffix so nothing is overwritten inside the ZIP.

4.q: Can I extract attachments from several PDFs at once?
4.a: Upload as many PDFs as you like and click Extract Attachments once. Everything found across all of them is placed in one extracted-attachments.zip, and the status message reports the total count and combined size.

5.q: What file types can be extracted?
5.a: Anything that was embedded: spreadsheets, XML data files, images, ZIP archives, other PDFs, and so on. The tool copies the bytes out exactly as they were stored and doesn't convert or open them.

6.q: Can I extract attachments from a password-protected PDF?
6.a: Encrypted PDFs prompt for their password when loaded, and extraction then runs on the decrypted copy held in memory. Without the correct password the embedded files can't be read.

7.q: Can I view or delete individual attachments instead of extracting all of them?
7.a: This tool extracts everything in one pass. To inspect, remove, or replace individual attachments inside the PDF use [0]Edit Attachments[/0], and to embed new ones use Add Attachments.

8.q: Are the embedded files uploaded during extraction?
8.a: No. The PDFs are parsed by a WebAssembly build of cpdf in a background worker in your browser, the ZIP is assembled locally, and the download comes straight from your device. Attachments often contain source data, so this keeps them off any server.

1.q: What format are the extracted images saved in?
1.a: Each image comes out in the format it's stored in inside the PDF, most often JPEG or PNG, with no re-encoding. Files are numbered in the order they're found, for example image_1.jpg and image_2.png, and Download All packs them into extracted-images.zip.

2.q: Why does the tool say no images were found?
2.a: It only pulls out embedded raster images. If the graphics are vector drawings, charts, or text drawn as paths, there's nothing to extract, and you'd need to render the page as a picture with [0]PDF to PNG[/0] instead.

3.q: Will I get the original full-resolution images?
3.a: You get the image data exactly as it's embedded, at its stored resolution rather than the size it appears on the page. If whoever made the PDF downsampled the images before embedding them, that lower resolution is all that exists in the file.

4.q: Can I extract images from a scanned PDF?
4.a: A scanned PDF stores each page as one large image, so you'll get one full-page picture per page rather than the individual photos or figures on it. Crop what you need from those page images afterward.

5.q: Why do I get duplicate images?
5.a: Images are collected page by page, so a logo or header graphic that's reused on many pages is extracted once for every page it appears on. Keep the first copy and discard the rest.

6.q: Can I extract images from several PDFs at once?
6.a: Upload as many PDFs as you want and click Extract once. Images from all the files are numbered continuously and shown in a single grid, and Download All puts everything into one ZIP.

7.q: Can I choose which images or pages to extract?
7.a: There are no page or selection options; every embedded image on every page is extracted. You can still save only the ones you want from the preview grid, since each thumbnail has its own download button.

8.q: Are my PDF's images uploaded during extraction?
8.a: No. The PDF is opened by a PyMuPDF engine running as WebAssembly inside your browser, and the images are pulled out of the file in memory on your device. The preview grid, the individual downloads, and the ZIP are all generated locally.

1.q: Can I choose which pages to extract?
1.a: Yes. Type page numbers and ranges separated by commas, such as 2, 4-6, 9, and only those pages are pulled out. Numbering starts at 1, and the total page count is shown next to the file so you can check the range before extracting.

2.q: Do the extracted pages come as one PDF or separate files?
2.a: Separate files. Each selected page becomes its own single-page PDF named like report_page_4.pdf, and they download together in a ZIP called report_extracted_pages.zip. To end up with one PDF that contains only certain pages, use [0]Delete Pages[/0] to remove the rest instead.

3.q: Does extracting keep the original quality?
3.a: Yes. Pages are copied, not re-rendered, so text, images, fonts, and vector graphics are unchanged from the source, and text stays selectable and searchable.

4.q: Are bookmarks, links, and annotations preserved?
4.a: Comments, highlights, and other annotations on the page travel with it. Bookmarks are not carried over, since each output is a new file built from the copied page, and links that jump to other pages of the original have nothing to point at.

5.q: Can I extract the same page more than once or in a different order?
5.a: Each page appears once in the ZIP no matter how often it's listed, and the files are named by their original page numbers rather than the order you typed. Use [0]Organize PDF[/0] if you need duplicates or a custom order inside a single document.

6.q: Can I extract pages from a password-protected PDF?
6.a: The tool prompts for the password when the file is loaded, then extracts normally. The extracted files are new PDFs without the password.

7.q: Is my PDF uploaded when I extract pages from it?
7.a: No. The document is opened and the pages are copied in your browser, and the ZIP is built locally, so nothing is transmitted. A 500-page file only takes as long as your own machine needs to copy the selected pages.

8.q: Can I extract hundreds of pages at once?
8.a: There's no hard limit, but every extracted page becomes a separate PDF inside the ZIP, so a large selection means many small files and more memory use in the browser tab. For cutting a whole document into chunks, [0]Split PDF[/0] is the better fit.

1.q: Which output format should I choose?
1.a: CSV opens in Excel, Google Sheets, or any database import. JSON gives an array of rows, each an array of cell strings, for scripts and APIs. Markdown gives a pipe table you can paste into GitHub, a wiki, or documentation.

2.q: What do I get when the PDF contains several tables?
2.a: Each table is saved as its own file, named like table_1_page3.csv, and all of them are bundled into filename_tables.zip. A single table downloads directly as filename_table.csv, .json, or .md. If you'd rather have every table in one file, use [0]PDF to CSV[/0].

3.q: Why does it say no tables were found?
3.a: Detection works on the document's text layer. Scanned PDFs contain only an image, so run them through [0]OCR PDF[/0] first. Text that only looks like a table because of spacing, with no table structure, may also go undetected.

4.q: A table continues over several pages. Will it come out as one file?
4.a: No. Each page is scanned separately, so a table that spans pages is exported as one file per page, each with the page number in its name. Join the pieces in a spreadsheet after extraction.

5.q: Can I extract tables from only some pages?
5.a: The whole document is always scanned, though the page number in each filename tells you where a table came from. To limit the scan, save the pages you need first with [0]Extract Pages[/0] and run this tool on the smaller file.

6.q: Does the CSV handle commas and line breaks inside cells?
6.a: Yes. Cells containing commas, quotes, or newlines are wrapped in double quotes with inner quotes doubled, so spreadsheet software reads them correctly. Empty cells are written as empty fields.

7.q: Can tables be extracted from a password-protected PDF?
7.a: If the file needs a password to open, you're asked for it before extraction starts, and the tables are read from a decrypted copy held in memory.

8.q: Is the PDF uploaded for table detection?
8.a: No. The detection engine (PyMuPDF compiled to WebAssembly) is downloaded from a CDN the first time you use it, then runs inside your browser. Your PDF stays on your device.

1.q: What is an FB2 file?
1.a: FB2 is the FictionBook 2 ebook format, an XML-based format that is common in Russia and Eastern Europe. It stores the book's text, chapter structure, and any embedded images in a single file, but many readers and phones outside that region can't open it, which is why converting to PDF helps.

2.q: Does the conversion keep chapters, formatting, and images?
2.a: Chapter breaks, basic text formatting, and images embedded in the FB2 file are all carried into the PDF. The PyMuPDF engine reads the XML structure directly, so nothing needs to be configured.

3.q: Can I convert an .fb2.zip file?
3.a: Not directly. The tool only accepts plain .fb2 files, so extract the archive first and upload the .fb2 inside it.

4.q: Can I convert several FB2 books at once?
4.a: Select or drop as many files as you like and click Convert to PDF. A single book downloads as a PDF with the same name, while several are packed into fb2-converted.zip with one PDF per book.

5.q: Can I change the page size or font before converting?
5.a: No. There are no layout options in this converter; the engine paginates the book with its default page size and typography. If you need a different page size afterward, run the result through [0]Fix Page Size[/0].

6.q: Will Russian or other Cyrillic text convert correctly?
6.a: FB2 files are Unicode XML and the converter renders Unicode text, so Cyrillic books convert with their original characters intact. The text stays selectable and searchable in the PDF.

7.q: Is my ebook uploaded during conversion?
7.a: No. The FB2 file is parsed and laid out by a PDF engine running in your browser, and only the finished PDF is saved to your device. Nothing is sent to a server, so the conversion also works for drafts and personal documents.

8.q: Why does the PDF have a different number of pages than my e-reader shows?
8.a: FB2 is a reflowable format, so page counts depend on screen size and font settings in each reader. The PDF fixes the layout at conversion time, which usually produces a different, and now permanent, page count.

1.q: What's the difference between Fit and Fill when resizing pages?
1.a: Fit scales each page until the whole page sits inside the target size, centers it, and pads any leftover space with the background color. Fill scales until the target is completely covered, which crops whatever spills past the edges. Use Fit when losing content isn't acceptable and Fill when you'd rather have edge-to-edge pages.

2.q: Can I convert a Letter document to A4 without distorting it?
2.a: Choose A4 as the target and keep Fit. Content is scaled proportionally, never stretched, so a Letter page ends up slightly narrower on A4 with a thin band of background color at the top and bottom. [0]Page Dimensions[/0] will confirm every page matches afterward.

3.q: What does the Auto orientation option do?
3.a: Auto looks at each page individually and keeps landscape pages landscape and portrait pages portrait, turning the target size to match. Portrait or Landscape forces every page into that orientation and scales the content to fit the new shape.

4.q: Can I set a custom page size?
4.a: Choose Custom as the target and enter the width and height in inches or millimeters, down to a hundredth of a unit. This covers trim sizes that aren't in the preset list, such as 6 x 9 inch book pages.

5.q: Does this keep the text selectable, or does it turn pages into images?
5.a: Pages are redrawn as vector content in a new document, so text stays sharp and selectable and nothing is rasterized. What doesn't carry over: annotations, form fields, links, and bookmarks, because only the page appearance is copied. Run [0]Flatten PDF[/0] first if filled-in form values need to survive.

6.q: My pages are almost Letter size but not quite. Will this fix them?
6.a: Yes. Pick Letter and Fit; a page that is 8.49 by 11.02 inches is scaled by a fraction of a percent to exactly 8.5 by 11, which is invisible to the eye but satisfies print shops and document systems that reject off-size pages.

7.q: What is the background color used for?
7.a: It fills the margins that Fit mode adds when the source page has a different shape than the target. White is the default; pick a dark color when your pages have dark backgrounds so the padding doesn't stand out.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded to fix the page sizes?
8.a: No. The resizing is done by a PDF library running in your browser, and the new file is assembled on your device. Nothing is sent anywhere.

1.q: What does flattening a PDF actually do?
1.a: It merges interactive elements into the page content: form fields, checkboxes, radio buttons, dropdowns, signature fields, comments, highlights, strikethroughs, sticky notes, stamps, and ink marks. The page looks the same afterward, but nothing can be edited, moved, or deleted.

2.q: Will the text still be selectable and searchable after flattening?
2.a: Yes, flattening doesn't turn pages into images. Regular text, images, bookmarks, and page dimensions are untouched; only form fields and annotations become static page content. If you want every page rasterized, use [0]Rasterize PDF[/0] instead.

3.q: I filled out a form and want to lock the answers. Is this the right tool?
3.a: Yes. Flatten the completed form and the values you entered become part of the page, so recipients can't change them. Do it only after you're finished, because there's no way to unflatten a PDF.

4.q: Why does it say no form was found?
4.a: That appears when the PDF has annotations but no form fields. It isn't an error; the annotations are still flattened and the file downloads normally.

5.q: Do hyperlinks and comments survive flattening?
5.a: Comments, highlights, and other markup are burned into the page and stay visible, but they lose their pop-up notes and can't be edited. Links are annotations too, so a clickable link may stop working even though its text remains on the page.

6.q: Can I flatten several PDFs at once?
6.a: Yes. Upload multiple files and click Flatten PDF; you get flattened_pdfs.zip with one file per PDF. A single file downloads directly with "flattened_" added to the front of its name.

7.q: Should I flatten before or after signing?
7.a: Before. Flatten first so form values and annotations can't be altered, then sign. Flattening rewrites page content, so doing it after a [0]digital signature[/0] makes readers report the document as changed.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded to flatten it?
8.a: No. Flattening runs with pdf-lib inside your browser, so the file and whatever you typed into the form stay on your device.

1.q: What does converting fonts to outlines do to a PDF?
1.a: Every character of text is replaced by a vector path that draws the same shape, and the output no longer references any font. It renders the same on any device or printer, even ones without the original typeface installed.

2.q: When should I outline fonts before printing?
2.a: Print shops often ask for outlined fonts to avoid font substitution or licensing problems on their equipment. Do it as the last step, after all text edits are finished, because the text can't be edited afterward.

3.q: Can I still select, search, or copy text after outlining?
3.a: No. Outlined text is just shapes, so selection, Ctrl+F search, copy and paste, and screen reader access all stop working. Keep the original PDF for anything that needs live text.

4.q: Can I convert outlines back to editable text?
4.a: No, the conversion is one-way. If you have lost the original, running [0]OCR[/0] on the outlined file adds a recognized text layer for searching, but it won't restore the original fonts or editable text.

5.q: Why is my PDF larger after outlining fonts?
5.a: Each character is stored as a bezier path instead of a short reference into a font program, and a page of body text can contain thousands of them. The file often grows noticeably; run it through [0]Compress PDF[/0] afterward if size matters.

6.q: Does outlining change how the document looks?
6.a: Fonts embedded in the PDF are traced exactly, so the appearance stays the same. If a font isn't embedded, Ghostscript substitutes a similar one before outlining, so check the result when a document relies on system fonts.

7.q: Can I outline fonts in several PDFs at once?
7.a: Yes. Upload multiple PDFs and convert them together; one file downloads as a PDF, and several download as outlined_pdfs.zip with one entry per input.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded during the font conversion?
8.a: No. Ghostscript runs as WebAssembly inside your browser, so the file is processed on your device and the outlined copy is written locally without any upload.

1.q: Can I add fillable fields to a PDF I already have?
1.a: Upload the PDF and its pages appear in the editor; pick a field type from the toolbar and click on the page to place it, then drag or resize it as needed. If the PDF already has form fields, they're detected and loaded so you can move, edit, or delete them alongside the new ones.

2.q: Can I make a form from scratch without an existing PDF?
2.a: Click Create Blank PDF and choose Letter, A4, A5, Legal, Tabloid, A3, or custom dimensions in points. Use Add Page for multi-page forms.

3.q: Which field types are available?
3.a: Text (single line, multi-line, or divided into comb boxes), checkbox, radio button groups, dropdown, list box, push button, signature, date, image, and barcode. Each field has a properties panel for name, default value, font size, text color, alignment, tooltip, and required or read-only flags. Signature fields are standard AcroForm signature fields, which only appear in viewers that support signing.

4.q: How do radio buttons get grouped so only one can be selected?
4.a: Every radio field has a group name, RadioGroup1 by default. Fields that share the same group name become one mutually exclusive set, so give each question its own group name and set a distinct export value on each option.

5.q: Can a button show or hide another field, or reset the form?
5.a: Button actions include Reset Form, Print Form, Open URL, Run JavaScript, and Show/Hide Field, which targets another field and can show, hide, or toggle it. They're stored as standard PDF actions, so they run in Acrobat and other viewers that support form scripting.

6.q: How does the date field work?
6.a: It's a text field with a date format attached, mm/dd/yyyy by default or a custom pattern such as dd/mm/yyyy. Viewers that support AcroForm JavaScript validate the typed value and format it; simpler viewers treat it as ordinary text.

7.q: Are barcodes and images real form fields?
7.a: A barcode (QR Code, Code 128, Code 39, EAN-13, UPC-A, DataMatrix, or PDF417) is generated from the value you enter and drawn onto the page as a fixed image, so the person filling the form can't change it. The image field is a button that lets the user pick a picture from their computer, which works in Acrobat and other viewers that support image import.

8.q: Is the form or the uploaded PDF stored on a server?
8.a: No. The editor runs in your browser, the fields are written into the PDF with pdf-lib on your device, and Download PDF Form saves the result locally under the original filename. You can test the result in [0]PDF Form Filler[/0].

1.q: How do I fill out a PDF form that won't let me type in it?
1.a: Upload the PDF and it opens in an embedded viewer that turns the form fields into live inputs, so you can type into text boxes, tick checkboxes, and pick from dropdowns and radio buttons. If nothing becomes editable, the document has no real form fields; add some with [0]Create PDF Form[/0] first.

2.q: What is an XFA form and can I fill one here?
2.a: XFA is an older XML-based form format that Chrome and most online tools can't render, which is why those forms show up as blank pages elsewhere. This form filler and Firefox both support XFA, so you can fill and save those forms here.

3.q: How do I save the filled form?
3.a: Click Save & Download Filled Form and the viewer writes your entries into the PDF's form fields and downloads the file. The values are stored in the fields themselves, so they show up in other PDF viewers, not just this one.

4.q: Can I sign the form after filling it in?
4.a: This tool fills fields only. Download the filled PDF, then open it in [0]Sign PDF[/0] to add your signature where the form expects one.

5.q: Can someone else edit my answers after I send the filled form?
5.a: The fields stay editable in the downloaded file, so a recipient could change them. To lock the answers in place, run the filled PDF through [0]Flatten PDF[/0], which turns the fields into fixed page content.

6.q: Can I save a partially completed form and finish it later?
6.a: Download the form with whatever you've filled in so far; the values are kept in the fields. Upload that same file again later and the viewer shows your earlier entries ready to continue.

7.q: Does the form filler work with password-protected forms?
7.a: If the PDF requires a password to open, the tool prompts for it before loading the form. The downloaded copy is saved without that password, so protect it again with [0]Protect PDF[/0] if the form needs to stay locked.

8.q: Is the information I type into the form sent anywhere?
8.a: No. The form is rendered by a PDF.js viewer embedded in the page, your entries are held in that viewer's memory, and the completed PDF is written and downloaded on your device. Nothing you type is transmitted, which is the point when the form holds tax, medical, or ID details.

1.q: How do I add Page X of Y to every page?
1.a: Type Page {page} of {total} in any of the six fields, usually Footer Center. {page} is replaced with that page's number and {total} with the page count, so a 12-page file gets Page 1 of 12 through Page 12 of 12.

2.q: Can I put different text on the left, center, and right?
2.a: Yes. There are six independent fields: header left, center, and right, plus footer left, center, and right. Fill only the ones you need, for example a company name at header left, the date at header right, and a confidentiality notice at footer center; empty fields are skipped.

3.q: Can I apply the header only to certain pages?
3.a: Yes. Enter a range like 1-3, 5 in the Page Range field and only those pages get the text; leave it empty to cover every page. The {page} value still reflects the real page number, so page 5 reads 5 even when pages 1 through 4 were skipped.

4.q: What font and size does it use?
4.a: Helvetica, at any size from 6 to 24 points (10 by default), in the color you pick. Because it uses the built-in PDF Helvetica, the text is limited to Latin characters; accented letters work, but scripts such as Cyrillic, Arabic, or Chinese don't.

5.q: Will it replace the header my document already has?
5.a: No. The text is drawn on top of the existing page content about 40 points (a bit over half an inch) from the edge, so if a page already has a running header in that spot the two will overlap. Check the result and pick a different position if they collide.

6.q: Is the header text selectable and searchable afterward?
6.a: Yes. It's added as real text rather than an image, so it can be selected, searched, and copied, and it stays sharp when printed at any size.

7.q: Is my document uploaded to add a header and footer?
7.a: No. The text is written into the PDF by your browser and the finished file is saved under its original name; the document never leaves your device.

8.q: Can I add page numbers without any other text?
8.a: Yes, put {page} alone in a field. [0]Page Numbers[/0] does the same job with a dedicated layout and font sizes up to 72 points, and Add Page Labels handles Roman numerals in the viewer's page display.

1.q: Does it work with HEIF files as well as HEIC?
1.a: Yes. Both .heic and .heif extensions are accepted, including HEIF screenshots and photos from iPhones and iPads. Files with any other extension are skipped when you add them.

2.q: Why is the PDF so much larger than my HEIC photos?
2.a: HEIC is heavily compressed, and the converter decodes each photo to a lossless PNG before placing it in the PDF at full resolution, so a 12 megapixel photo can take tens of megabytes. Run the result through [0]Compress PDF[/0] if you need a smaller file.

3.q: How are the photos arranged, and what size are the pages?
3.a: Each photo becomes its own page in the order listed. The page is sized to the photo's pixel dimensions at one point per pixel, so a 4032 by 3024 photo produces a page about 56 by 42 inches, which viewers and printers scale to fit.

4.q: Is the GPS location or other EXIF data kept in the PDF?
4.a: No. The decoded image is stored as plain pixels, so location, camera model, and capture date from the phone aren't carried into the PDF.

5.q: What about burst shots or HEIC files that contain several images?
5.a: Only the first image in the container is converted; additional frames stored in the same file are ignored. For a Live Photo, the still image is used and the video part, which lives in a separate .mov file, isn't involved.

6.q: Why does the first HEIC file take longer to convert?
6.a: The HEIC decoder is libheif compiled to WebAssembly and loads in the browser when first needed. Later conversions in the same session skip that step, though large photos still take a few seconds each to decode.

7.q: Can I combine HEIC photos with JPG or PNG images in one PDF?
7.a: Not here; this tool accepts only HEIC and HEIF. [0]Images to PDF[/0] accepts HEIC alongside JPG, PNG, WebP, and other formats in a single batch.

8.q: Are my photos uploaded to convert them?
8.a: No. Decoding and PDF creation happen in your browser, so private photos never leave your phone or computer.

1.q: Which image formats can I combine into a PDF?
1.a: JPG, JPEG, PNG, BMP, GIF, TIFF, PNM, PGM, PBM, PPM, PAM, JXR, JPX, JP2, PSD, SVG, HEIC, HEIF, and WebP. You can mix formats in one batch, and each image becomes its own page in a single images_to_pdf.pdf file.

2.q: What do the High, Medium, and Low quality settings change?
2.a: High Quality embeds your images as they are, with no resizing or re-encoding. Medium re-encodes each image as a JPEG at 75% quality and caps the longest side at 2500 pixels, and Low uses 50% quality with a 1500 pixel cap, which gives much smaller files for email.

3.q: Will transparent PNGs keep their transparency?
3.a: Only at High Quality, where files are embedded untouched. Medium and Low convert every image to JPEG, which has no alpha channel, so transparent areas are flattened rather than kept.

4.q: How do I control the page order?
4.a: Pages follow the order of the file list, which is the order you selected or dropped the images. To change it, remove an image with the trash icon and add it again with Add More Files so it goes to the end.

5.q: Can I set the page size to A4 or Letter?
5.a: Not in this tool. Each page takes the dimensions of its image, so a tall phone photo produces a tall page and a landscape scan a wide one. If you need uniform paper sizes afterward, run the result through [0]Fix Page Size[/0].

6.q: Do iPhone HEIC photos need converting first?
6.a: No. HEIC and HEIF files are decoded in the browser and turned into PNG before they're embedded, and WebP is handled the same way. This happens automatically and doesn't need an extra step.

7.q: Are my photos uploaded anywhere?
7.a: No. Decoding, compression, and PDF assembly all run in your browser, so the images never leave your device. Large batches of full-resolution photos take longer and use more memory on your machine because of that.

8.q: Is there a separate tool if all my images are JPGs?
8.a: [0]JPG to PDF[/0] gives the same result with a simpler interface, and there are dedicated PNG, HEIC, WebP, and TIFF converters as well. This tool is the one to reach for when your files are in mixed or less common formats such as PSD, JXR, or PNM.

1.q: What happens to photos and colored graphics when I invert a PDF?
1.a: Every pixel is flipped to its complementary value, so photos look like film negatives and brand colors shift (blue turns orange, red turns cyan). The tool suits text-heavy documents where you want light text on a dark page; for brightness or contrast changes without inverting images, use [0]Adjust Colors[/0].

2.q: Will I still be able to select or search text after inverting?
2.a: No. Each page is rendered as an image, inverted, and rebuilt as an image-only PDF, so the text layer is gone. If you need searchable text again, run the inverted file through [0]OCR PDF[/0].

3.q: Does the inverted PDF look blurry?
3.a: Pages are rendered at 1.5x scale, roughly 108 dots per inch. That's sharp on a screen at normal zoom, which is where dark-mode reading happens, but it can look soft if you print the file or zoom in far.

4.q: Why is the output file larger than the original?
4.a: The inverted pages are stored as full-page PNG images instead of text and vector drawings, which often takes more space. For a smaller file, pass the result through [0]Compress PDF[/0].

5.q: Are hyperlinks, bookmarks, and form fields kept?
5.a: No. Because the output is a fresh image-based document, interactive elements such as links, form fields, comments, and bookmarks are not carried over. Keep the original if you need them.

6.q: Can I invert only some pages?
6.a: Not with this tool; it processes every page. If you only want a few pages inverted, separate them first with [0]Split PDF[/0], invert that part, and merge the pieces back together.

7.q: Does it work on scanned documents?
7.a: Yes. Scans are already images, so they invert cleanly, and it can rescue a scan captured as a negative or with reversed exposure. Grayscale scans keep their gray levels, just reversed.

8.q: Is my document uploaded to be inverted?
8.a: No. Rendering and pixel inversion happen on a canvas in your browser, and the new PDF is assembled locally. Nothing leaves your computer, and there's no server queue, so the speed depends only on your device.

1.q: Can I combine multiple JPG files into one PDF?
1.a: Yes. Select or drag in as many JPGs as you need and each image becomes its own full-size page in a single file named from_jpgs.pdf. Pages follow the order of the file list, so remove and re-add a file if you want it in a different spot.

2.q: What does the JPG quality setting actually change?
2.a: High Quality passes your original JPEG data through unchanged. Medium (the default) re-encodes each image at 75% JPEG quality and scales the longest side down to 2500 pixels if it's larger; Low uses 50% quality and a 1500 pixel limit. For phone photos, Medium is usually 40 to 60% smaller than High with no visible difference on screen.

3.q: Does it support JPEG 2000 (.jp2 and .jpx) files?
3.a: Yes. JPEG 2000 files are accepted alongside .jpg and .jpeg, which is useful for medical imaging and geospatial data. If your browser can't decode a JPEG 2000 file for recompression, the original file is embedded as is, whichever quality you chose.

4.q: What page size will my JPGs get in the PDF?
4.a: Each image is placed as a full-size page with the image's own proportions, so portrait photos give portrait pages and landscape scans give landscape pages. There's no fixed A4 or Letter option in this tool.

5.q: Which quality setting is best for scanned documents?
5.a: Medium works for most scans that will be read on screen or printed at normal size, since 2500 pixels on the long side keeps text crisp. Choose High if the scans must stay at full resolution for OCR or archiving, and Low for quick sharing where size matters more than detail.

6.q: Why were some of my files skipped?
6.a: Only .jpg, .jpeg, .jp2, and .jpx files are accepted, so PNG, HEIC, WebP, and other formats are left out with a notice. Use the matching converter for those, or [0]Image to PDF[/0] for a mixed set of formats.

7.q: Can I make the PDF on my phone?
7.a: Yes. The tool runs in a mobile browser; tap the upload area to pick photos from your camera roll. Medium quality keeps the resulting PDF a reasonable size for a large set of photos.

8.q: Are my photos uploaded to create the PDF?
8.a: No. Recompression happens on a canvas in your browser and the PDF is assembled by the PyMuPDF engine running as WebAssembly, so the photos never leave your device.

1.q: Can I convert any JSON file into a PDF with this tool?
1.a: No. It only rebuilds PDFs from JSON files created by BentoPDF's [0]PDF to JSON[/0] tool, which stores the document's full internal structure. A JSON export from an API, a database, or a config file will fail with an error.

2.q: How do I turn API data or a config file into a readable PDF instead?
2.a: Paste or upload the JSON as plain text in [0]Text to PDF[/0], which lays it out as formatted text on pages. JSON to PDF is only for round-tripping documents that started out as PDFs.

3.q: Will the rebuilt PDF match the original?
3.a: The JSON produced by PDF to JSON captures the document's objects, so converting it back reproduces the pages, text, and images of the source. Converting back and comparing is also a quick way to confirm that an export captured everything.

4.q: What is the output when I convert multiple JSON files?
4.a: Every conversion downloads as jsons-to-pdf.zip, even for a single file. Inside, each PDF carries the name of its source JSON, so report.json becomes report.pdf.

5.q: Can I edit the JSON before converting it back?
5.a: Yes, as long as the structure stays valid for the CPDF engine. Programmatic changes to the JSON, such as edited metadata or text objects, are rebuilt into the PDF; a malformed edit produces a conversion error.

6.q: Why does the tool say the CPDF engine isn't available?
6.a: The conversion depends on the CPDF WebAssembly build. On bentopdf.com it's included, but a self-hosted copy needs the CPDF WASM files configured in [0]WASM settings[/0] before this tool will run.

7.q: Is my JSON file uploaded to a server?
7.a: No. The files are read in your browser and rebuilt into PDFs by a Web Worker running the CPDF engine locally, so nothing is transmitted and the page stays responsive during large conversions.

1.q: What does linearizing a PDF actually change?
1.a: QPDF rewrites the file so the objects needed for the first page come first, adds a linearization dictionary and hint tables, and rebuilds the cross-reference table. The pages, fonts, images, links, and form fields are unchanged; only the byte order inside the file is different.

2.q: Does this fix a PDF that shows Fast Web View: No in Acrobat?
2.a: Fast Web View is Acrobat's name for linearization, and running the file through this tool sets it to Yes. That holds only if you don't edit the PDF again afterward, because almost any later change, such as merging, adding pages, or resaving from most editors, removes the linearization.

3.q: Does linearizing make the file smaller?
3.a: No. It's a structural reorder, not compression, and the hint tables add a small amount, typically under 1 percent. To shrink the file, run [0]Compress PDF[/0] first and linearize last.

4.q: Will my web server or viewer actually load it faster?
4.a: Only if the server supports HTTP byte-range requests, which most static hosts and CDNs do. A viewer such as pdf.js or a browser's built-in viewer can then fetch the first page and start rendering while the rest downloads, instead of waiting for the whole file.

5.q: Why did I get a ZIP when I only uploaded one PDF?
5.a: The tool always packages its output as linearized-pdfs.zip, with each file inside renamed to linearized- followed by the original name. Unzip it to get the PDF.

6.q: What if a file fails to linearize?
6.a: The batch continues with the other files, and the completion message tells you how many succeeded and how many failed. Damaged files are the usual cause; run them through [0]Repair PDF[/0] and try again.

7.q: Are the PDFs uploaded to be optimized?
7.a: No. QPDF runs as WebAssembly inside your browser, reading and writing the files in memory on your device, and the ZIP is generated locally. Nothing is sent to a server even though the output is meant for web publishing.

1.q: How do I convert a Markdown file to PDF?
1.a: Click Upload and pick a .md, .markdown, or .txt file, or paste the text into the left pane, and the rendered preview appears on the right. Click Export PDF or press Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on a Mac), then choose Save as PDF as the destination in the print dialog that opens.

2.q: Can I change the page size or margins of the PDF?
2.a: Set those in the print dialog: choose Letter, A4, or another paper size, adjust the margins, and lower the scale if a wide table gets cut off. Turn off Headers and footers there too if you don't want the date and URL printed on each page.

3.q: Does it support code blocks, tables, and diagrams?
3.a: Fenced code blocks get syntax highlighting for JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Go, Rust, Java, C#, C++, SQL, Bash, YAML, JSON, HTML, and CSS, and standard pipe tables render as tables. Mermaid code blocks are drawn as flowcharts, sequence diagrams, and other chart types in both the preview and the PDF.

4.q: Which Markdown extensions work beyond the basics?
4.a: Task lists, footnotes, definition lists, abbreviations, subscript and superscript, ==highlight== and ++insert++ marks, emoji shortcodes like :smile:, and automatic linking of bare URLs. The settings dialog has switches for raw HTML, line breaks, autolinking, and typographic quotes.

5.q: Does the dark theme affect the exported PDF?
5.a: No. The theme toggle only changes the editor colors on screen; the print stylesheet forces a white background and dark text, so the PDF looks the same either way.

6.q: Can I add a table of contents to the PDF?
6.a: Put ${toc} on its own line where you want it and a table of contents is generated from your headings when the document renders. Headings also get anchor IDs, so in-document links to a heading work in the preview.

7.q: Can I include images in the PDF?
7.a: Use standard Markdown image syntax with a full image URL or a data URI and the image renders in the preview and prints into the PDF. Relative paths to files on your disk won't load, because the editor has no access to your local folders.

8.q: Is my Markdown text uploaded to a server to make the PDF?
8.a: No. The Markdown is rendered to HTML by markdown-it in your browser and the PDF is created by the browser's print function, so neither the text nor the finished PDF touches a server. Notes, drafts, and internal docs stay on your machine.

1.q: Does merging keep bookmarks?
1.a: Yes. The merge is done with the CoherentPDF engine, which carries each file's bookmarks into the combined document so the outline stays navigable. Page content and annotations are copied as they are.

2.q: Can I merge only some pages from each file?
2.a: Yes. In File Mode, type a range such as 1-3, 5 in the Pages box next to a file to include just those pages, or leave it blank for the whole file. In Page Mode every page from every file appears as a thumbnail you can drag into any sequence, including interleaving pages from different documents.

3.q: What order will the files be in?
3.a: The order shown in the list, top to bottom. Drag entries to rearrange them before merging, and use Add More Files to append documents without losing the arrangement you already have.

4.q: Why do page numbers look wrong in the merged PDF?
4.a: By default the merged file uses plain numbering from 1 to N. If the originals used page labels such as i, ii, iii or A-1, turn on Keep original page labels to preserve them, keeping in mind that two files with the same labels will produce duplicates. To print visible numbers on the pages themselves, use [0]Page Numbers[/0].

5.q: Why is the merged file so large?
5.a: Each file's fonts and images are copied as they are, so the result is roughly the combined size of the inputs, and when several files embed the same font each copy is kept. Check Remove duplicate fonts to fold identical fonts into one; for more savings, run the result through [0]Compress PDF[/0].

6.q: Can I merge PDFs that have different page sizes or orientations?
6.a: Yes. Pages keep their own size and rotation, so a landscape A3 drawing can follow a portrait Letter page without being scaled. For a uniform size afterward, run the merged file through [0]Fix Page Size[/0].

7.q: Are the PDFs uploaded to a server to be merged?
7.a: No. The files are combined inside your browser by the CoherentPDF WebAssembly module and the merged PDF is written to your downloads folder, so contracts and statements never leave your machine.

8.q: Can I merge password-protected PDFs?
8.a: If a file needs a password to open, the tool asks for it when you add the file and then merges the decrypted pages. The merged output has no password; add one afterward with [0]Protect PDF[/0] if needed.

1.q: Can I convert books bought from the Kindle store?
1.a: Only if they're DRM-free. Most Kindle store purchases carry DRM and the tool can't open them. Personal documents, public domain books, and titles from DRM-free stores convert normally.

2.q: Does it accept AZW, AZW3, or KFX files?
2.a: No. Only files with the .mobi extension are accepted. Convert other Kindle formats to MOBI or EPUB with another program first; EPUB files can then go through [0]EPUB to PDF[/0].

3.q: Will the page count match my Kindle's page numbers?
3.a: No. MOBI text reflows to fit whatever screen it's on, so the engine lays it out onto fixed-size pages of its own. PDF page numbers won't line up with Kindle locations, and there's no setting for page size or font size.

4.q: Are images and formatting preserved?
4.a: Headings, bold and italic text, lists, and embedded images carry over. The text stays real text rather than an image, so it's selectable and searchable in the PDF.

5.q: Can I convert more than one book at a time?
5.a: Yes. One file downloads as a PDF named after the book; several files are converted one after another and delivered as mobi-converted.zip with one PDF each.

6.q: Why did my conversion fail?
6.a: The usual cause is DRM. Corrupted downloads and files that were renamed to .mobi without actually being MOBI files also fail. If the same book opens in Calibre, converting it there to a fresh MOBI usually produces a file this tool can handle.

7.q: Is the ebook uploaded to a server?
7.a: No. The conversion engine (PyMuPDF compiled to WebAssembly) is downloaded from a CDN the first time you use it and then runs inside your browser, so the book itself never leaves your device.

1.q: How many pages can I put on one sheet?
1.a: Choose 2-up (1x2), 4-up (2x2), 9-up (3x3), or 16-up (4x4) from the Pages per Sheet menu. Pages are placed left to right and top to bottom in document order, and the last sheet has empty cells if the page count doesn't divide evenly.

2.q: What paper size and orientation will the output have?
2.a: Pick Letter, A4, Legal, or A3 for the output sheet and Portrait, Landscape, or Auto for orientation. Auto uses landscape for a 2-up layout of landscape pages and portrait for everything else.

3.q: Will my pages be stretched or cropped?
3.a: Neither. Each page is scaled proportionally to fit its cell and centered, so pages whose shape doesn't match the cell get some white space around them instead of being distorted.

4.q: Does the text stay sharp after N-up?
4.a: The original pages are embedded as vector content rather than converted to images, so text and line art stay crisp at any print size. In dense layouts like 16-up the text is still tiny on paper, which is a readability limit rather than a quality one.

5.q: Can I add margins or a border around each page?
5.a: Add Margins leaves a half-inch margin around the sheet and a small gap between cells, which helps when a printer can't print to the edge. Add Border draws a one point outline around each placed page in a color you pick.

6.q: How do I print 4 PowerPoint slides per page?
6.a: Export the slides to PDF first, or use [0]PowerPoint to PDF[/0], then upload that PDF here and choose 4-up. Landscape slides on a portrait sheet fit well in a 2x2 grid.

7.q: Is N-up the same as booklet printing?
7.a: No. N-up only reduces pages into a grid in reading order. A booklet needs pages reordered and paired so they fold into a book, which is what [0]PDF Booklet[/0] does.

8.q: Does the PDF get uploaded to make the N-up layout?
8.a: No. The new sheets are built in your browser with pdf-lib and downloaded under the original file name, so the document never leaves your device.

1.q: How do I know if my PDF needs OCR?
1.a: Open the file in any viewer and try to select a line of text. If nothing highlights or search finds no matches, the pages are just images (a scan or a photo) and OCR is what adds the missing text. A PDF that already has selectable text doesn't need this tool.

2.q: Which languages can it recognize?
2.a: Over 100 Tesseract language packs are listed, from English and Spanish to Arabic, Hindi, Japanese, and Chinese. Tick every language that appears in the document; the packs are loaded together so mixed-language pages are recognized in one pass. Some self-hosted deployments bundle a shorter list and say so above the language picker.

3.q: Does OCR change how my document looks?
3.a: No. The original pages are copied unchanged and an invisible text layer is drawn on top, positioned word by word to match the scan. You see the same image as before, but you can now search, select, and copy the text.

4.q: Which resolution setting should I use?
4.a: High (288 DPI) is the default and handles typical office documents. Drop to Standard (192 DPI) when speed matters or the file is long, and use Ultra (384 DPI) for small print, footnotes, or poor scans. Higher settings take noticeably longer since every page is rendered at that size before recognition.

5.q: What does the character whitelist do?
5.a: It restricts the output to a fixed set of characters, which cuts down on errors like a lowercase l being read as a 1. The Invoice preset allows only digits and the symbols $ . , / - # :, Numbers Only suits serial numbers or meter readings, and Custom lets you type your own set.

6.q: Can it read handwriting?
6.a: Not reliably. Tesseract is trained on printed text, so neat block capitals sometimes work but cursive mostly produces noise. Results are best on clean, well-lit printed pages; the Binarize option helps with faded or low-contrast scans, and [0]Deskew PDF[/0] straightens tilted ones first.

7.q: Can I get just the recognized text instead of a PDF?
7.a: Yes. When OCR finishes, the extracted text appears in a box where you can review it, copy it to the clipboard, or download it as ocr-text.txt. The searchable PDF download is separate, so you can take either or both.

8.q: Does OCR upload my scans to a server?
8.a: No. Tesseract runs as WebAssembly inside your browser; the only downloads are the OCR engine and the language packs you selected, fetched the first time they're needed. The scanned pages and the recognized text stay on your device.

1.q: Do I need LibreOffice installed to convert an ODG file?
1.a: No. A LibreOffice engine compiled to WebAssembly runs inside your browser, so you don't need LibreOffice, OpenOffice, or a plugin on your computer, and it works on any operating system.

2.q: Are the drawings kept as vectors or turned into images?
2.a: Shapes, connectors, lines, and text boxes stay as vectors in the PDF, so the drawing scales cleanly to any print size and the text remains selectable.

3.q: Does the PDF keep the original page size?
3.a: Yes. The page dimensions from the ODG file are preserved, including landscape and custom sizes, so a diagram laid out for A3 or Tabloid prints at that size.

4.q: Can I convert several ODG files at once?
4.a: Yes. Add multiple files and the results download as odg-to-pdf.zip, one PDF per drawing. A single file downloads directly with the same base name and a .pdf extension.

5.q: Why does the first ODG conversion take longer than the next ones?
5.a: On first use the browser downloads the LibreOffice engine, around 75 MB compressed, and starts it. Conversions later in the same session skip that step and finish much faster.

6.q: Will fonts look the same as in LibreOffice Draw?
6.a: The engine renders with the fonts bundled inside it rather than the fonts installed on your computer, so an unusual font may be replaced by a similar one. Check the output if the drawing depends on a specific typeface.

7.q: Does it work with files from Apache OpenOffice Draw?
7.a: Yes. Any .odg file works, including ones saved by OpenOffice Draw, since both programs use the same OpenDocument Graphics format.

8.q: Is my drawing uploaded anywhere?
8.a: No. The conversion runs entirely in your browser tab; the only download is the engine itself, and the ODG file never leaves your device.

1.q: Can I convert a Google Slides presentation to PDF with this tool?
1.a: Yes, if you first download it from Google Slides as an ODP file using File > Download > ODP Document. Upload that .odp here and each slide becomes one PDF page.

2.q: Are speaker notes included in the PDF?
2.a: No. Only the slides themselves are rendered, one per page. Export the notes separately from Impress or Google Slides if you need them alongside the slides.

3.q: What happens to animations and slide transitions?
3.a: They're dropped, since a PDF page is static. Text, images, shapes, and slide backgrounds all appear as they do on the slide, but nothing moves or fades.

4.q: Does the PDF keep the slide size and layout?
4.a: Each slide is rendered at its original dimensions, so a 16:9 deck produces wide pages and a 4:3 deck produces squarer ones. Content is placed where it sits in the presentation.

5.q: Can I convert PowerPoint files here too?
5.a: This tool only accepts .odp files. For .pptx and .ppt decks use [0]PowerPoint to PDF[/0], which runs on the same LibreOffice engine.

6.q: Why is the first ODP conversion slower than later ones?
6.a: The LibreOffice engine has to download the first time you use it in a session, which the notice on the page mentions. Later conversions reuse the cached engine and start immediately.

7.q: What do I get if I convert several presentations at once?
7.a: A single presentation downloads directly as a PDF. Several are bundled into odp-to-pdf.zip, with one PDF named after each source file.

8.q: Are my slides uploaded to a server during conversion?
8.a: No. The LibreOffice engine runs in your browser as WebAssembly, so the presentation is rendered and saved as a PDF on your own device. Unreleased decks and internal material stay local.

1.q: Does the PDF include every sheet in the workbook?
1.a: All sheets are included, in the order they appear in the workbook, following the print layout saved in the file. Hidden sheets and print ranges are handled the way LibreOffice Calc would handle them when printing.

2.q: Why does my wide spreadsheet get split across several pages?
2.a: The converter uses the page style stored in the ODS file, so columns that don't fit the page width continue on following pages, the same way Calc prints them. To keep a table on one page, set landscape orientation, a print scale, or narrower columns in Calc before converting.

3.q: Can I change page size or orientation during conversion?
3.a: There are no conversion settings; the PDF follows the paper size, orientation, margins, and scaling saved in the spreadsheet. Adjust those in Calc under Format and Page Style, save the file, and convert again.

4.q: Will charts, merged cells, and cell colors come through?
4.a: The conversion is done by LibreOffice itself running in your browser, so cell formatting, borders, merged cells, and embedded charts are rendered the way Calc would print them.

5.q: Can I convert a Google Sheets file?
5.a: Download the sheet from Google Sheets as OpenDocument (.ods) and upload that file. XLSX files aren't accepted here; use [0]Excel to PDF[/0] for those.

6.q: Why does the first ODS spreadsheet take longer to convert?
6.a: The LibreOffice engine is a large WebAssembly download that's fetched the first time you convert in a session, and the progress bar shows it loading. Once it's loaded, further conversions in the same tab start right away.

7.q: What is the output called when I convert several files?
7.a: One file downloads under the same name with a .pdf extension. Two or more are converted in sequence and packaged as ods-to-pdf.zip with one PDF per spreadsheet.

8.q: Is my spreadsheet uploaded to a LibreOffice server?
8.a: No. The conversion engine is a WebAssembly build of LibreOffice that runs in a worker inside your browser, so budgets, timesheets, and financial records stay on your computer for the whole process.

1.q: How do I convert an ODT file to PDF without LibreOffice installed?
1.a: Drop the .odt file on the page and click Convert to PDF. A build of LibreOffice compiled to WebAssembly loads inside your browser and does the conversion, so you don't need LibreOffice, OpenOffice, or Word on the computer.

2.q: Why is converting the first ODT file slower?
2.a: The LibreOffice engine is roughly 75 MB compressed and has to be downloaded and started the first time you convert in a session; a progress indicator shows the percentage. Once it's loaded, further conversions in the same session start right away.

3.q: Will my formatting, tables, and images be preserved?
3.a: The conversion uses LibreOffice's own PDF export, so styles, tables, images, and page layout come through the way Writer would print them. Documents with embedded OLE objects or fonts that aren't available may render slightly differently, so check one sample before converting a large batch.

4.q: Can I convert multiple ODT files at once?
4.a: Add as many .odt files as you like, remove any you don't want from the list, and convert them in one go. A single file downloads as a PDF named after the original; two or more arrive in odt-converted.zip with one PDF per file.

5.q: What about .docx, .doc, or .ott files?
5.a: This page accepts only .odt. Word documents go through [0]Word to PDF[/0], which uses the same engine, and an .ott template should be opened and saved as .odt before converting.

6.q: Will the PDF text be selectable and searchable?
6.a: The PDF is exported from the document's actual text rather than a picture of the page, so the text can be selected, copied, and searched in any viewer.

7.q: Does it work with ODT files from OpenOffice or other programs?
7.a: Any standard OpenDocument Text file is accepted regardless of which program saved it, including LibreOffice Writer, Apache OpenOffice, and other word processors that write .odt.

8.q: Is my ODT document uploaded to convert it?
8.a: No. The LibreOffice engine runs entirely inside your browser, so the .odt file is read and the PDF is written on your own device. That makes it usable for confidential contracts, theses, and anything else you'd rather not put on a conversion server.

1.q: How do I move a page to a different position?
1.a: Drag its thumbnail to the new spot in the grid; the page number labels update as you go. For a whole-document rearrangement, type the new order in the page order box, for example 3, 1, 2, 4, and click Apply.

2.q: What does the page order box expect?
2.a: A comma-separated list of the original page numbers in the order you want them, and it must mention every page exactly once. 3, 1, 2 for a three-page file works; 3, 1 (a page missing) or 1, 1, 2 (a repeat) is rejected. Use the duplicate and delete buttons for copies and removals.

3.q: Can I duplicate a page more than once?
3.a: Yes. Each click on the green duplicate button adds another copy right after the page, and every copy can then be dragged anywhere independently. This is handy for putting several blank copies of a form page in one file.

4.q: Can I delete pages here too?
4.a: Yes. Click the red delete button on a thumbnail to drop it from the output; the only rule is that the last remaining page can't be deleted. For removing many pages by range, [0]Delete Pages[/0] is quicker.

5.q: Does reordering pages keep my bookmarks?
5.a: Page content, images, and annotations on each page are kept. Bookmarks aren't, because the reorganized file is assembled fresh from copied pages, so a document with a navigation outline will lose it. Recreate it afterward with the [0]Bookmark[/0] tool if needed.

6.q: Is the quality of the pages affected?
6.a: No. Pages are copied as-is rather than re-rendered, so text stays selectable and images keep their original resolution. The output is saved under the same name as the original file.

7.q: Is my PDF uploaded while I rearrange its pages?
7.a: No. The thumbnails are rendered by your browser and the new file is assembled locally, so nothing is sent anywhere, even for large documents.

8.q: Can I organize pages from more than one PDF at once?
8.a: No, this tool works on a single file. To pull pages from several documents into one sequence, use [0]Merge PDF[/0] in Page Mode, which shows thumbnails from every file in one grid.

1.q: How do I apply the overlay to only some pages?
1.a: Type a range in the Apply to pages field using the base document's page numbers, for example 1-5, 8, 10-z, where z stands for the last page. Leave it empty to cover every page.

2.q: What happens when the two PDFs have different page counts?
2.a: With the loop option on, the overlay's pages repeat in order until every base page is covered, so a 2-page overlay on a 5-page document is applied as 1, 2, 1, 2, 1. With it off, pages are matched one to one and base pages beyond the overlay's length are left unchanged.

3.q: Do the page sizes need to match?
3.a: No. An overlay page larger than the base page is scaled down to fit and a smaller one is centered without being enlarged. There are no controls for position, scale, or opacity, so build the overlay PDF at the size and transparency you want before combining.

4.q: Does the base PDF stay searchable and editable?
4.a: Yes. The base document's text, links, form fields, and bookmarks are untouched; the overlay is added to each page as an extra drawing layer, and any text in it remains selectable too.

5.q: Are links, form fields, or comments from the overlay PDF copied over?
5.a: No. Only the visible page content of the overlay is used. Annotations on the overlay pages, including links, form fields, and comments, don't transfer to the result.

6.q: Which mode should I use for a letterhead?
6.a: Underlay, so the letterhead sits behind the page content, with the loop option on if the letterhead is a single page. For text or image watermarks with adjustable opacity, rotation, and placement, [0]Add Watermark[/0] gives more control.

7.q: Why does it fail on a password-protected PDF?
7.a: The tool doesn't ask for passwords. If either file needs a password to open, remove it first with the [0]password removal tool[/0], then apply the overlay to the copy without the password.

8.q: Do both PDFs get uploaded?
8.a: No. The overlay is applied by qpdf compiled to WebAssembly, which runs entirely in your browser, so neither the base document nor the overlay file leaves your device. The combined PDF downloads under the base document's filename.

1.q: How do I check whether my PDF is A4 or Letter?
1.a: Upload the file and the analysis runs immediately. The summary shows the total page count and how many distinct sizes appear, and the table lists each page's width and height next to the matched standard size, so a plain A4 or Letter document shows one size across all pages.

2.q: Which standard paper sizes does it recognize?
2.a: A3, A4, A5, Letter, Legal, and Tabloid, in either portrait or landscape, matched within one point of the official dimensions. Anything else is reported as Custom with its exact measurements.

3.q: What does the Mixed Sizes warning mean?
3.a: More than one width and height combination was found in the document, and the summary breaks down how many pages use each. A rotated page counts as a separate size from its upright twin, so a landscape A4 page in a portrait A4 file triggers the warning. To make everything uniform, use [0]Fix Page Size[/0].

4.q: Can I see the sizes in inches or millimeters instead of points?
4.a: Use the units menu to switch the whole table between points, inches, millimeters, and pixels. Pixels are calculated at 96 PPI, which matches how browsers and most screen tools treat PDF pages.

5.q: What does the Rotation column tell me?
5.a: It shows the rotation attribute stored on the page, in degrees. A page can look upright in a viewer while carrying a 90 or 270 degree rotation, which trips up some print and conversion workflows, and [0]Rotate PDF[/0] can normalize it.

6.q: Can I export the results?
6.a: Click Export to CSV to download page-dimensions.csv with one row per page: page number, width, height, standard size, orientation, aspect ratio, area, and rotation, in whichever unit is selected. It opens directly in Excel or Google Sheets.

7.q: Does this tool change my PDF?
7.a: No. It only reads the page tree and reports what it finds; nothing is rewritten, and the only download offered is the optional CSV.

8.q: Is the PDF uploaded for analysis?
8.a: No. The file is parsed in your browser and the measurements are computed locally, which is also why the results appear as soon as the file is loaded.

1.q: Where on the page can the numbers go?
1.a: Six positions: bottom center, bottom left, bottom right, top center, top left, and top right. The margin adjusts to the page size automatically (about 4 percent of the page, between 8 and 40 points), so numbers stay clear of the edge on both small and large pages.

2.q: Can I show the total page count, like 3 of 12?
2.a: Choose the "page X of Y" format and each page prints as 3 / 12. The other format prints only the number. There's no free-form template here; for wording such as "Page 3 of 12", [0]Header & Footer[/0] accepts custom text with {page} and {total} placeholders.

3.q: Can I start numbering from a page other than the first, or skip a cover page?
3.a: Not here; numbering always starts at 1 on the first page and runs to the last. To leave a cover unnumbered, split it off, number the rest, and merge the two back together. For Roman numerals on front matter, [0]Add Page Labels[/0] sets the numbers viewers display instead of printing them on the page.

4.q: What font is used, and can I change it?
4.a: Numbers are set in Helvetica at the size you choose, from 6 to 72 points, in any color from the color picker. The typeface itself is fixed.

5.q: Are the numbers permanent?
5.a: They're drawn directly into the page content, not added as annotations, so every viewer shows them and they print with the document. That also means they can't be switched off later, so keep your unnumbered original.

6.q: Will numbers land in the right spot on cropped or mixed-size pages?
6.a: Each page is measured individually, using its crop box when one is set, so a document that mixes Letter and A4 or portrait and landscape pages still gets numbers inside the visible area at the chosen corner.

7.q: Can I add a prefix like EXHIBIT-A or legal Bates numbers?
7.a: This tool prints plain numbers only. For prefixed, zero-padded numbering such as ABC000123 used in legal productions, use [0]Bates Numbering[/0], which has templates, padding, and multi-file support.

8.q: Does the tool upload my PDF to add the numbers?
8.a: No. The numbers are written by a PDF library running in your browser and the file never leaves your device, which makes it fine for contracts and confidential reports.

1.q: Do I need a Mac or the Pages app to convert a .pages file?
1.a: No. The conversion runs on a LibreOffice engine inside your browser, so it works on Windows, Linux, Chromebooks, and Macs without Pages installed.

2.q: Why is the first Pages document slow to convert?
2.a: The engine has to be downloaded on first use, around 75 MB compressed, and then started. Later conversions in the same session reuse it and start right away.

3.q: Can I convert several Pages documents at once?
3.a: Yes. Add multiple .pages files and click Convert to PDF; you get pages-to-pdf.zip with one PDF per document. Files that share a name get a numbered suffix such as Report (1).pdf so nothing is overwritten.

4.q: Will the PDF look exactly like it does in Pages?
4.a: Usually close, but not guaranteed. A LibreOffice import filter reads the file rather than Pages itself, so complex layouts, some fonts, and newer Pages features may render differently. Check the output before sending it on.

5.q: What will the PDF be named?
5.a: The same base name as the Pages document with a .pdf extension, so Resume.pages becomes Resume.pdf.

6.q: What should I do if the conversion fails?
6.a: An error message shows the reason the engine reported. Make sure the file is a real .pages document and not corrupted; if it still fails, open it in Pages and export it again, or export to PDF from Pages directly.

7.q: Can I convert a Pages file to Word instead of PDF?
7.a: This tool only produces PDF. If you need a .docx, convert the Pages file here first and then run the result through [0]PDF to Word[/0].

8.q: Is my Pages document uploaded to a server?
8.a: No. The LibreOffice engine reads and renders the document in your browser; the only network transfer is downloading the engine itself. Your file never leaves your device.

1.q: How does booklet page order work when I print?
1.a: In the default 1x2 (Booklet) mode, two pages sit side by side on each side of a sheet in saddle-stitch order: the first sheet's front carries the last page and page 1, its back carries page 2 and the second-to-last page, and so on inward. Print double-sided with the flip-on-short-edge setting, fold the stack in half, and the pages read in sequence.

2.q: What if my page count isn't a multiple of 4?
2.a: The count is rounded up to the next multiple of 4 and the missing slots are left blank, which lands them at the end of the booklet. A 10-page document becomes a 12-page booklet on three sheets, and the preview marks the empty slots as blank.

3.q: Which paper sizes can I use?
3.a: Pick from Letter, Legal, Tabloid, Ledger, Executive, Folio, and the ISO A, B, and C series from A0 down to C7. Letter is the default, and each source page is scaled to fit its slot on the sheet with a small margin.

4.q: Should the output be portrait or landscape?
4.a: Auto picks landscape for booklet mode, so two portrait pages sit side by side on a landscape sheet, and portrait for the grid modes. You can force either orientation; the source pages are scaled proportionally to fit whichever you choose.

5.q: What are the 2x2, 2x4, and 4x4 grid modes?
5.a: They place 4, 8, or 16 pages per sheet in reading order rather than booklet order, which is useful for handouts or thumbnail proof sheets. Only 1x2 reorders pages for folding; for more grid layouts see [0]N-Up PDF[/0].

6.q: Can I rotate landscape pages so they fit the booklet?
6.a: The Source Rotation option turns every page 90 degrees clockwise or counter-clockwise before imposition, or alternates the direction between odd and even pages for documents scanned head-to-head. Click Generate Preview to check the layout before downloading.

7.q: Does the booklet lose quality?
7.a: No. Pages are embedded as vector content from the original PDF rather than rasterized, so text stays sharp at any zoom and the file prints at full quality.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded to create the booklet?
8.a: No. The page reordering, scaling, and preview rendering all run in your browser, and the finished booklet PDF is saved from your device without passing through a server.

1.q: What are PDF layers, and why does my PDF have none?
1.a: Layers are Optional Content Groups (OCGs): named groups of page content that a viewer can show or hide, common in CAD exports, maps, and print files with separate language or markup layers. Most PDFs from office software have none, and the tool then shows an empty list with the option to add one.

2.q: Does hiding a layer delete its content?
2.a: No. Unchecking a layer changes the default visibility state saved in the PDF, so it opens hidden but can be switched back on in any viewer with a layers panel. Deleting a layer with the X button removes the layer group itself from the document's layer list.

3.q: Why can't I toggle or delete some layers?
3.a: Layers shown with a lock icon were marked locked by the PDF's creator, so their visibility can't be changed and the add-child and delete buttons are hidden for them. That lock is part of the file and the tool respects it.

4.q: Can I add a new layer and put content on it?
4.a: You can add top-level layers and nested child layers by name, and they're saved into the PDF's layer configuration. This tool doesn't draw content onto a layer; it manages the layer list, so a new layer stays empty until another application assigns content to it.

5.q: Will the changes show in Acrobat and other viewers?
5.a: Layer names and visibility states are written into the PDF's standard optional content dictionary, so any viewer with layer support reads them. Viewers without a layers panel still honor the default visibility, so a layer you hid stays hidden there.

6.q: What is the downloaded file called?
6.a: Download Modified PDF saves the edited document under the same filename as the original, so rename it afterward if you want to keep both versions.

7.q: Can I inspect layers in a password-protected PDF?
7.a: You're prompted for the password on upload, and the layer editor works on the decrypted copy. The saved file isn't encrypted.
