8.q: Is the drawing uploaded when I edit its layers?
8.a: No. The PDF is opened by PyMuPDF running as WebAssembly in your browser, layer changes are applied in memory, and the download is written on your device, which matters for CAD drawings and site plans that are often confidential.

1.q: What can I do with the PDF Multi Tool that the single-purpose tools can't?
1.a: It puts merging, reordering, rotating, duplicating, deleting, inserting, and splitting in one page grid, so you can do several of them in a single pass without downloading and re-uploading between steps. Every action is covered by undo and redo, so you can experiment before you export.

2.q: How do I combine pages from several PDFs into one document?
2.a: Upload all the source files and their pages appear together in one grid, in upload order. Drag pages into the order you want, delete the ones you don't need, and click Export PDF to download the result as a single file.

3.q: Can I add images as pages?
3.a: Drop JPG, PNG, WebP, HEIC, TIFF, BMP, GIF, or SVG files alongside your PDFs and each image becomes a page you can move, rotate, or delete like any other. Blank A4 pages can also be appended with the Add Blank Page button.

4.q: How do I split one PDF into several files?
4.a: Click the scissors icon on a page to place a split marker after it; a dashed line shows where the document will be divided. Export then produces split-documents.zip containing document - 1.pdf, document - 2.pdf, and so on.

5.q: Does rotating pages here reduce quality?
5.a: No. Rotation is stored as a page attribute in 90-degree steps rather than re-rendering the content, so text, vectors, and images are untouched. For angles other than 90, 180, or 270 degrees, use [0]Rotate by Custom Degrees[/0].

6.q: Can I export only some of the pages?
6.a: Tick the checkboxes on the pages you want and use Download selected to get just those pages as selected-pages.pdf. The workspace stays as it is, so you can keep working and export the rest later.

7.q: What happens to bookmarks when I export?
7.a: The export rebuilds the document page by page, so bookmarks from the source files aren't carried into the new PDF. Page content, including text and images, is copied as-is.

8.q: Are my PDFs uploaded when I use the Multi Tool?
8.a: No. Page thumbnails are rendered and the final PDF or ZIP is assembled in your browser, and damaged files are repaired locally before loading too. Nothing you drop into the grid leaves your computer.

1.q: What resolution are the BMP images?
1.a: Pages render at a fixed 2x scale, so a Letter page (8.5 x 11 inches) becomes a 1224 x 1584 pixel image, about 144 pixels per inch. There's no DPI setting on this tool; for an adjustable scale use [0]PDF to PNG[/0].

2.q: How is a multi-page PDF delivered?
2.a: A one-page PDF downloads as a single .bmp named after the file. A multi-page PDF downloads as a ZIP named filename_bmps.zip containing page_1.bmp, page_2.bmp, and so on, one image per page.

3.q: Why are the BMP files so large?
3.a: BMP stores raw pixel data without compression, so a page takes the same space whether it's blank or full of detail, and files are far larger than a PNG or JPG of the same page. If your target software accepts PNG, that format is lossless too at a fraction of the size.

4.q: Can I convert several PDFs to BMP in one batch?
4.a: No, one PDF per run; if you drop several files only the first is used. Convert them one after another, or pick the pages you need first with Extract Pages so each run stays small.

5.q: Does the conversion keep transparency or vector quality?
5.a: No. Every page becomes a flat raster image on a white background, and text becomes pixels, so the BMP can't be searched or enlarged without softening. Keep the original PDF for editing.

6.q: Can I convert a password-protected PDF to BMP?
6.a: Yes, if you know the password: the tool prompts for it when the file loads and then renders the pages normally. A file with an unknown password can't be opened.

7.q: Is my PDF uploaded to convert it to BMP?
7.a: No. Rendering happens on a canvas in your browser and the images are packed into the ZIP locally, so the document never leaves your computer. Large PDFs just take longer because your own machine does the rendering.

8.q: Which tool should I use instead if BMP isn't required?
8.a: For lossless output with small files, PDF to PNG; for photos and the smallest files, [0]PDF to JPG[/0]; for multi-page fax or scanning systems, PDF to TIFF. BMP mainly makes sense when a legacy application or device insists on it.

1.q: What scale should I use?
1.a: Scale multiplies the page's native size, from 1.0x to 4.0x with 2.0x as the default. 2.0x suits phones and most tablets; 3.0x or 4.0x gives sharper pages on high-resolution screens at the cost of a much larger file and a longer conversion.

2.q: Why is my CBZ bigger than the original PDF?
2.a: Every page is rendered to a bitmap at the chosen scale, which discards the PDF's compact vector text and compression. Lowering the scale, choosing JPEG or WebP at around 80% quality, or turning on grayscale for black-and-white content all bring the size down.

3.q: What does Manga mode change?
3.a: It writes a right-to-left reading direction flag into the ComicInfo.xml metadata so readers that honor the flag page from right to left. The page images themselves are unchanged.

4.q: Will the pages stay in the right order?
4.a: Yes. Images are named with zero-padded numbers, such as 01.jpg or 001.jpg depending on the page count, so readers that sort filenames alphabetically keep the sequence even past page 100.

5.q: Which metadata will Calibre pick up?
5.a: Calibre reads the metadata.opf file inside the archive: title, author, publisher, year, tags, and series with its index. Komga, Kavita, CDisplayEx, Mylar, and ComicRack use ComicInfo.xml, and a ComicBookInfo record in the ZIP comment covers older readers. Fill in Series and Number so libraries group issues correctly.

6.q: Can I convert several PDFs to CBZ in one go?
6.a: No. This tool handles one PDF per run, and adding another file replaces the current one. Convert them one at a time.

7.q: Can a password-protected PDF be converted to CBZ?
7.a: If the PDF needs a password to open, you're prompted for it and the pages are rendered from a decrypted copy held in memory.

8.q: Are the comic pages rendered on a server?
8.a: No. Pages are drawn with PDF.js in your browser and zipped locally, so the comic never leaves your device.

1.q: How does the tool find tables in a PDF?
1.a: It runs PyMuPDF's table detection on every page, which looks for the ruling lines and aligned text that make up a table. Each table it finds is written to the CSV row by row, and all pages are scanned in one pass.

2.q: What happens if my PDF has several tables?
2.a: All of them are written into one .csv file in page order, with the rows of one table following the rows of the previous one and no separator between them. If you need each table in its own file or on its own sheet, use [0]PDF to Excel[/0] instead.

3.q: Why does PDF to CSV say no tables were found?
3.a: Usually the PDF lays out its data with spaces and tabs that only look like a table, without the structure the detector needs, or the page is a scan with no text layer at all. For scans, run [0]OCR PDF[/0] first so there is text to detect.

4.q: How are commas, quotes, and line breaks inside cells handled?
4.a: Cells that contain a comma, a double quote, or a newline are wrapped in double quotes, and any quotes inside them are doubled, following RFC 4180. The file is saved as UTF-8, so accented characters and non-Latin scripts survive the trip into a spreadsheet.

5.q: Will the CSV keep the formatting from the PDF?
5.a: No. CSV is plain text, so bold text, colors, merged cells, and column widths are dropped and only the cell values remain. Numbers are exported as the text shown in the PDF, including any currency symbols or thousands separators.

6.q: Can I extract tables from a password-protected PDF?
6.a: You'll be asked for the password after upload, and extraction continues once it's entered. The password is used only to open the file in your browser.

7.q: Is the PDF uploaded to extract the tables?
7.a: No. The table detection engine is loaded into your browser as WebAssembly and the CSV is generated locally, so the document never leaves your device. The first run takes a little longer while the engine loads.

8.q: How do I open the CSV in Excel without breaking the columns?
8.a: Double-clicking the file works in most setups, since the tool uses the standard comma delimiter. If your Excel is set to a locale that expects semicolons, use Data > From Text/CSV and pick comma as the delimiter.

1.q: Why does PDF to Excel say no tables were found?
1.a: The detector looks for table structure such as ruling lines and aligned cells. Text arranged in columns with spaces, or a table that exists only as part of a scanned image, doesn't register. For scans, run [0]OCR PDF[/0] first; for loosely formatted text, PDF to Text gets you the raw content to tidy up by hand.

2.q: How are multiple tables organized in the spreadsheet?
2.a: Each detected table gets its own worksheet, named Table 1 (Page 3), Table 2 (Page 5), and so on, so you can see which page it came from. A PDF with a single table produces one sheet called Table. Sheet names are cut at 31 characters because Excel allows no more.

3.q: Are formatting, colors, and merged cells preserved?
3.a: No. Only the cell text is transferred; fonts, fills, borders, column widths, and merged cells aren't reproduced. Numbers may arrive as text cells, so if a column won't sum, select it and use Excel's Convert to Number prompt.

4.q: Can I convert only certain pages to Excel?
4.a: There are no page options; every page is scanned and all tables found are exported. If you only need one table, pull those pages into a separate PDF first, or use [0]Extract Tables[/0], which previews each table and lets you download them one at a time.

5.q: What's the difference between PDF to Excel, PDF to CSV, and Extract Tables?
5.a: PDF to Excel packs every table into one .xlsx workbook with a sheet per table. [0]PDF to CSV[/0] produces flat comma-separated files, and Extract Tables previews each table and offers per-table downloads in several formats. Pick Excel when you want everything in one workbook with page references.

6.q: Does it handle password-protected PDFs?
6.a: If the file needs a password to open, the tool asks for it before extraction starts. The output .xlsx is not password-protected.

7.q: Is my financial data uploaded during conversion?
7.a: No. Table detection runs in a PDF engine loaded into your browser as WebAssembly, and the spreadsheet is built locally by a JavaScript library. Bank statements and invoices never leave your machine.

1.q: Does converting a PDF to grayscale make it smaller?
1.a: Often, yes. Each page is stored as a grayscale JPEG at 90% quality, which is smaller than a color image, so color-heavy files usually shrink. A text-only PDF can grow instead, because its compact vector text becomes a full-page image.

2.q: Will the text still be selectable after conversion?
2.a: No. Every page is rendered at 2x scale, desaturated, and re-embedded as a JPEG image, so the output is image-based and text can't be selected or searched. If you need searchable text again, run the result through [0]OCR PDF[/0].

3.q: Can I adjust brightness or contrast, or keep some pages in color?
3.a: Not here. This tool has no options and converts every page using a standard luminance formula. For brightness, contrast, or saturation controls use [0]Adjust Colors[/0], and to convert only some pages, split those out first and merge the results afterward.

4.q: Is grayscale the same as black and white?
4.a: No. Grayscale keeps shades of gray, so photos, shaded charts, and highlights stay readable, while true black and white drops everything to two tones; this tool produces grayscale. If you need 1-bit output, [0]PDF to TIFF[/0] has a Black & White mode.

5.q: Does the page size or print quality change?
5.a: The page dimensions are preserved. Pages are rendered at 2x scale, about 144 dpi, which looks fine on screen and is acceptable for office printing, but fine detail won't be as crisp as the vector original.

6.q: Why convert a PDF to grayscale before printing?
6.a: A grayscale file prints the same on any printer and avoids color charges, and some print shops, courts, and government portals require grayscale submissions. Converting first also shows how colored charts and highlights will look in gray before you print.

7.q: What happens to annotations, form fields, and links?
7.a: They're flattened into the page image. Form fields stop being fillable, comments become part of the picture, and clickable links no longer work.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded to convert it?
8.a: No. Rendering and the grayscale filter run on a canvas in your browser tab, and the new PDF is assembled there too. Nothing is sent to a server.

1.q: Can I convert just one page of a PDF to JPG?
1.a: The tool converts every page in the file. To get a single page, pull it out first with [0]Extract Pages[/0] and convert that one-page PDF; it downloads as a plain .jpg instead of a ZIP.

2.q: What resolution are the JPG images?
2.a: Pages render at 2x their PDF size, which works out to about 144 DPI: a standard 8.5 by 11 inch page becomes roughly a 1,224 by 1,584 pixel image. There is no separate DPI setting.

3.q: What JPG quality setting should I use?
3.a: The slider runs from 10% to 100% with a default of 90%. Around 80 to 90% is hard to tell from the original on screen, while lower values shrink the files noticeably at the cost of compression artifacts around text and sharp edges.

4.q: Why did I get a ZIP file instead of images?
4.a: A PDF with more than one page produces filename_jpgs.zip containing page_1.jpg, page_2.jpg, and so on, one image per page. Only single-page PDFs download as a lone .jpg.

5.q: Should I choose JPG or PNG for my PDF pages?
5.a: JPG is lossy and produces smaller files, which suits photos and scans meant for email or chat. For text, diagrams, or anything that needs exact pixels, [0]PDF to PNG[/0] is lossless.

6.q: Will the text in the images be editable or searchable?
6.a: No. A JPG is a flat picture of the page, so text, links, and form fields become pixels. Keep the PDF if you need those.

7.q: Can I convert a scanned PDF with this tool?
7.a: Yes. Scanned pages are already images inside the PDF, and they're rendered at 2x page scale like any other page. If the scan was low resolution to begin with, the JPG won't add detail.

8.q: Are my PDF pages uploaded to convert them to JPG?
8.a: No. The pages are drawn onto a canvas and encoded to JPG entirely in your browser, and the images or ZIP are created on your device.

1.q: What does the JSON contain?
1.a: The full object structure of the PDF as cpdf reads it: the trailer, catalog, page tree, every dictionary, and each page's content stream parsed into a list of drawing and text operators. It's a complete dump of the file, not a summary.

2.q: Is this the right tool to get the text out of a PDF as JSON?
2.a: Usually not. The text here is scattered across content stream operators in the order it was drawn, with fonts and positions but no paragraphs. For readable page text in a structured format use [0]Prepare PDF for AI[/0], and for plain text use PDF to Text.

3.q: Can I convert the JSON back into a PDF?
3.a: Not with BentoPDF. The output follows cpdf's own JSON format, which the cpdf command line tool can read back into a PDF, but the browser tool only goes in one direction.

4.q: Why is the JSON so much bigger than the PDF?
4.a: Content streams are expanded into operator arrays, binary stream data such as images is encoded as text, and every object is written out with its keys, so a JSON file several times the size of the source is normal. Large or image-heavy PDFs produce very large files.

5.q: Can I convert multiple PDFs to JSON at once?
5.a: Select as many as you like; each is converted in a background worker and the results are packaged into pdfs-to-json.zip with one .json per PDF, named after the source file. A single PDF also arrives as a ZIP.

6.q: Does it work on encrypted PDFs?
6.a: You're asked for the password before conversion starts and the decrypted copy is serialized. Without the password the object structure can't be read.

7.q: What is this useful for?
7.a: Inspecting a PDF's internals when debugging a generator, checking what a page's content stream contains, comparing two versions structurally, or feeding the object tree into a script. For document properties alone, [0]View Metadata[/0] is quicker.

8.q: Is the PDF uploaded to produce the JSON?
8.a: No. cpdf runs as WebAssembly in a web worker in your browser, and the JSON is written and zipped on your device before download.

1.q: How well does PDF to Markdown preserve the document structure?
1.a: Headings, paragraphs, lists, and basic bold and italic formatting are converted, and each page is separated by a horizontal rule (---) in the output. Heading levels are inferred from font sizes, so a document with inconsistent styling may come out with some headings at the wrong level.

2.q: What does the Include Images option do?
2.a: When it's checked, pictures from the PDF are embedded directly in the Markdown as base64 data, so the single .md file is self-contained but can get large. Leave it off for text-heavy documents to keep the output small and readable in a plain editor.

3.q: Why is the Markdown empty or almost empty?
3.a: The converter reads the PDF's text layer, so a scanned document that's only images has nothing to convert. Run it through [0]OCR PDF[/0] first to add a text layer, then convert the result.

4.q: How does it handle multi-column layouts, footnotes, and sidebars?
4.a: Complex layouts are the weak spot: multi-column text can be interleaved, and sidebars or footnotes may land in the wrong place. Expect to review and tidy the output for magazine-style pages, while single-column documents need little cleanup.

5.q: Can I convert several PDFs to Markdown at once?
5.a: Upload multiple PDFs and click Convert once. One file downloads as filename.md; several come back as markdown-files.zip with one .md per PDF, and duplicate names get a numbered suffix.

6.q: Is this the same as PDF to Text?
6.a: No. [0]PDF to Text[/0] gives you raw text with no structure, which is better for feeding into scripts. PDF to Markdown keeps headings, lists, and emphasis so the result is ready to paste into Obsidian, a wiki, or a static site generator.

7.q: Can I convert a password-protected PDF?
7.a: If the file needs a password to open, you're prompted for it before conversion starts and the text is extracted as usual. The password isn't stored anywhere, and the Markdown output has no protection of its own.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded to convert it to Markdown?
8.a: No. Conversion runs on a PyMuPDF engine loaded into your browser as WebAssembly, and the .md file or ZIP is generated on your machine. Research papers, contracts, and internal docs stay private.

1.q: Which PDF/A version should I choose?
1.a: PDF/A-2b, the default, suits most archiving and accepts transparency and JPEG 2000 images. Pick PDF/A-1b only when a recipient demands it, since it's the strictest level and forbids transparency and layers, and PDF/A-3b when the archive needs to carry embedded files, such as the XML data used by e-invoicing formats.

2.q: What does the conversion actually change in my file?
2.a: Ghostscript rewrites the PDF so it meets the standard: every font is embedded as a subset, colors are converted to device-independent color with an sRGB output intent, and features the chosen level forbids are dropped rather than failing the whole run. Page content stays intact and text remains selectable.

3.q: Why is the PDF/A file bigger than the original?
3.a: PDF/A requires all fonts to be embedded, so any font the original referenced but didn't include is now stored inside the file, and the sRGB color profile is added too. [0]Compress PDF[/0] can reduce the size; re-validate afterward if strict compliance matters.

4.q: When should I turn on Pre-flatten?
4.a: Only if the normal conversion fails. Pre-flatten renders every page to a 300 DPI image before Ghostscript runs, which gets around broken fonts or unusual transparency but leaves you with no selectable text, so try without it first. It also needs the PyMuPDF module, which loads on first use.

5.q: Is the output guaranteed to pass a PDF/A validator?
5.a: Not guaranteed. Ghostscript produces conformant output for the vast majority of files, but it isn't a validator, so if a court, repository, or auditor requires proof, check the result with a dedicated PDF/A validator such as veraPDF.

6.q: Can I convert multiple PDFs to PDF/A at once?
6.a: Yes. Add multiple files and they're converted one after another with the same settings; a single file downloads directly and several download together as pdfa-converted.zip.

7.q: Are my records uploaded to a server for PDF/A conversion?
7.a: No. Ghostscript runs as a WebAssembly module inside your browser, so the conversion happens on your machine and the files never leave it. The module itself is fetched from a CDN the first time you use the tool, which is why the first run takes a little longer.

8.q: Can I convert a password-protected PDF to PDF/A?
8.a: The tool asks for the open password first, then converts the decrypted file. PDF/A itself forbids encryption, so the output is always unprotected; a password-protected PDF/A isn't possible.

1.q: What resolution do the PNGs have?
1.a: Scale 1.0x renders at 72 pixels per inch of page, so a Letter page becomes 612 by 792 pixels. The default 2.0x doubles that to 1224 by 1584, and 3.0x gives 1836 by 2376, which is 216 pixels per inch.

2.q: Can I export at 300 DPI for print?
2.a: Not directly. The slider tops out at 3.0x, about 216 DPI on a standard page, and there's no field for entering a custom DPI in this tool.

3.q: Is the background transparent?
3.a: No. Pages are drawn onto a white background, so areas with no content come out white rather than transparent, even though PNG supports transparency.

4.q: Can I convert only certain pages to PNG?
4.a: Every page is converted; there's no page-range field. Pull out the pages you need with [0]Extract Pages[/0] first, then convert that smaller file.

5.q: How are the files named?
5.a: A one-page PDF downloads as filename.png. Multi-page documents download as filename_pngs.zip containing page_1.png, page_2.png, and so on in document order.

6.q: Why are the PNG files so large?
6.a: PNG is lossless, so a full page at 2.0x is often several megabytes, especially for scans and photos. If some compression is acceptable, [0]PDF to JPG[/0] or PDF to WebP produce far smaller images from the same pages.

7.q: Do annotations and filled form fields appear in the images?
7.a: Visible markup such as highlights, stamps, and filled form fields is rendered as it appears on the page. The text inside pop-up comments isn't drawn, only the note icon.

8.q: Is the PDF rendered on a server?
8.a: No. Rendering uses PDF.js inside your browser and the ZIP is built locally, so the document never leaves your computer. If the PDF needs a password, you're asked for it first.

1.q: Is the text in the SVG still selectable?
1.a: No. Each page is exported with text drawn as vector outlines, so it scales cleanly and doesn't depend on fonts being installed, but it isn't live text you can select or search. If you need the words themselves, use [0]PDF to Text[/0] alongside the SVG.

2.q: Do I get one SVG for the whole document or one per page?
2.a: One per page, since SVG has no concept of pages. A single-page PDF downloads as filename.svg, a multi-page PDF becomes filename_svg.zip containing page_1.svg, page_2.svg and so on, and several PDFs at once download as pdf_to_svg.zip.

3.q: Can I edit the result in Illustrator or Inkscape?
3.a: The output is standard SVG that opens in Inkscape, Illustrator, Figma, and any web browser. Shapes, paths, and text outlines arrive as editable vector objects, while photos embedded in the PDF stay as raster images inside the file.

4.q: Why is my SVG file so large?
4.a: Scanned or photo-heavy PDFs produce big SVGs because every raster image is embedded in the file as base64 data, and pages with thousands of tiny vector paths add up too. For image-based pages, [0]PDF to PNG[/0] gives a smaller and more practical result.

5.q: Can I convert multiple PDFs at once?
5.a: Drop as many PDFs as you like into the tool and click Convert. Each file is processed in turn and the results are collected in pdf_to_svg.zip, named after their source document.

6.q: Are there any options like page range or size?
6.a: No. Every page of every uploaded file is converted at its native page size, with no scaling or range selection. To convert only certain pages, split them out first with [0]Extract Pages[/0].

7.q: Can I convert a password-protected PDF to SVG?
7.a: You're prompted for the password after upload, and conversion proceeds once it's accepted. The SVG files themselves carry no password.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded for the conversion?
8.a: No. PyMuPDF runs inside your browser as WebAssembly and writes the SVG files locally, so the PDF never leaves your machine. The engine is fetched on first use, which is why the first conversion takes a moment longer.

1.q: Why is the .txt file empty?
1.a: The PDF is most likely a scan or a photo, which has no text layer to extract. Run it through [0]OCR PDF[/0] first; that tool adds a text layer and also offers a .txt download directly.

2.q: Does the text come out in the right order?
2.a: Text is read left to right, top to bottom, following the PDF's internal structure, which is correct for most single-column documents. Multi-column layouts, sidebars, and tables can come out interleaved, and headers, footers, and page numbers are included with everything else on the page.

3.q: Is any formatting kept?
3.a: No. The output is plain UTF-8 text, so accented characters, Cyrillic, CJK, and Arabic are preserved, but bold, headings, links, and images are not, and line breaks follow the PDF's lines rather than paragraphs. For headings and lists kept as Markdown, use [0]PDF to Markdown[/0].

4.q: Can I extract text from several PDFs at once?
4.a: Yes. Add as many PDFs as you like and click Extract once; each becomes its own .txt file named after the source, and they download together as pdf-to-text.zip. A single PDF downloads directly as filename.txt.

5.q: How are pages separated in the output?
5.a: Pages follow one another with a line break between them. There are no page markers or form feeds, so the file reads as one continuous stream of text.

6.q: Can I pick specific pages or a page range?
6.a: No, this tool always extracts every page. Pull the pages you need into a separate PDF first with [0]Extract Pages[/0], then convert that file.

7.q: Does it work on password-protected files?
7.a: If a PDF asks for a password when you open it, the tool prompts you for that password before extracting. Without the password, the text can't be read.

8.q: Do my documents get uploaded to extract the text?
8.a: No. Extraction runs in a PDF engine loaded into your browser as WebAssembly, so contracts, medical records, and anything else stay on your device from start to finish.

1.q: Can I get all pages in a single multi-page TIFF?
1.a: Yes. Check "Save as multi-page TIFF (single file)" and every page is written into one .tiff named after the PDF. Leave it unchecked and a multi-page PDF downloads as a ZIP containing page_1.tiff, page_2.tiff, and so on; a one-page PDF always gives a single .tiff.

2.q: What DPI should I use?
2.a: The slider runs from 72 to 600 and defaults to 300, the usual choice for print and archival scans. Fax and document management systems typically expect 200 to 300, and 150 is enough for screen use. Very high DPI on large pages can run the browser out of memory, and you'll see an error if that happens.

3.q: Which compression should I choose?
3.a: LZW, the default, and Deflate are lossless and suit any content. CCITT Group 4 gives the smallest files for black-and-white scans and automatically switches the color mode to 1-bit. JPEG is lossy (quality 85) but keeps photo-heavy pages small, and PackBits or None are there for older systems that require them.

4.q: How do I make a black-and-white TIFF for fax or e-filing?
4.a: Set Color Mode to "Black & White (1-bit)" and Compression to CCITT Group 4, then pick 200 or 300 DPI. That combination is what most fax gateways and document management systems expect, and it produces very small files.

5.q: Why is my TIFF so large?
5.a: TIFF stores a bitmap of every page. An uncompressed 300 DPI color Letter page is roughly 25 MB, so lower the DPI, switch the color mode to grayscale or black and white, or use CCITT Group 4 for text scans. If you only need lossless images for the screen, [0]PDF to PNG[/0] makes smaller files.

6.q: Can I batch-convert PDFs to TIFF?
6.a: No. This tool takes one PDF at a time; if you drop several, only the first is used. Convert them one after another.

7.q: Will a password-protected PDF convert to TIFF?
7.a: Yes. If the PDF needs a password to open, you're asked for it before conversion, and the pages are rendered once it's entered. The TIFF output itself has no password protection.

8.q: Are my pages uploaded to convert them?
8.a: No. Pages are rendered with PDF.js and encoded with libvips compiled to WebAssembly, all inside your browser. That does require a browser with SharedArrayBuffer support, which is why the tool must run over HTTPS.

1.q: Why choose WebP over JPG for PDF pages?
1.a: WebP files are typically 25 to 35% smaller than JPG at the same visual quality, which matters for web pages and social posts where file size counts. If you need images for older software or email clients, [0]PDF to JPG[/0] is the safer choice.

2.q: What WebP quality setting should I use?
2.a: The slider runs from 10% to 100% and defaults to 85%. Values between 80 and 85% usually look identical to the original on screen, and going higher mainly adds file size.

3.q: What resolution are the WebP images?
3.a: Each page is rendered at 2x its PDF dimensions, so a letter-size page comes out at roughly 1,224 by 1,584 pixels. There is no separate DPI or size setting.

4.q: Does it convert all pages, or can I pick some?
4.a: All pages are converted. A one-page PDF downloads as filename.webp; a longer document downloads as filename_webps.zip containing page_1.webp, page_2.webp, and so on. To convert only certain pages, pull them out first with [0]Extract Pages[/0].

5.q: Will the WebP images open everywhere?
5.a: Current versions of Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge display WebP, as do most modern image editors. Some older desktop programs and email clients don't, so fall back to JPG or PNG for those.

6.q: Is the WebP output lossy?
6.a: The quality slider controls lossy compression, so fine text edges lose a little detail at low settings. For an exact copy of a page, use [0]PDF to PNG[/0], which is lossless.

7.q: Are my PDF pages uploaded when converting to WebP?
7.a: No. Rendering and WebP encoding happen in your browser, and the resulting images or ZIP are created on your own device.

1.q: Will the Word document look like the PDF?
1.a: Text, basic formatting, and page layout are reconstructed into a .docx that stays close to the original for simple documents. Multi-column layouts, text placed over graphics, embedded forms, and unusual fonts may shift, so open the result and tidy it in Word or Google Docs.

2.q: Why is my converted Word file empty?
2.a: The PDF is a scan with no text layer, so there's nothing for the converter to reconstruct and you get blank pages or a few stray characters. Run the file through [0]OCR PDF[/0] first to add a text layer, then convert the OCR'd PDF.

3.q: Can I edit the text after converting?
3.a: The output is a normal .docx with real paragraphs, not an image of the page, so you can edit, restyle, and copy from it in Word, LibreOffice Writer, or Google Docs.

4.q: Does it handle CMYK or print-ready PDFs?
4.a: Before conversion the PDF is passed through Ghostscript to convert it to RGB, which avoids the image errors that CMYK print files otherwise cause in the converter. If that step fails, the original file is used as is.

5.q: Can I convert many PDFs at once?
5.a: Add as many files as you want; they're converted one after another and downloaded as converted-documents.zip with one .docx per PDF. A single file downloads directly under its own name with a .docx extension.

6.q: What about password-protected PDFs?
6.a: You're prompted for the password when conversion starts, and the decrypted copy is converted. The resulting .docx isn't password protected.

7.q: Do I need Microsoft Word installed to convert PDF to Word?
7.a: No. The conversion is done by PyMuPDF and pdf2docx running in your browser, and the .docx it produces opens in Word, LibreOffice Writer, Pages, and Google Docs. To go the other way, use [0]Word to PDF[/0].

8.q: Is the PDF uploaded to convert it to Word?
8.a: No. The whole pipeline, from reading the PDF to writing the .docx, runs in WebAssembly inside your browser, so contracts and reports stay on your device.

1.q: What does PDFs to ZIP actually do to my files?
1.a: Nothing beyond packaging. The PDFs are copied into a single pdfs_archive.zip with their original names, unchanged, in the order you added them, so what comes out of the ZIP is byte for byte what went in.

2.q: Does zipping make the PDFs smaller?
2.a: No. The archive is written without compression, since PDF content is already compressed internally and would barely shrink anyway, so expect the ZIP to be about the combined size of the files. To reduce the size, run them through [0]Compress PDF[/0] first and zip the results.

3.q: What's the difference between zipping PDFs and merging them?
3.a: A ZIP keeps each PDF as a separate file inside one container that the recipient unpacks. Merging joins the pages into one PDF document, which is what you want when the files should be read as a single document; use [0]Merge PDF[/0] for that.

4.q: What if two of my files have the same name?
4.a: Duplicate names are handled automatically: the second file becomes name (1).pdf, the third name (2).pdf, and so on, so nothing gets overwritten inside the archive. Rename the files before uploading if you'd rather have meaningful names.

5.q: Can I add non-PDF files to the archive?
5.a: No. Only files with a .pdf extension or a PDF file type are accepted; anything else you drop in is ignored. For a mixed bundle, use your operating system's built-in zip feature instead.

6.q: Will the recipient need special software to open the archive?
6.a: No. The output is a standard ZIP file that Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android open without extra software; double-click or tap it to unpack the PDFs.

7.q: Are my PDFs uploaded to build the ZIP?
7.a: No. The archive is assembled in your browser, so the files are read from your disk and the ZIP is written back to it without any network transfer. Bundling invoices, contracts, or medical records this way keeps them on your device.

1.q: What is the PDF Workflow Builder for?
1.a: It chains several PDF operations into one run. Instead of opening a tool, downloading, and feeding the result into the next tool for each step, you connect nodes on a canvas, such as PDF Input, Compress, Watermark, and Download, set each node's options, and click Run to process everything in sequence.

2.q: Can I run the same workflow on many PDFs at once?
2.a: Yes. The PDF Input node accepts multiple files; a Merge node combines them into one document, while other nodes process each PDF separately. When more than one file comes out the end, the Download node bundles them into a ZIP automatically.

3.q: Why won't it let me connect two nodes?
3.a: Sockets are typed: PDF (a single document), MultiPDF (several documents), and Image. A node that expects a single PDF won't accept a MultiPDF output, so put a Merge node in between, and image outputs only feed nodes that take images. Connections always run from the bottom of one node to the top of the next.

4.q: Why does it complain that Encrypt must be the last step?
4.a: Once a PDF is encrypted, later nodes can't read it, so the engine rejects a workflow where anything other than the output sits after Encrypt. Move Encrypt to just before Download. Password-protected inputs are the opposite case: the run pauses and asks for the password.

5.q: What happens if one step fails?
5.a: The run stops at that node, which turns red with an error message, and nothing downstream is produced. Fix the setting or the input and run again; it's easiest to build a two-node version first and add steps once that works.

6.q: Can I save a workflow and reuse it later?
6.a: Yes. Save stores it as a named template in your browser's local storage, and Load brings it back in a later session on the same browser. Export writes the layout to a workflow.json file you can back up or send to a colleague, and Import restores nodes, positions, connections, and settings from that file.

7.q: Does a saved workflow contain my documents?
7.a: No. Templates and exported JSON files hold only the node types, their settings, positions, and connections; the PDFs are chosen fresh each time you run. Settings are saved as typed, so avoid exporting a workflow with a password entered in an Encrypt node if you plan to share it.

8.q: Are the files processed on a server?
8.a: No. Every node runs in your browser with the same engines as the individual tools, and the only network activity is fetching a processing module such as Ghostscript the first time a node needs one. Your PDFs never leave the machine, even in a long multi-step run.

1.q: What does the quality setting do for PNG images?
1.a: High embeds each PNG as-is, losslessly and at full size. Medium re-encodes the image as JPEG at 75% quality and shrinks anything larger than 2500 pixels on its longest side; Low uses JPEG at 50% with a 1500 pixel limit.

2.q: Which setting should I use for screenshots?
2.a: High. Screenshots and diagrams have sharp edges and small text, and the JPEG compression at Medium or Low adds visible blur and artifacts around them. Medium or Low make sense mainly for photos where file size matters more.

3.q: What happens to transparent areas?
3.a: At High the PNG keeps its alpha channel and transparent regions show the page behind them, which viewers display as white. Medium and Low convert to JPEG, which has no transparency, so use High for images with transparent backgrounds.

4.q: What page size will each page be?
4.a: The page matches the image's pixel dimensions at one point per pixel, so a 1920 by 1080 screenshot gives a page about 26.7 by 15 inches; at Medium or Low a downscaled image gives a proportionally smaller page. Use [0]Fix Page Size[/0] afterward if you need A4 or Letter.

5.q: Can I put several PNGs into one PDF and control the order?
5.a: Yes. Every file you add becomes one page in the order shown in the list; remove and re-add files to change the order. The output is always a single PDF, not one file per image.

6.q: Why is the PDF about the same size as my PNGs?
6.a: At High the PNG data is stored unchanged, so the PDF is roughly the sum of the image sizes plus a little overhead. If that's too large, choose Medium or Low, or run the PDF through [0]Compress PDF[/0].

7.q: What if a PNG can't be embedded?
7.a: PNGs with unusual color profiles or bit depths that the PDF library rejects are redrawn and stored as JPEG at 90% quality instead, so the conversion still completes with a small quality trade-off.

8.q: Are the images uploaded?
8.a: No. Each PNG is read, optionally recompressed, and embedded with pdf-lib inside your browser, so screenshots of internal tools or private conversations never leave your device.

1.q: How do I print a large PDF across several A4 or Letter sheets?
1.a: Set Rows and Columns to the grid you want, for example 2 rows and 2 columns to split a page into four sheets, choose the output page size, and click the button. Each grid cell becomes one page in the new PDF, ready to print on ordinary paper and tape together. For the opposite job, fitting several pages onto one sheet, use [0]N-Up PDF[/0].

2.q: What is the overlap setting for?
2.a: Overlap extends each tile a little into its neighbors, in points, inches, or millimeters, so the sheets share a strip you can glue or tape without a gap at the seam. Leave it at 0 if you want tiles that meet edge to edge.

3.q: What's the difference between Fit and Fill when posterizing?
3.a: Fit scales each tile so the whole thing lands on the output page, leaving white margins if the shapes don't match. Fill (Crop) scales the tile up until it covers the page completely, which removes margins but can cut off edges.

4.q: Can I posterize just one page of the document?
4.a: Type the pages in the Page range box, for example 1 or 1-3, 5. Only those pages are split and included in the output; pages outside the range are left out entirely, so extract them separately if you still need them.

5.q: Is the output still vector, or is it turned into images?
5.a: Each page is rendered at double resolution and the tiles are saved as PNG images, so the result is raster rather than vector. That's fine for printing at poster sizes, but the text is no longer selectable and very large scale factors can look soft.

6.q: How many pages will the result have?
6.a: Rows multiplied by columns for every page you posterize, so a 3x3 grid turns one page into nine and a 2x2 grid applied to a three page document produces twelve. Tiles are ordered row by row from left to right.

7.q: What output sizes and orientations can I use?
7.a: A4, Letter, Legal, A3, or A5, with orientation set to Portrait, Landscape, or Automatic, which follows the shape of the source page. The preview shows dashed red lines where the cuts will fall so you can adjust the grid before processing.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded to tile it?
8.a: No. The rendering, tiling, and assembly happen in your browser, and the new PDF downloads under the original file name. Because pages are rendered locally, big grids on large pages take more memory on your machine.

1.q: Why does my first PowerPoint conversion take a while?
1.a: The converter is a full LibreOffice build compiled to WebAssembly, about 75 MB, that your browser downloads and starts the first time you convert. Once loaded it stays ready, so a second presentation in the same session converts far faster.

2.q: Will animations, transitions, and embedded videos show up?
2.a: No. Every slide is captured as a static page, so animations and transitions are dropped and a video appears only as whatever the slide shows in its place. Replace videos with a screenshot before converting if you need a visual.

3.q: Are speaker notes included?
3.a: Not in this export; only the slides are rendered, one per page. If you need a notes version, print to PDF from PowerPoint's notes view instead.

4.q: Which file types are accepted?
4.a: Modern .pptx, legacy .ppt, and OpenDocument .odp presentations, in any mix, several at a time. Keynote and Google Slides decks need to be exported to .pptx first.

5.q: What page size do the PDF pages have?
5.a: Each page matches the slide's own dimensions, so a 16:9 deck produces landscape pages in that ratio rather than being forced onto Letter or A4. If you need a standard paper size for printing, run the result through [0]Fix Page Size[/0].

6.q: Why do some fonts look different in the PDF?
6.a: The in-browser engine ships with its own fonts and can't see fonts installed on your computer, so a deck that uses a font it doesn't have is rendered with a substitute, which can shift line breaks. Sticking to common fonts keeps the layout closest to the original.

7.q: What do I get when I convert several presentations at once?
7.a: Each file becomes a separate PDF with the original name, and they're bundled into powerpoint-converted.zip. A single file downloads straight away as a PDF.

8.q: Is my presentation uploaded to a server?
8.a: No. The LibreOffice engine is downloaded to your browser and runs there; the presentation is opened and converted on your own machine. Confidential pitch decks and internal reviews never leave your device.

1.q: What does the JSON output contain?
1.a: It follows the LlamaIndex document schema: one document per page with that page's text and metadata fields. It's produced by PyMuPDF's LlamaIndex integration, so it can be loaded directly into LlamaIndex or any pipeline that accepts per-page text with metadata.

2.q: How is this different from PDF to Text or PDF to Markdown?
2.a: [0]PDF to Text[/0] gives one plain text stream, and PDF to Markdown keeps headings and structure for reading. This tool splits the content page by page and wraps it in structured JSON with metadata, which is what retrieval pipelines need for chunking and citing sources.

3.q: Does it work on scanned PDFs?
3.a: Only if they already have a text layer. Scanned images produce empty or near-empty output, so run them through [0]OCR PDF[/0] first and then extract.

4.q: Can I process a whole batch of PDFs?
4.a: Yes. Upload multiple files and you get pdf-for-ai.zip containing one yourfile_llm.json per PDF; a single file downloads as yourfile_llm.json directly. If one file in the batch fails, the rest still complete and the summary tells you how many failed.

5.q: Can I choose which pages to extract or control the chunk size?
5.a: No. There are no options; every page is extracted with its full text and metadata. Do chunking in your own pipeline, where you can pick sizes that fit your embedding model, and drop pages you don't need there.

6.q: Can I prepare a password-protected PDF for AI tools?
6.a: Yes. If a file is encrypted, you're prompted for its password before extraction starts, and the text is pulled from the decrypted copy.

7.q: Is my document sent to an AI service?
7.a: No. Despite the name, nothing is sent to an AI provider or any server; the extraction runs with PyMuPDF compiled to WebAssembly inside your browser. You decide afterward where the JSON goes.

8.q: What can I do with the JSON file?
8.a: Feed it to a RAG pipeline, build a knowledge base for a chatbot, run LLM analysis over reports, or turn a PDF collection into training data. Because the content is split per page with metadata, answers can point back to the page they came from.

1.q: What is the difference between the user password and the owner password?
1.a: The user password is required and is what anyone must type to open the file. The owner password is optional; when you set a different one, the PDF also gets usage restrictions, so someone who opens it with only the user password can't print, copy, edit, annotate, fill forms, or rearrange pages.

2.q: What encryption does Protect PDF use?
2.a: 256-bit AES, applied with QPDF's implementation of the PDF 2.0 encryption standard. There is no option to pick a weaker cipher, so the strength of the protection comes down to how strong your password is.

3.q: What happens if I forget the password?
3.a: There is no recovery. AES-256 can't be brute-forced in any practical time, and BentoPDF keeps no copy of the file or the password. Store the password somewhere safe and keep an unprotected original for yourself.

4.q: Do I still get restrictions if I only enter a user password?
4.a: No. With only a user password the file needs the password to open, but once opened there are no limits on printing, copying, or editing. Add a separate owner password if you want those restrictions.

5.q: Can I restrict printing or copying without requiring a password to open the file?
5.a: Not with this tool, because the user password is mandatory here. Use [0]Change Permissions[/0] instead, which applies restrictions while leaving the file openable without a password.

6.q: How do I remove the password later?
6.a: Open the protected file in the [0]password removal tool[/0], enter the password, and download a copy with the encryption removed. You need the password to do this; there is no bypass.

7.q: Will the protected PDF open in any reader?
7.a: Any current PDF reader, including Adobe Reader, Preview, Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, opens AES-256 encrypted files. Very old readers released before AES-256 support was added may refuse the file.

8.q: Is my PDF or my password sent anywhere?
8.a: No. QPDF runs as WebAssembly in your browser, so the file is encrypted on your device and neither the document nor the passwords are transmitted. Share the password with your recipient through a different channel than the file itself.

1.q: Do I need Photoshop installed?
1.a: No. The PSD is read by PyMuPDF running in your browser, which uses the flattened composite image stored inside the file, so the conversion works on any computer with a modern browser.

2.q: Are the layers kept in the PDF?
2.a: No. The PDF contains one flattened image of the composite, so individual layers, adjustment layers, masks, and layer effects can't be toggled or edited afterward. It's a picture of the document as it looked when the PSD was saved.

3.q: Why does my PSD convert to a blank or wrong-looking page?
3.a: The converter relies on the composite image Photoshop writes when Maximize Compatibility is on. If that option was off when the file was saved, the composite may be missing or stale; resave the PSD with Maximize Compatibility enabled and convert again.

4.q: What resolution will the PDF have?
4.a: The composite is embedded at its full pixel dimensions with no downsampling, so a 300 DPI print file stays at print quality. That also means large artwork produces a large PDF; run it through [0]Compress PDF[/0] if you need a smaller proof.

5.q: What happens when I convert several PSDs together?
5.a: They're combined into one PDF named psd_to_pdf.pdf, with each PSD becoming a page in the order listed. To get separate PDFs, convert the files one at a time.

6.q: Can I convert other Photoshop or image formats here?
6.a: Only files with a .psd extension are accepted. For PNG, JPG, TIFF, or WebP exports use [0]Images to PDF[/0], which also lets you set page size and margins.

7.q: Are my design files uploaded?
7.a: No. The PSD is decoded and the PDF written by PyMuPDF compiled to WebAssembly in your browser, so unreleased designs and client work never leave your machine.

1.q: How do I open a .pub file without Microsoft Publisher?
1.a: Upload the .pub file here and click Convert to PDF. A LibreOffice engine compiled to WebAssembly runs in your browser, reads the Publisher file, and writes a PDF you can open on any device, so you don't need Publisher or any other Microsoft software installed.

2.q: Will the layout look the same as in Publisher?
2.a: Text, images, and text boxes are placed according to the original layout, and most flyers and newsletters convert well. Layered text boxes and tightly positioned elements can shift slightly, and fonts that aren't standard system fonts may be substituted, so check the output when exact positioning matters.

3.q: Why does the first Publisher file take longer?
3.a: The conversion engine is roughly 75 MB compressed and is downloaded and started the first time you convert in a session, with a progress indicator showing how far along it is. After that, additional files convert much faster.

4.q: Can I convert several Publisher files at once?
4.a: Add multiple .pub files, remove any you don't want, and convert them together. A single file downloads as a PDF with the same base name; several are packaged into pub-to-pdf.zip, with duplicate names given a numbered suffix.

5.q: Can I convert a PDF back into a Publisher file?
5.a: No, the conversion is one way, from .pub to PDF. If you need an editable result, convert the PDF with [0]PDF to Word[/0] afterward and rebuild the layout there.

6.q: Is the text in the converted PDF selectable?
6.a: The PDF is generated from the document's text objects, so text stays selectable and searchable rather than being flattened into an image. Text that was placed in the original as a picture stays a picture.

7.q: Is my Publisher file uploaded to a server?
7.a: No. The whole conversion happens inside your browser, so the .pub file and the resulting PDF never leave your computer. Client artwork, unreleased newsletters, and event programs stay private.

1.q: What does rasterizing a PDF actually do?
1.a: Every page is rendered to a bitmap and the bitmaps are reassembled into a new PDF. The result looks the same but contains no text objects, fonts, layers, form fields, or hidden content, only a picture of each page, much like a photocopy.

2.q: Which DPI should I choose when rasterizing?
2.a: 150, the default, is fine for reading on screen and ordinary office printing. Use 300 for print-quality output or when someone will zoom in on fine print, 600 only for archival or professional printing, and 72 when the smallest possible file matters more than sharpness.

3.q: PNG or JPEG?
3.a: PNG is lossless, so text edges stay crisp, but files are bigger. JPEG (saved at quality 95) is noticeably smaller and works well for scanned or photographic pages, but can leave faint artifacts around sharp text. Grayscale is available with either and shrinks files further for black-and-white documents.

4.q: Why is the rasterized file bigger than the original?
4.a: A text PDF stores a few kilobytes of font and glyph data per page, whereas a 300 DPI image of a Letter page is 2550 x 3300 pixels. Lower the DPI, switch to JPEG, or run the result through [0]Compress PDF[/0] if size matters.

5.q: Can I make the text selectable again afterward?
5.a: Not from the rasterized file itself; the operation is one-way, so keep the original. You can add a searchable text layer back with [0]OCR PDF[/0], though recognized text is never as exact as the original.

6.q: How is this different from flattening a PDF?
6.a: Flattening merges form fields and annotations into the page but keeps text as text. Rasterizing goes further and turns everything, text included, into pixels. If you only need to lock form fields or comments, [0]Flatten PDF[/0] keeps the file searchable and much smaller.

7.q: Are my confidential documents uploaded to be rasterized?
7.a: No. Rendering is done by the PyMuPDF WebAssembly module running in your browser, so the pages are drawn and repacked on your own machine. That's what makes the tool a safe way to strip hidden text and layers from a sensitive file before sharing it.

8.q: Can I rasterize several PDFs at once?
8.a: Yes. Add as many as you like; each is processed with the same DPI, format, and grayscale settings, and the results download together as rasterized-pdfs.zip. A single file downloads on its own.

1.q: What counts as an annotation here?
1.a: Everything stored in a page's annotation list: sticky notes and comments, highlights, underlines, strikethroughs, freehand ink, stamps, shapes, text boxes, clickable links, and file attachments. Page text, images, and vector graphics are never touched.

2.q: Will my form fields survive?
2.a: No. Form fields are stored as widget annotations, so they're removed along with everything else and any typed-in values disappear with them. If you want the filled-in values to stay visible, run [0]Flatten PDF[/0] first, then remove annotations.

3.q: Does it remove watermarks?
3.a: Only watermarks that were added as annotations. Watermarks drawn into the page content itself stay in place, since they're part of the page graphics rather than a separate object.

4.q: Can I remove only some annotations instead of all of them?
4.a: Not with this tool; it clears every annotation on every page in one pass. To delete individual comments or highlights, open the file in the [0]PDF Editor[/0] and remove them one at a time.

5.q: Why are some highlights still there after processing?
5.a: They were flattened: a previous tool merged them into the page graphics, so they're no longer separate annotation objects. Flattened markup can't be removed by this tool.

6.q: Does the text stay selectable, and do bookmarks survive?
6.a: Yes to both. The file is edited at the object level without re-rendering pages, so text remains selectable and searchable, and bookmarks, page order, and page sizes are unchanged. Links lose their click action, though the visible link text stays.

7.q: Will a digital signature stay valid?
7.a: No. Signature fields are annotations and are removed, and saving a modified copy invalidates an existing signature anyway. Remove annotations before signing, not after.

8.q: Is the PDF uploaded to strip the comments?
8.a: No. The annotations are removed with pdf-lib in your browser and the cleaned copy downloads under the original filename, so a heavily annotated contract never leaves your machine.

1.q: How does the tool decide a page is blank?
1.a: Each page is rendered at reduced size and the tool counts pixels that are noticeably darker than white. If that share is below the limit set by the sensitivity slider, the page is flagged, so pages with faint scanner noise can still count as blank.

2.q: What does the sensitivity slider actually change?
2.a: It sets how much ink a page may contain and still count as blank. At 100% only pages with under 0.1% non-white pixels are flagged, at 0% pages with up to 5% are, and the default 80% sits at about 1%.

3.q: It missed pages that look blank, or flagged pages I want to keep. What now?
3.a: Lower the sensitivity if pages that look empty were missed, and raise it if pages with a light header, footer, or watermark were flagged. Then click Detect Blank Pages again and check the thumbnails.

4.q: Can I review the pages before they're removed?
4.a: After detection the tool shows a thumbnail of every flagged page, and clicking a thumbnail deselects it so it stays in the document. Only the pages that remain selected are removed when you confirm.

5.q: Will a page with only a page number be treated as blank?
5.a: A lone page number covers well under 0.1% of the page, so even the strictest setting can flag it as blank. That's why the thumbnail review matters when such pages need to stay.

6.q: Are the remaining pages changed in any way?
6.a: The kept pages are copied over exactly, with their content, fonts, and order untouched. Bookmarks aren't carried into the new file, since the pages are assembled into a fresh PDF, so rebuild them with [0]Edit Bookmarks[/0] if you need them.

7.q: Why does detection take a while on long documents?
7.a: Every page has to be rendered to pixels before it can be measured, so the time grows with page count and page complexity. Progress is shown while it works, and nothing else is needed from you until the thumbnails appear.

8.q: Does the PDF leave my computer for the scan?
8.a: No. Pages are rendered and analyzed in your browser, and the cleaned PDF is written locally. That's also why the scan speed depends on your own device rather than a server.

1.q: What metadata exactly gets removed?
1.a: The document info fields (Title, Author, Subject, Keywords, Creator, Producer, and the creation and modification dates), the XMP metadata stream, the document ID pair in the trailer, and application-specific PieceInfo left behind by tools like Illustrator or InDesign. There are no options; it always clears all of these.

2.q: What stays in the file?
2.a: All visible content, plus form fields, annotations, bookmarks, links, and any file attachments. Names stored inside those elements, such as the author on a sticky-note comment, are not touched. To strip comments, scripts, and attachments as well, use [0]Sanitize PDF[/0].

3.q: Does it remove metadata from images inside the PDF?
3.a: No. Image data is left as it is, so any EXIF or XMP information a photo carried when it was placed into the PDF stays with that image. If that matters, [0]Rasterize PDF[/0] re-renders every page as a fresh image, at the cost of selectable text.

4.q: How can I confirm the metadata is gone?
4.a: Open the cleaned file in [0]View Metadata[/0] and check that the fields are blank. Running the same check on the original first shows you exactly what is about to be removed.

5.q: Can this be undone?
5.a: No. The cleaned file keeps no record of the removed values. Keep your original copy if you may need the author, dates, or other details later.

6.q: Will removing metadata reduce the file size?
6.a: A little, since the XMP block and info fields are dropped, usually only a few kilobytes. For a real reduction, follow up with [0]Compress PDF[/0].

7.q: Does it remove comments, annotations, or hidden text?
7.a: No, it only targets metadata. Comments and markup are annotations, which stay; [0]Remove Annotations[/0] handles those. Hidden or white text remains part of the page content, so review the document itself if it went through several revisions.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded while the metadata is removed?
8.a: No. The file is opened and rewritten by a PDF library in your browser, which is the point when the goal is anonymity: the document never touches a server, and no server log records what you cleaned.

1.q: What is the difference between Remove Restrictions and Unlock PDF?
1.a: Use [0]Unlock PDF[/0] when a PDF asks for a password before it will open. Use this tool when the PDF opens but blocks printing, copying, editing, or commenting; it strips those restrictions and writes a copy with no encryption at all.

2.q: Do I need the owner password?
2.a: If the PDF opens without asking for a password, leave the field empty and the restrictions are removed as is. If a password is required, enter it in the Owner Password field. The tool doesn't crack, guess, or brute-force passwords.

3.q: What restrictions exactly get removed?
3.a: Password protection, printing limits, editing locks, text and image copying restrictions, annotation and commenting limits, and the usage restrictions attached to some digitally signed PDFs. The output has zero encryption, so anyone who receives it can open it freely.

4.q: Is it legal to remove restrictions from a PDF?
4.a: That depends on your rights to the document and on local law. Removing restrictions from files you own or are licensed to use, for example to run accessibility tools or copy quotes for notes, is the intended use. Don't use it to get around someone else's copyright or licensing terms.

5.q: Will the content of the PDF change?
5.a: No. QPDF rewrites only the encryption layer; pages, text, images, bookmarks, and form fields are untouched, and the output keeps the original file name.

6.q: Why does it say the PDF may require the correct owner password?
6.a: That error appears when QPDF can't open the file with the password you entered, or with no password. Check for typos and caps lock, and if the file needs a password to open, enter that one.

7.q: Can I keep the PDF encrypted but allow printing?
7.a: Not with this tool, which removes all security. To keep a password and adjust individual permissions such as printing or copying, use [0]Change Permissions[/0] instead.

8.q: Does removing restrictions upload my PDF or password?
8.a: No. QPDF runs as WebAssembly inside your browser tab, so the file and any password you enter stay on your device.

1.q: What kinds of damaged PDF can this fix?
1.a: It rebuilds the file's internal structure, which recovers broken or missing cross-reference tables, wrong object numbers and stream lengths, endings cut off by an incomplete download, and quirks left by buggy PDF generators. If the actual content data is still in the file, it usually comes back.

2.q: What can't Repair PDF recover?
2.a: Files where most of the content bytes are gone, files that aren't really PDFs despite the extension, and encrypted files whose password you don't have. It also can't regenerate image data: a corrupted picture inside an otherwise fixed PDF stays corrupted.

3.q: How does the repair work?
3.a: Each file is passed through QPDF, which reads whatever structure it can find, reconstructs the object table, and writes a clean new PDF. The rewritten file downloads as repaired-<original name>.pdf.

4.q: Can I repair a password-protected PDF?
4.a: Yes, if you know the password. You're asked for it before the repair starts, and the repaired copy is written without encryption, so run it through [0]Protect PDF[/0] again if it still needs a password.

5.q: Can I repair several PDFs at once?
5.a: Yes. One repaired file downloads directly, and several download together as repaired_pdfs.zip. Files that couldn't be repaired are listed by name in a message, and the rest still download.

6.q: The repair failed. What else can I try?
6.a: Open the file in a web browser such as Chrome or Firefox, which have their own recovery logic, and use the browser's print or save function to write a new PDF. If the file is encrypted, remove the password first with the [0]password removal tool[/0] and then repair the result.

7.q: Will repairing change how my PDF looks?
7.a: No. The page content, fonts, and images are carried over as they are; only the surrounding file structure is rewritten.

8.q: Is my damaged PDF uploaded to a server for repair?
8.a: No. QPDF runs as WebAssembly inside your browser, so the broken file is read and rewritten on your own device. A file that fails to repair here was never copied anywhere either.

1.q: When would I need to reverse the page order of a PDF?
1.a: Most often after a scanner or a print-to-PDF job fed the sheets last page first, or when a document assembled from images ended up backwards. The tool flips the whole sequence so the last page becomes page 1.

2.q: Does it change the content or rotation of the pages?
2.a: No. Each page is copied as is, including its size, rotation, and any annotations on it; only the order changes.

3.q: Are bookmarks preserved?
3.a: Page content and page-level annotations are kept, but the output is rebuilt page by page, so document-level bookmarks aren't carried over. Add them back with [0]Edit Bookmarks[/0] if you need them.

4.q: What is the reversed PDF's filename?
4.a: A single PDF downloads with its original filename, so it replaces the source if you save it to the same folder. Several files are reversed independently and downloaded together as reversed_pdfs.zip.

5.q: Can I move just a few pages instead of reversing the whole document?
5.a: Use [0]Duplicate & Organize[/0] to drag pages into any order, duplicate, or delete them. Reverse Pages is a one-click full reversal with no per-page controls.

6.q: Can I reverse the pages of a password-protected PDF?
6.a: You're asked for the password when processing starts and the decrypted copy is reversed. The output isn't encrypted.

7.q: Is the PDF uploaded to reverse it?
7.a: No. The pages are copied into a new document by pdf-lib running in your browser, and the file is downloaded from there; nothing is transmitted.

1.q: Can I rotate a PDF page by an angle other than 90 degrees?
1.a: That's what this tool is for. Type any angle from -360 to 360 degrees, in steps of 0.1, into the box under a page and the thumbnail turns to match; positive values rotate clockwise and negative values counterclockwise.

2.q: How do I straighten a slightly crooked scan?
2.a: Enter a small correction such as 1.5 or -2 for the tilted page and watch the preview until the lines of text look level, then click Apply Rotations. If a whole scanned document is skewed, [0]Deskew PDF[/0] detects and corrects the angle on every page automatically.

3.q: What happens to the page size when I rotate by an odd angle?
3.a: For 90, 180, and 270 degrees the rotation is stored as a page attribute and the page just turns. For any other angle the content is placed on a new page sized to the rotated bounding box, so the page gets larger and the corners around the content are left blank.

4.q: Does rotating by a custom angle turn my text into an image?
4.a: No. The page content is embedded as vector content and drawn at the new angle, so text stays sharp, selectable, and searchable at any zoom level. Links, form fields, and comments on pages rotated by a non-90-degree angle aren't carried over, though.

5.q: How do I rotate every page by the same angle?
5.a: Type the angle in the Batch Rotation box at the top and click Apply to All. That overwrites the angle on every page, so make any per-page tweaks after the batch step, not before.

6.q: What do the minus and plus buttons next to each page do?
6.a: They nudge that page's angle by one degree in either direction and are handy for fine-tuning after typing a rough value. For finer control, type the value directly; the field accepts tenths of a degree.

7.q: Can I rotate just one page and leave the rest alone?
7.a: Each page has its own angle field, so set the value on the page you want and leave the others at 0. Pages left at 0 are copied through unchanged.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded to rotate the pages?
8.a: No. The thumbnails are rendered and the rotated PDF is rebuilt in your browser, and the file downloads under its original name straight from the page. Nothing is sent to a server.

1.q: Can I rotate just one page instead of the whole document?
1.a: Yes. Every page shows as a thumbnail with its own left and right buttons, so a single sideways scan in a 40-page file can be fixed on its own. The buttons at the top rotate every page at once when the whole document is the wrong way up.

2.q: How do I rotate a page 180 degrees?
2.a: Click the same direction twice. Rotations add up in 90-degree steps, so two clicks give 180 and three clicks give 270, the same as one click the other way. The thumbnail updates so you can see the current state before saving.

3.q: Does rotating reduce the quality of the pages?
3.a: No. The tool changes each page's rotation attribute rather than re-rendering anything, so text stays selectable, images keep their resolution, and the file size stays about the same.

4.q: Will the rotation stick when I open the file in another app or print it?
4.a: Yes. The rotation is written into the PDF page itself, which every viewer and printer honors, unlike the temporary rotate button in a viewer that resets when you close the file.

5.q: Can I rotate by an angle other than 90 degrees, like to straighten a tilted scan?
5.a: Not here; this tool works in 90-degree steps only. Use [0]Rotate by Custom Degrees[/0] for arbitrary angles, or Deskew PDF to straighten scans automatically.

6.q: Can I rotate only the odd or even pages?
6.a: There's no page selection or range field in this tool; you either rotate pages one at a time with their buttons or all of them together. For selecting groups of pages, [0]PDF Multi Tool[/0] is the better fit.

7.q: Is my PDF uploaded to rotate its pages?
7.a: No. The thumbnails are rendered by your browser and the rotated file is written locally, so the document never leaves your computer. The rotated PDF downloads under the original file name.

8.q: Does rotating keep my bookmarks?
8.a: Page content, images, and annotations come through unchanged, but bookmarks are not carried over, because the rotated file is built from copied pages. A document that relies on its outline will need it added back with the [0]Bookmark[/0] tool.

1.q: Why does the first RTF file take longer to convert?
1.a: The converter is LibreOffice compiled to WebAssembly, and the engine is about 77 MB compressed. It's downloaded and started the first time you convert in a session; after that, each file takes only a few seconds.

2.q: What RTF formatting is preserved in the PDF?
2.a: Font styles such as bold and italic, paragraph alignment, lists, tables, and embedded images come through as they would if you exported the file from LibreOffice Writer. Embedded OLE objects, such as inserted spreadsheets, may not render fully.

3.q: Will my fonts look the same?
3.a: Only fonts bundled with the engine are available, which covers common Latin, Arabic, and Hebrew faces. Fonts that aren't bundled are replaced with the closest substitute, so line breaks and spacing can shift slightly.

4.q: Can I convert many RTF files at once?
4.a: Yes. One file downloads as a PDF with the same base name; several files download together as rtf-converted.zip with one PDF per file, and duplicate names are numbered automatically.

5.q: What's the difference between this and Word to PDF?
5.a: Both use the same LibreOffice engine and produce the same result for RTF. [0]Word to PDF[/0] also accepts .doc, .docx, and .odt, so use it when you have a mix of formats in one batch.

6.q: Does it handle RTF from WordPad, TextEdit, or legal and medical software?
6.a: RTF written by any standard word processor converts, including files from WordPad, TextEdit, and exports from records systems. Proprietary extensions inside such files may be dropped, but the text and standard formatting still convert.

7.q: What about text in Chinese, Japanese, Korean, or Indic scripts?
7.a: Those fonts aren't bundled with the browser engine, so text in these scripts may render with a fallback font or as boxes. Latin, Arabic, and Hebrew scripts are covered.

8.q: Is my document sent to a LibreOffice server?
8.a: No. The whole LibreOffice engine runs inside your browser tab as WebAssembly. Your file is converted locally, and the only thing downloaded is the engine itself.

1.q: What does Sanitize PDF actually remove?
1.a: Ten things, each with its own checkbox: form fields are flattened, and metadata, annotations, JavaScript, embedded files, layers, links, the structure tree, MarkInfo, and optionally embedded fonts are stripped. Everything except font removal is checked by default.

2.q: Will the sanitized PDF look different?
2.a: The page content itself is untouched, but some interactive parts become static. Form fields turn into plain text, hyperlinks stop being clickable, and comments, highlights, and sticky notes disappear, so check the result before sending it.

3.q: Should I check Remove Embedded Fonts?
3.a: Usually not. It deletes the font programs the PDF relies on, and if the reader can't substitute a matching font the text can render incorrectly or not at all. Leave it unchecked unless you have a specific reason and have tested the result.

4.q: Does it remove the author name, creation date, and editing software?
4.a: Remove Metadata clears the Info dictionary, the XMP metadata stream, the document ID, and application-specific PieceInfo, so the author, title, dates, and producing software are gone. If that's all you need, [0]Remove Metadata[/0] does only this step.

5.q: Does it stop scripts that run when the PDF is opened?
5.a: Remove JavaScript deletes the document's script tree, its open action, and the automatic actions attached to the document, pages, annotations, and form fields. That covers the usual places a PDF can hide code that runs on open, print, or field changes.

6.q: Does sanitizing redact sensitive text on the pages?
6.a: No. It strips hidden and interactive data around the content, not the visible words or images, so anything you can read on the page is still there. If you need the page content reduced to a flat picture with no selectable text underneath, use [0]Rasterize PDF[/0].

7.q: Can I sanitize a password-protected PDF?
7.a: You'll be asked for the password after upload. The sanitized copy is written without encryption, so if the document should stay protected, run it through [0]Protect PDF[/0] afterward.

8.q: Is it safe to sanitize a PDF I don't trust here?
8.a: The file is parsed as data in your browser and never uploaded, and the tool doesn't execute any script inside it. Keep the original in case a stripped element turns out to be needed, since sanitizing can't be undone from the output.

1.q: Which settings give the most realistic scan look?
1.a: Subtle values work best: noise around 10 to 20, a rotation of about 0.5 degrees with a little Rotate Variance so each page tilts differently, and a touch of blur. Turn on Grayscale for a photocopier look, add Border for the dark edge a flatbed leaves, and drop Resolution to 100 to 150 DPI for a fax-like result.

2.q: What does Rotate Variance do?
2.a: It adds a random amount, up to the value you set (0 to 3 degrees), to the base rotation on every page, so a ten-page document doesn't have ten identically tilted pages. The preview shows only the base rotation; the variation is applied when you click Apply.

3.q: Can I still select or search the text afterward?
3.a: No. Each page is rendered, processed as pixels, and saved as a JPEG image, so the output is image-only. That's usually the point of a scan effect, but keep the original if you need editable text later.

4.q: Why does the preview look different from the final file?
4.a: The preview renders the first page at screen resolution and ignores the Resolution slider, so noise and blur can look slightly stronger or weaker in the final output, and it can't show the per-page rotation variance. The other settings match what you'll get.

5.q: How does the Resolution setting affect the file?
5.a: It sets the DPI at which pages are rendered before the effects are applied, from 72 to 300. Lower values make pages softer and more pixelated, like a cheap scanner, and produce smaller files; 300 DPI keeps text crisp but makes a much larger PDF.

6.q: Can I make the paper look old or yellowed?
6.a: Raise the Yellowish slider to add a warm tint that mimics aged or recycled paper. Combine it with Grayscale for a photocopy-of-a-photocopy look, and nudge Brightness down and Contrast up to imitate a tired toner cartridge.

7.q: Does it process more than one PDF at a time?
7.a: No. This tool works on a single PDF per run, applying your settings to every page of that file. Load the next file after the first download finishes.

8.q: Does my document get uploaded to apply the effect?
8.a: No. Rendering, noise, blur, and rotation are all applied on a canvas in your browser, and the output PDF is assembled locally, so the file never leaves your computer.

1.q: How do I create my signature?
1.a: The built-in viewer offers three ways: draw it freehand with a mouse, trackpad, or finger; type your name and pick a signature font; or upload an image of your handwritten signature. Then click the page where it belongs and drag or resize it into place.

2.q: Can I sign on more than one page or add initials?
2.a: Yes. You can place as many signatures as you need on any pages of the document, so you can initial each page of an agreement and sign the last one in the same session.

3.q: What does the Flatten PDF option do?
3.a: With flattening on, the signature is permanently merged into the page content so it can't be moved or deleted in another viewer. With it off, the signature is saved as an annotation that compatible viewers can still edit. Turn it on before sending a signed document to someone else.

4.q: Is this a legally binding electronic signature?
4.a: It places an image of your signature on the page, which is widely accepted for everyday forms, NDAs, and agreements, but it carries no cryptographic proof of who signed. Whether it's binding depends on your jurisdiction and the agreement. If you need a verifiable, certificate-based signature, use [0]Digital Signature[/0].

5.q: What image should I upload for my signature?
5.a: A PNG with a transparent background gives the cleanest result because the page shows through around the strokes. An image with a solid white background will cover whatever sits underneath it.

6.q: Can I fill in form fields and sign at the same time?
