6.a: This tool is built for placing signatures. If the document has fillable fields, complete them in [0]Form Filler[/0] first, download the result, then sign it here.

7.q: Does signing work on a phone or tablet?
7.a: Yes. The viewer accepts touch input, so you can draw your signature with a finger or stylus, which often gives a more natural result than a mouse.

8.q: Is my signature or document uploaded?
8.a: No. The viewer, the signature tools, and the save step all run in your browser, so the PDF and your signature image never leave your device.

1.q: How do I extract a range of pages from a PDF?
1.a: Choose Extract by Page Range and type the pages you want, such as 1-5, 8, 11-13. By default the selected pages are combined into one PDF; switch the output to One PDF per range and each comma-separated range becomes its own file inside split-pages.zip.

2.q: Can I split a PDF into one file per page?
2.a: Yes. Pick Split All Pages into Separate Files and every page is written to its own PDF, named page-1.pdf, page-2.pdf, and so on, bundled in split-pages.zip.

3.q: How do I split a PDF every N pages?
3.a: Choose Split N Times and enter the chunk size. A 23-page file split every 5 pages produces five PDFs, and the tool warns you beforehand that the last one will hold only 3 pages. The files download as split-n-times.zip.

4.q: Can I split a PDF by chapters or bookmarks?
4.a: Yes, if the PDF has bookmarks. Choose Split by Bookmarks and a level (All, or level 0 through 3), and a new file starts at each bookmark's page, giving you split-1.pdf, split-2.pdf, and so on in split-by-bookmarks.zip. A PDF with no bookmarks at the chosen level shows an error instead.

5.q: How do I separate odd and even pages?
5.a: Select Split by Even/Odd Pages and pick even or odd; the matching pages are extracted into one PDF in their original order. This is a common step for double-sided printing on a single-sided printer.

6.q: Can I pick pages visually instead of typing numbers?
6.a: Yes. Select Pages Visually shows a thumbnail of every page; click the ones you want and they're extracted in page order. Combined output gives one PDF, and the separate option gives one file per page in a ZIP.

7.q: Does splitting reduce the quality of the pages?
7.a: No. Pages are copied by QPDF without re-rendering, so text, images, fonts, and vector graphics stay exactly as they were in the original.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded when I split it?
8.a: No. The page extraction and ZIP packaging run in your browser, and the resulting files are saved directly from your device.

1.q: Is the PDF vector or an image?
1.a: An image. Each SVG is rendered by your browser onto a canvas and the bitmap is placed on a PDF page, so the result won't scale without loss and the text isn't selectable. If you need true vector output, export the PDF from a vector editor such as Inkscape instead.

2.q: What size will the page be?
2.a: The page matches the SVG's width and height attributes in pixels, one pixel per PDF point. An SVG with no width and height (only a viewBox) renders at 800 by 600, so set explicit dimensions in the file for predictable results.

3.q: What do the quality settings change for SVG conversion?
3.a: High keeps the lossless PNG at full size. Medium re-encodes it as JPEG at 75 percent quality and limits the longest side to 2500 pixels; Low uses 50 percent and 1500 pixels, which also shrinks the page. For line art and text, High avoids JPEG artifacts.

4.q: Can I control the output resolution, for example 300 DPI?
4.a: There is no DPI setting; the render uses the SVG's own pixel dimensions. To get more pixels, increase the width and height attributes in the SVG source while keeping the viewBox, then convert.

5.q: Why did my SVG come out with missing text, fonts, or images?
5.a: The SVG is rendered from its own markup, so references to external files (linked images, imported fonts, external CSS) can't be loaded in that context and fall back or disappear. Embed images as data URIs and convert text to paths before converting.

6.q: Is transparency kept?
6.a: No. The canvas is filled with white before the SVG is drawn, so transparent areas become white in the PDF.

7.q: Can I put several SVGs into one PDF?
7.a: Upload multiple files and they become consecutive pages of a single from_svgs.pdf, in the order shown in the file list. Each page takes the size of its own SVG.

8.q: Is the SVG uploaded to be converted?
8.a: No. Rendering happens on a canvas in your browser and the PDF is built with pdf-lib on your device; nothing is sent anywhere.

1.q: How do I add a table of contents page to a PDF?
1.a: Upload a PDF that has bookmarks, set the title, font size, and font, and click Generate Table of Contents. A new page listing every bookmark with its page number is inserted at the front of the document, and the file downloads under its original name.

2.q: Why does it say my PDF has no bookmarks?
2.a: The TOC is built entirely from the PDF's bookmark outline, not from headings in the text, so a document without bookmarks has nothing to list. Create them first with [0]Edit Bookmarks[/0], then run this tool on the saved result.

3.q: Are the entries in the table of contents clickable?
3.a: Each entry links to the page it refers to, so readers can jump straight there in any viewer that supports links, and the printed page number is there for paper copies.

4.q: Does it handle nested bookmarks?
4.a: Sub-bookmarks are indented under their parent entries, so a chapter and section hierarchy comes through as a multi-level list.

5.q: Which fonts and sizes can I use?
5.a: You can pick from the 12 standard PDF fonts, which are Times, Helvetica, and Courier in regular, bold, italic, and bold italic, at sizes from 10pt to 72pt; Helvetica at 12pt is the default. These built-in fonts cover Latin text, so bookmark titles in other scripts may not display correctly.

6.q: Will the new TOC page mess up my existing bookmarks or page numbers?
6.a: Existing bookmarks are kept and still point at the right pages after the new page goes in at the front. Numbers printed on your pages don't change, so a page labeled 1 is now the second physical page; tick Add bookmark for TOC page if you want the TOC itself listed in the outline.

7.q: Can I add a table of contents to a PDF I just merged?
7.a: As long as the merged file has bookmarks, it works like any other PDF. Generate the TOC as the last step so the page numbers match the final page order.

8.q: Is my PDF uploaded to generate the table of contents?
8.a: No. The bookmark outline is read and the TOC page is typeset by a cpdf engine running as WebAssembly in a background thread of your browser, and the updated file is downloaded from there. The document never leaves your device.

1.q: How does it know which pixels are text?
1.a: It doesn't read the text; each page is rendered to an image and every dark pixel (red, green, and blue all below 120 on a 0 to 255 scale) is repainted in your chosen color. Black and dark gray type is caught, while light gray text, colored text, and photos are left alone.

2.q: Why did lines, borders, and my logo change color too?
2.a: Because the tool works on dark pixels rather than text objects, any dark element, including table rules, underlines, and black artwork, is recolored along with the text. There's no way to exclude regions in this tool.

3.q: Can I recolor only certain words or paragraphs?
3.a: No. One color is applied to all dark content on every page. To change individual words or headings while leaving the rest alone, edit the text directly in the [0]PDF Editor[/0].

4.q: Will the text still be selectable and searchable?
4.a: No. The output is image-based: each page is rendered at 2x and embedded as a PNG, so text can no longer be selected, searched, or copied. Keep the original if you need an editable version, or run [0]OCR PDF[/0] on the result to add a text layer back.

5.q: Why did the file get much bigger?
5.a: A page of text weighs a few kilobytes as text but becomes a full-page PNG image when recolored, so multi-page documents can grow many times over. [0]Compress PDF[/0] can shrink the result at the cost of some sharpness.

6.q: Can I turn black text white for a dark background?
6.a: Yes, any color works, including white, but the page background isn't changed, so white text on the original white page disappears. Choose a color that contrasts with the background the page already has.

7.q: Is my document uploaded to change the text color?
7.a: No. Each page is rendered and recolored on a canvas in your browser, and the new PDF is assembled there too, so the file never leaves your device. A progress indicator shows which page is being processed.

8.q: Why is colored or light gray text unchanged?
8.a: Only pixels dark enough to pass the threshold are repainted. Red headings, blue links, mid-gray captions, and anti-aliased edges lighter than the cutoff keep their original color, which can leave a faint halo around recolored letters.

1.q: Does it handle multi-page TIFFs?
1.a: Yes. Every page (IFD) inside a TIFF becomes a separate PDF page, so a 10-page fax file gives a 10-page PDF without splitting it first. Pages from several TIFF files are appended in list order into one document.

2.q: Which TIFF variants are supported?
2.a: Grayscale and RGB images at 8, 16, or 32 bits per channel, with or without an alpha channel, stored uncompressed or with LZW or Deflate compression. TIFFs using CCITT Group 3 or 4 fax compression, PackBits, or JPEG compression can't be decoded; re-save those as uncompressed or LZW TIFF in an image editor first.

3.q: What do the quality options do?
3.a: High stores each page as lossless PNG, keeping every pixel. Medium and Low re-encode pages as JPEG at 75% and 50% quality, which is much smaller for scanned photos but can blur fine text. Pixel dimensions stay the same in all three.

4.q: What page size does a converted TIFF get?
4.a: The page is sized to the pixel dimensions at one point per pixel, and the TIFF's own DPI tag is ignored. A 300 DPI Letter scan of 2550 by 3300 pixels therefore becomes a page about 35 by 46 inches; run the result through [0]Fix Page Size[/0] to get true Letter or A4 pages.

5.q: Will the PDF be searchable?
5.a: No. Scanned TIFFs are images, and the PDF contains the same images with no text layer. Run the output through [0]OCR PDF[/0] to make it searchable and copyable.

6.q: What happens with 16-bit or floating-point images?
6.a: They're reduced to 8 bits per channel for the PDF, so medical or scientific TIFFs lose their extended range. WhiteIsZero grayscale files are inverted correctly so black stays black.

7.q: Why does a large TIFF take so long or fail?
7.a: The whole file is decoded into browser memory and each page is expanded to raw pixels before being re-encoded. Files of several hundred megabytes can exhaust that memory, so split very large TIFFs or convert them a few at a time.

8.q: Are my scans uploaded?
8.a: No. The TIFF is decoded with a JavaScript decoder in your browser and the PDF is assembled locally, so medical images or confidential faxes never leave your device.

1.q: Which timestamp servers can I use?
1.a: The menu offers five public RFC 3161 authorities: DigiCert, Sectigo, SSL.com, FreeTSA, and MeSign. There is no field for a custom URL, so the choice is limited to those presets.

2.q: Does timestamping work offline?
2.a: No. The tool has to contact the chosen TSA over the internet to obtain the signed timestamp token; everything else, including hashing the file and embedding the token, happens in your browser. If the request fails you can pick another server and try again.

3.q: What's the difference between a timestamp and a digital signature?
3.a: A digital signature proves who signed the document and needs your own certificate, while a document timestamp proves only when the document existed, vouched for by the TSA. If you need both, sign first with [0]Digital Sign PDF[/0] and then add the timestamp here.

4.q: Can I timestamp a PDF that is already signed?
4.a: The timestamp is appended as an incremental update rather than a rewrite of the file, so an existing signature stays intact and verifiable, and the timestamp shows as its own entry in the reader's signature panel.

5.q: Will anything appear on the page?
5.a: No. The timestamp is invisible; it lives in the file's signature data and shows up in the signature panel of Acrobat and similar readers, not as a stamp on the page. The downloaded file keeps its original name.

6.q: Why did I get a Timestamp Failed error?
6.a: Most often the TSA didn't respond or your connection dropped, so try another server from the list. On self-hosted copies of BentoPDF served over HTTPS, the servers that only offer HTTP endpoints need a CORS proxy configured at build time; FreeTSA uses HTTPS and works without one.

7.q: How long does the timestamp stay valid?
7.a: Readers validate the token against the TSA's certificate chain, so it verifies as long as that chain is trusted. This tool doesn't embed long-term validation (LTV) data, so verification years later depends on the reader still being able to check the TSA's certificates.

8.q: How do I check the timestamp after downloading?
8.a: Open the signature panel in Adobe Acrobat Reader or another signature-aware viewer; the timestamp is listed there with its time and the authority that issued it. If the reader trusts the TSA's certificate chain, it reports the timestamp as valid.

1.q: Can I type text instead of uploading a file?
1.a: Yes. Switch the toggle to Type Text, paste or type into the editor, and click Create PDF. It's the quickest way to turn clipboard content into a PDF without saving a .txt file first.

2.q: Which fonts and page sizes are available?
2.a: Four fonts: Helvetica (sans-serif), Tiro and Times (serif), and Courier (monospace), at any size from 6 to 72 points. Page sizes cover the ISO A, B, and C series from A0 to C10 plus US Letter, Legal, Tabloid, Ledger, and 11 x 17, with A4 as the default.

3.q: What happens if I upload several .txt files?
3.a: Their contents are joined into a single PDF, in the order listed, with a blank line between each file. There's no page break between files, so if each one needs its own pages, convert them one at a time.

4.q: Does it handle right-to-left languages like Arabic or Hebrew?
4.a: Yes. When the text contains Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, or Urdu characters, the direction switches to right-to-left and the text is right-aligned, both in the editor and in the PDF.

5.q: Can I change the margins?
5.a: No. Margins are fixed at 1 inch (72 points) on every side, and text wraps to fit within them at the chosen font size. Pick a larger page size if you need more text per page.

6.q: Will long lines wrap or get cut off?
6.a: Lines wrap automatically at the right margin, and line breaks from the source are kept. Courier gives every character the same width, which suits code and logs.

7.q: What filename does the PDF made from my text file get?
7.a: The download is always named text_to_pdf.pdf, regardless of the input file name. Rename it after downloading if you're producing several.

8.q: Is the text I type sent to a server?
8.a: No. The PDF is generated by a PDF engine running in your browser, so notes, logs, or credentials pasted into the editor never leave your device. The engine itself is downloaded on first use, which is why the first conversion pauses briefly.

1.q: Can Unlock PDF remove a password I don't know?
1.a: No. It needs the current password and doesn't crack, guess, or brute-force anything. If the PDF opens without a password but blocks printing or copying, use [0]Remove Restrictions[/0] instead.

2.q: Does it work with the owner password or only the open password?
2.a: Either. Enter whichever password you have; the tool authenticates with it and saves a copy with the encryption removed entirely, so no residual restrictions remain.

3.q: Can I remove the password from several PDFs at once?
3.a: Yes, as long as they share the same password. Upload them all, enter the password once, and you get decrypted-pdfs.zip with the files under their original names. PDFs with different passwords need separate batches; any file that fails is counted in the summary while the rest still download.

4.q: Why do I get a password error?
4.a: The password didn't match the file. Check caps lock and trailing spaces, and make sure you're using this file's password rather than one from a similar document. A damaged file shows a Decryption Failed message instead; [0]Repair PDF[/0] may help there.

5.q: Will removing the password change the document?
5.a: No. Pages, text, images, forms, and bookmarks are kept; only the encryption layer is removed, and the file keeps its name. The output has no security at all, so re-protect it with [0]Protect PDF[/0] if it needs a new password.

6.q: Why would I remove the password from my own PDF?
6.a: Common reasons: a document management system that rejects encrypted files, merging with other PDFs (many merge tools can't read encrypted input), long-term archiving, or a password that's no longer needed.

7.q: Is my password or file sent anywhere?
7.a: No. Decryption runs in your browser with WebAssembly PDF engines (CoherentPDF, with PyMuPDF as a fallback), so the file and the password stay on your device.

8.q: Is this the same tool that was called Decrypt PDF?
8.a: Yes. Decrypt PDF was renamed to Unlock PDF; it's the same tool with the same behavior.

1.q: How do I check whether a signed PDF was changed after it was signed?
1.a: Upload the PDF and validation starts on its own. For each signature the tool hashes the bytes the signature covers, compares that hash with the digest stored inside the signature, and then verifies the signature against the signer's public key; any change to the covered bytes makes the status Invalid with the reason shown on the card. Every signature in the file gets its own card, and the summary at the top counts how many were found.

2.q: What do Valid, Invalid, and Unverified mean?
2.a: Valid means the signature was cryptographically verified, covers the whole file, and uses a secure digest. Invalid means verification ran and failed, for example because the bytes changed or the key doesn't match. Unverified means the signature uses an algorithm the tool can't check, such as Ed25519 or SM2, so confirm it in Adobe Acrobat or with openssl before relying on it.

3.q: Which signature algorithms are supported?
3.a: RSA with PKCS#1 v1.5 padding, RSA-PSS, and ECDSA on the P-256, P-384, and P-521 curves, with SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512 digests. Signatures hashed with MD5 or SHA-1 are flagged with an Insecure Digest status and never reported as valid, because both algorithms have published collision attacks.

4.q: Why does the card say Signer Identity Not Verified?
4.a: The tool has no built-in list of certificate authorities, so on its own it can confirm the signature is intact but not who is behind the certificate. Upload your organization's root or intermediate certificate as a .pem, .crt, .cer, or .der file and validation reruns: signatures whose certificate matches it or chains back to it get a Trusted badge, and the summary counts those as valid.

5.q: Does partial coverage mean the document was tampered with?
5.a: It means bytes were appended after this signature was applied. The part that was signed is still intact, so the tool shows a Modified After Signing warning instead of marking the signature invalid. That is not proof of tampering by itself: a second signature or an incremental save produces the same result, and only the last signature added can cover the entire file. Treat it as a reason to look at what was added.

6.q: Does it check whether the signing certificate was revoked?
6.a: No. The tool checks the certificate's validity dates, the trust chain against a certificate you provide, and the cryptographic integrity of the signature, but it doesn't query OCSP responders or certificate revocation lists. For a revocation check, verify the file in a desktop tool with network access.

7.q: What happens if the certificate has expired since the document was signed?
7.a: Expiry is judged against today's date, so a certificate that is now past its Valid Until date shows a Certificate Expired status and isn't counted as valid in the summary, even if the signature itself checks out. Compare the Signed On time with the Valid From and Valid Until dates on the card to see whether the certificate was current at signing.

8.q: Is the signed PDF or my trusted certificate uploaded anywhere?
8.a: No. Signature parsing and the cryptographic checks run in your browser using node-forge and the Web Crypto API, so the document and any certificate you add stay on your device.

1.q: What information can a PDF reveal about me?
1.a: The Info dictionary often holds the author's name (usually the operating system or Office username), the software used, and creation and modification timestamps. XMP metadata can add document IDs, revision history, and application details, and filled form field values are shown too. If you're about to publish or share the file, run [0]Remove Metadata[/0] afterward.

2.q: What is the difference between the Info dictionary and XMP metadata?
2.a: The Info dictionary is the older set of fixed fields: Title, Author, Subject, Keywords, Creator, Producer, and dates. XMP is an XML block with namespaces such as Dublin Core, xmp, and pdf, and it can hold far more. The two are meant to agree but often don't, which is why the tool shows both.

3.q: Why are the dates shown differently from what Acrobat displays?
3.a: PDF dates are stored as strings like D:20240101120000Z. The tool converts them to a readable date in your local time zone, so the hour can differ from a viewer that shows the raw value or uses a different zone.

4.q: How can I tell which program created the PDF?
4.a: Look at the Creator field (the application that made the original document, such as Word or InDesign) and the Producer field (the library that wrote the PDF, such as Acrobat Distiller or a PDF engine). The XMP section usually repeats them as xmp:CreatorTool and pdf:Producer.

5.q: Does it show the values filled into form fields?
5.a: The Interactive Form Fields section lists each field name with its current value, or Not Set when empty, which is a quick way to check what data a filled form contains before sending it.

6.q: Can I copy or export the metadata?
6.a: The Copy Metadata as JSON button puts the Info dictionary fields on your clipboard as a JSON object. The XMP tree and form field values are displayed on the page but aren't included in the copied JSON.

7.q: Can I change what I see here?
7.a: This tool is read-only. Use [0]Edit Metadata[/0] to change the title, author, keywords, and dates, or Remove Metadata to strip everything before publishing.

8.q: Is the PDF uploaded to read its metadata?
8.a: No. The file is parsed by pdf.js in your browser as soon as you select it, and nothing is transmitted, so you can inspect a sensitive document before deciding where it goes.

1.q: How do I open a Visio file without Visio?
1.a: Upload the .vsd or .vsdx file and click Convert to PDF. A LibreOffice engine compiled to WebAssembly loads in your browser, renders the diagram, and downloads a PDF you can open, print, or share on any device without a Visio license.

2.q: Which Visio formats are supported?
2.a: Both the legacy binary .vsd format from Visio 2003 and earlier and the XML-based .vsdx format from Visio 2013 and later, and you can mix them in one batch. Files saved as .vsdm or .vdx aren't accepted, so re-save those as .vsdx first.

3.q: Does a multi-page Visio diagram become a multi-page PDF?
3.a: Each Visio page becomes one PDF page, and the page size and orientation from the drawing are kept, so a landscape network diagram stays landscape.

4.q: Why does my old .vsd file look slightly different after conversion?
4.a: Older .vsd files generally convert with lower fidelity than .vsdx, so unusual shapes, custom stencils, or text formatting can render a little differently. Fonts that aren't available are substituted, which can shift labels; check the output if the diagram is going into formal documentation.

5.q: Can I convert several diagrams at once?
5.a: Add as many .vsd and .vsdx files as you need, remove any you don't want, and convert them together. One file downloads as a PDF with the same base name; several come back in vsd-to-pdf.zip, with duplicate names given a numbered suffix.

6.q: Why is my first Visio conversion slow?
6.a: The engine is roughly 75 MB compressed and has to be downloaded and started once per session, with a progress percentage shown while it loads. Later conversions in the same session skip that step and finish quickly.

7.q: Is the text in the PDF selectable?
7.a: Shape labels and connector text are written into the PDF as text, so you can select, copy, and search them. The diagram itself is drawn as vector shapes, so it stays sharp when zoomed or printed.

8.q: Is my Visio file uploaded to convert it?
8.a: No. The conversion engine runs entirely in your browser, so network diagrams, floor plans, and org charts are rendered on your own machine and the PDF is saved from there. Nothing is transmitted to a server.

1.q: Does each WebP image become its own page?
1.a: Yes. Every image is placed on a separate page sized to the image itself, in the order the files appear in the list, and the whole set downloads as one file named from_webps.pdf.

2.q: What page size will my WebP images get in the PDF?
2.a: The page matches the image's pixel dimensions at one point per pixel, so a 1600 x 1200 image produces a 1600 x 1200 point page, roughly 22 x 17 inches. To get standard A4 or Letter pages, run the result through [0]Fix Page Size[/0].

3.q: What do the quality settings change for WebP images?
3.a: High keeps the full pixel dimensions with the lightest compression. Medium, the default, re-encodes as JPEG at about 75 percent and scales images down so the longest side is at most 2500 pixels; Low uses about 50 percent and a 1500 pixel cap, which gives the smallest files.

4.q: Will transparent areas stay transparent?
4.a: No. Images are re-encoded through the browser's canvas as JPEG when they're embedded, and JPEG has no alpha channel, so see-through regions come out as a solid background. Flatten the image onto a white background in an image editor first if that matters.

5.q: Can I convert an animated WebP?
5.a: Only the first frame is used, since the browser decodes the file as a still image before it's placed on the page. Each animation becomes a single static page.

6.q: Can I mix WebP with JPG or PNG files in the same PDF?
6.a: Not on this page; the file picker accepts .webp only. Use [0]Images to PDF[/0], which takes WebP, JPG, PNG, and other formats together in a single conversion.

7.q: Are my images uploaded to make the PDF?
7.a: No. Each WebP is decoded by your browser's own image engine and written into the PDF locally, so the pictures never leave your device.

8.q: Can I reorder or remove images before converting?
8.a: You can remove any file from the list with its delete icon, but there's no drag reordering on this page, so pages follow the order in which you selected the files. Pick them in the order you want them to appear.

1.q: Do I need Microsoft Word installed to convert Word to PDF?
1.a: No. The conversion is done by LibreOffice compiled to WebAssembly running inside your browser, so it works on any computer, tablet, or phone with a modern browser and no Office license. The engine is about 77 MB and downloads on first use, so the first conversion of a session takes longer.

2.q: Can I convert Google Docs or Apple Pages files?
2.a: For Google Docs, download the document as .docx from File > Download and convert that. Pages files aren't supported; export them as Word or PDF from Pages first. The tool accepts .doc, .docx, .odt, and .rtf.

3.q: Will headings become PDF bookmarks, and do links stay clickable?
3.a: Yes, as long as the headings use Word's heading styles; LibreOffice's PDF export turns them into an outline, and hyperlinks in the document remain clickable in the PDF.

4.q: Why do fonts look different in the PDF?
4.a: Only fonts bundled with the engine are available, so a document set in a font that isn't embedded in the file is rendered with the closest substitute. The layout stays close, but line breaks can shift; embedding fonts in the .docx before converting avoids this.

5.q: Do tracked changes and comments appear in the PDF?
5.a: The document is rendered the way LibreOffice Writer displays it, so accept or reject tracked changes and delete comments in Word before converting if you want a clean PDF.

6.q: Can I convert several documents at once?
6.a: Yes. A single file downloads as a PDF with the same base name; multiple files are delivered as word-converted.zip with one PDF each, and duplicate names are numbered automatically.

7.q: What doesn't convert well?
7.a: Macros, ActiveX controls, and complex SmartArt may not render correctly, and Chinese, Japanese, Korean, or Indic text may show fallback fonts or boxes because those fonts aren't bundled. Standard text, tables, images, headers, footers, and footnotes convert reliably.

8.q: Is my document uploaded to a server for conversion?
8.a: No. The LibreOffice engine runs entirely inside your browser tab, so a resume, contract, or medical letter is converted on your own device and never sent anywhere.

1.q: Do I need WordPerfect installed to convert WPD files?
1.a: No. The tool loads a LibreOffice engine into your browser, and LibreOffice's WordPerfect filter reads the file directly, so nothing needs to be installed on your computer.

2.q: Which WordPerfect versions are supported?
2.a: All major WordPerfect versions that use the .wpd extension, including files from the DOS and early Windows era that current software often refuses to open. The file must actually end in .wpd; other extensions aren't accepted by the picker.

3.q: Why is the first WordPerfect conversion slow?
3.a: The LibreOffice engine is around 75 MB compressed and is downloaded the first time you convert, with a progress percentage shown while it loads. Later conversions in the same session skip that step and are much faster.

4.q: What is preserved from the original document?
4.a: Text, page layout, and basic formatting such as fonts, bold and italic, and indents carry over to the PDF. WordPerfect macros and reveal codes are not preserved, since they have no equivalent in a PDF.

5.q: Can I convert several WPD files in one go?
5.a: Select or drop multiple files and click Convert to PDF. One file downloads as a PDF with the same name; several are packed into wpd-to-pdf.zip with a PDF for each document.

6.q: Can I turn a WordPerfect file into a Word document instead?
6.a: Not from this tool. Convert to PDF here first, then run the result through [0]PDF to Word[/0] if you need an editable .docx.

7.q: Are my old legal or government documents uploaded?
7.a: No. The conversion engine runs entirely in your browser, so the WPD files and the resulting PDFs stay on your device. Only the engine itself is downloaded, not your documents.

8.q: Why did a file fail to convert?
8.a: Damaged files and files that aren't really WordPerfect despite the .wpd extension are the usual causes. If the file opens in desktop LibreOffice, it should convert here as well, since the same import filter is used.

1.q: Which WPS files does this tool convert?
1.a: Word processor documents saved by Microsoft Works, the office suite bundled with consumer PCs in the late 1990s and 2000s. Files from Kingsoft's WPS Office use the same .wps extension but are a different format, and this converter is built around the Microsoft Works one; for WPS Office files, save as .docx from that program and use [0]Word to PDF[/0].

2.q: Do I need Microsoft Works installed?
2.a: No. The conversion runs on a LibreOffice engine loaded into your browser, which reads the Works format on its own. That's the main reason to use this tool: Works was discontinued in 2009, and current versions of Word no longer open its files.

3.q: What WPS formatting is preserved in the PDF?
3.a: Text, basic formatting such as bold, italic, alignment, and paragraph spacing, and embedded images come through. Anything more elaborate may render differently, so check the PDF before you discard the original.

4.q: Why is converting the first WPS file slower?
4.a: The LibreOffice engine (roughly 75 MB) has to download and start before the first file converts. It stays loaded for the rest of your session, so converting a folder of old documents goes quickly after the first one.

5.q: Can I convert Works spreadsheets (.wks) or databases (.wdb) too?
5.a: No. Only .wps word processor files are accepted; other Works file types are rejected at upload. For other legacy word processor formats, there are separate tools such as [0]WPD to PDF[/0] for WordPerfect files.

6.q: Can I convert many WPS files at once?
6.a: Yes. Add as many as you like and convert them in one batch; each becomes a PDF with the original name, and two or more files download together as wps-to-pdf.zip.

7.q: Are my old documents uploaded anywhere?
7.a: No. The engine runs inside your browser and the .wps file is read and converted on your own computer. Decades-old letters, school papers, and financial records never leave your device.

1.q: How does the tool decide what the PDF looks like?
1.a: It parses the XML, groups repeating sibling elements by tag name, and renders each group as a table with one column per child element, using element names as the headers. If the root has no repeating children, you get a two-column Property and Value table. The output is landscape A4 with the root element's name as the title.

2.q: What kind of XML works best?
2.a: Data-style XML: records with the same set of child elements repeated under one parent, such as database exports, invoice line items, product feeds, RSS feeds, or sitemaps. Deeply nested or document-style XML is flattened, so nested values are joined into a single cell and lose their hierarchy.

3.q: Why do I get an Invalid XML error?
3.a: The file isn't well-formed: an unclosed tag, a missing root element, an unescaped & or < character, or a bad encoding. The message includes the parser's reason, so fix the file in an editor or validator and try again.

4.q: Are XML attributes included in the PDF?
4.a: Partly. In the table view only child elements become columns, so attributes on the repeated records are not shown. In the Property and Value view for a non-repeating root, attributes are listed after the child values.

5.q: Can I convert multiple XML files at once?
5.a: Yes. Add several files and they're converted in one batch into xml-to-pdf.zip with one PDF per file. A single file downloads directly with the same base name and a .pdf extension.

6.q: Does it apply my XSLT stylesheet or CSS?
6.a: No. Stylesheet instructions and DOCTYPE declarations are stripped before parsing, and the layout is generated from the data structure alone. If you need the styled rendering, open the XML in a browser that applies the stylesheet and print it to PDF from there.

7.q: Will Chinese, Arabic, Cyrillic, or other non-Latin text render?
7.a: Not reliably. The PDF is built with jsPDF's standard Helvetica font, which covers Latin characters, so text in other scripts may show up as wrong or missing characters.

8.q: Is the XML file uploaded to convert it?
8.a: No. Parsing uses a JavaScript XML parser and the PDF is generated with jsPDF, both inside your browser, so invoices, transaction logs, and other sensitive data in the file never leave your device.

1.q: What is the difference between XPS and OXPS, and does it matter here?
1.a: XPS is Microsoft's original format from Windows Vista and 7; OXPS is the ECMA-388 OpenXPS variant that Windows 8 and later write by default. Both extensions are accepted, can be mixed in one batch, and produce the same kind of PDF.

2.q: Why can't I open my XPS file anymore?
2.a: Microsoft no longer installs the XPS Viewer by default, and macOS, Linux, and phones never supported the format. Converting to PDF makes the document readable in any browser or PDF reader.

3.q: Does the conversion keep the quality of the original?
3.a: Yes. Page dimensions, vector graphics, fonts, and images are carried into the PDF without resampling, so a document printed to XPS at high resolution keeps that resolution in the PDF.

4.q: Will text stay selectable in the PDF?
4.a: Text in the XPS is written to the PDF as text with its fonts rather than as a picture of the page, so you can select, search, and copy it in a PDF reader.

5.q: Can I convert several XPS files at once?
5.a: Yes. Add as many .xps or .oxps files as you need; a single file downloads as a PDF, and multiple files are bundled into xps-converted.zip with one PDF per document.

6.q: Does the converter install anything on my computer?
6.a: No. The PyMuPDF engine is loaded into your browser as WebAssembly the first time you convert, and nothing is installed on your system.

7.q: Can I convert a PDF back to XPS?
7.a: No, this tool only goes from XPS or OXPS to PDF. On Windows you can print any PDF to the Microsoft XPS Document Writer if you need an XPS copy.

8.q: Is my XPS document uploaded for conversion?
8.a: No. The PyMuPDF engine runs locally in your browser, so the XPS file is parsed and the PDF written on your own device. Old corporate or government documents never leave your machine.
